The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, and Project Tiger (1973) created national parks and sanctuaries from which many people were relocated, often with inadequate compensation, while those who remained lost rights of cultivation, grazing and collection; critics have called this model “fortress conservation”. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, slowed the diversion of forests to industry but was also used against forest dwellers whose land had never been recorded, and made even a school or a well in a forest village depend on central clearance. The National Forest Policy of 1988 for the first time made the domestic needs of tribal and other forest-dependent people the first charge on forest produce, and Joint Forest Management, promoted from 1990, gave village committees a share of produce, though the committees were created and controlled by the forest department. Only the Forest Rights Act, 2006, recognised forest dwellers’ rights in law, including the right to manage community forests, and required that any relocation from protected areas be voluntary and with the informed consent of the gram sabha (Section 11.4).

docs.title: 2.8.1 Colonial Forestry on the Ground
docs.text:
Historians have shown how these policies worked in practice. Mahesh Rangarajan’s study of the Central Provinces between 1860 and 1914 traces how the forest department reserved forests, restricted shifting cultivation and grazing, and sought to eliminate “vermin” such as tigers and wolves, while forest dwellers resisted through evasion, petition and occasionally revolt (Rangarajan 1996). K. Sivaramakrishnan’s history of forests in colonial Bengal and the Jungle Mahals shows how foresters’ own ideas, about fire for instance, changed through argument and experience, and how forest management was shaped by local negotiations as much as by central policy (Sivaramakrishnan 1999). These studies complicate the picture of a single, all-powerful colonial state imposing its will, but they confirm that the burden of the new order fell heavily on Adivasi communities.

The history shows a slow shift from a view of forest dwellers as a threat to the forest towards a view of them as rights-holders and partners. The shift is incomplete, and conflicts between conservation authorities and forest communities remain sharp, especially in tiger reserves.

docs.title: 2.9 Seeds and Agrobiodiversity
docs.text:
Adivasi farmers maintain a large share of India’s remaining traditional crop varieties, especially of rice and millets. The Jeypore tract of Koraput district in southern Odisha has long been regarded by rice scientists as an important centre of rice diversity; large collections of local varieties were made there in the mid-twentieth century, and in 2012 the Food and Agriculture Organization recognised the Koraput traditional agriculture system as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System. Kondh, Paraja, Gadaba and other cultivators continue to grow many local varieties, chosen for particular fields, seasons, tastes and ritual uses.

In many communities women are the main keepers of seed: they select, store and exchange it, and know which variety suits which field and dish. Non-governmental organisations in Odisha, Jharkhand, the Deccan and the North-East have supported community seed banks and seed fairs to strengthen these practices. The knowledge that goes with a variety (how to grow it, process it and cook it) is lost when the variety is abandoned; seed banks can conserve the grain but not this knowledge.

docs.title: 2.10 Insects
docs.text:
Insects are food, livelihood and indicators of the seasons. Many communities in central and north-eastern India eat insects: the red weaver ant (Oecophylla smaragdina), whose eggs and adults are made into a sour chutney (chāpṛā) in Bastar and neighbouring regions; termites, collected when the winged forms swarm after the first rains; the larvae of bees and wasps; and silkworm pupae.

Lac, the resin secreted by the lac insect (Kerria lacca) on host trees such as kusum (Schleichera oleosa), palāś (Butea monosperma) and ber (Ziziphus mauritiana), has been cultivated and traded for centuries, and Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh are major producers. Lac cultivators must know host trees, the insect’s life cycle and the timing of inoculation and harvest. Tasar silk is produced from the cocoons of the wild silkworm Antheraea mylitta, reared on asan (Terminalia) and arjun trees by Santal, Ho, Munda and other communities.

Honey-gathering communities such as the Jenu Kuruba (“honey Kuruba”) of Karnataka and the Kurumba and Irula of the Nilgiris collect honey from the giant rock bee (Apis dorsata) on cliffs and tall trees. Their knowledge of where the colonies nest, when the flowering seasons bring the best honey, and how to harvest with smoke at night is considerable; so are the risks of the work.

docs.title: 2.11 Gender and Ecological Knowledge
docs.text:
Ecological knowledge is divided by gender. In most Adivasi communities women gather food plants, fuelwood, fodder and many forest products, fetch water, and select and store seed; men clear land, hunt, plough (where ploughing is practised) and cut timber. As a result women often know more than men about the edible and medicinal plants near the village, and men more about distant forest and animals. Because outside researchers and officials have usually spoken to men, women’s knowledge has been under-recorded, and women have been under-represented in forest committees and decisions.

Women have also been at the forefront of forest protection. In the most famous episode of the Chipko movement, in 1974 at Reni in the Garhwal Himalaya, Gaura Devi and other women of the village confronted contractors’ men who had come to fell trees, while the village men were away, and prevented the felling (Guha 1989). In Odisha’s self-initiated forest protection (Section 2.7.1), women’s groups have often taken on patrolling and the enforcement of rules. Recognising women’s knowledge and giving them a voice in forest governance is now a stated aim of forest policy, though one still far from realised.

docs.title: 2.12 Living with Wild Animals
docs.text:
Forest communities live alongside animals that can destroy their crops, kill their livestock and threaten their lives. In Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Assam, conflict with elephants has grown as forests have been fragmented by mines, roads and settlements: elephants raid fields and granaries, damage houses and kill people, while elephants themselves are killed by electrocution, trains and poisoning. Leopards, bears and wild pigs cause losses elsewhere.

Communities have long-standing ways of coping: watching fields from platforms at night, drums, fires and noise to drive animals away, knowledge of the routes and habits of elephant herds, and, in many places, religious respect for the elephant or tiger that discourages retaliation. Government compensation for losses is often slow and inadequate. Conservationists increasingly recognise that the willingness of local people to tolerate wild animals is essential to conservation, and that this depends on fair treatment, prompt compensation and secure rights, not only on traditional attitudes.

docs.title: 2.13 Living Root Bridges
docs.text:
In the southern Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, among the wettest places on earth, villagers have for generations built bridges from the living roots of the rubber fig (Ficus elastica). Aerial roots are guided across a stream, often along a framework of bamboo or the hollowed trunk of an areca palm, until they reach the far bank and take root; over decades they thicken and interweave, and stones are laid to form a walkway. Some bridges have two levels. A root bridge takes many years to become usable but, unlike timber bridges, grows stronger with age and resists the floods of the monsoon. Their construction requires knowledge of the tree, patience across generations and collective maintenance by the village. The bridges have become a major tourist attraction, which brings income but also risks damage from crowds.

The first systematic scientific study of the bridges was made by the architect Ferdinand Ludwig, the botanist Thomas Speck and their colleagues, working with the root-bridge researcher Wilfrid Middleton and with the villages concerned (Ludwig et al. 2019). They inventoried seventy-four bridges, at altitudes from under a hundred metres to about 1,200 metres, and from 2 to more than 50 metres long. Their measurements explain why the bridges strengthen with age. Roots that bear load respond with secondary growth, thickening and changing their cross-section according to the direction in which they are trained; and roots that touch can graft together (inosculation), so that a bridge gradually becomes a single, self-repairing network. The builders achieve this by choices that rest on long experience: which trees to use, how to guide young roots across a stream, how long to wait before a root can bear weight, and how to keep reinforcing the structure as it grows. The bridges are thus, in the study’s terms, both a technology and a form of plant cultivation, and they have attracted the interest of architects who hope to use living plants in buildings. In 2022 the “living root bridge cultural landscapes” of Meghalaya, known in Khasi as jingkieng jri, were placed on India’s Tentative List for World Heritage nomination. As with sacred groves (Chapter 3), the knowledge that matters for their future is the village’s knowledge of how to grow and maintain them, and the village’s authority to do so.

docs.title: 2.14 The Apatani Valley: Rice, Fish and Forest
docs.text:
In the hills of central Arunachal Pradesh, where most communities practised shifting cultivation, the Apatani of the Ziro valley built something quite different: a permanently cultivated valley floor of irrigated rice fields, surrounded by managed groves and forest, supporting a population far denser than that of their jhum-cultivating Nyishi neighbours. The Apatani speak a language of the Tani group of Tibeto-Burman, and their own traditions describe a migration into the valley from the north, after which the marshy valley floor was drained and turned into fields. The irrigation network is outlined in Section 4.3; this section looks at the system as a whole (Figure 2.2), and at what it shows about the variety of Adivasi agriculture.

Figure 2.2. A schematic cross-section of the Apatani landscape of the Ziro valley, after the descriptions summarised in Section 2.14. Not to scale; the arrangement of land uses and the flows of water and organic matter into the fields are simplified (Fürer-Haimendorf 1962; Kumar and Ramakrishnan 1990).

docs.title: 2.14.1 An Integrated Landscape
docs.text:
The Apatani landscape is organised in rings. On the valley floor lie the bunded rice fields, levelled with great precision so that water can be passed from field to field, with finger millet often planted on the bunds. Near the villages are kitchen gardens and small dry fields; on the lower slopes, groves of pine and bamboo planted and owned by clans and households, which supply timber, poles and the bamboo used for pipes, fences and houses; above them, forest used for firewood, timber and hunting under clan and village rules. Fish are raised in the flooded rice fields during the growing season; today the main species is the introduced common carp. Fertility is maintained largely by recycling: household refuse, the dung of pigs and poultry, crop residues and leaf litter carried down from the slopes are worked into the fields, so that the plots nearest the villages, which receive most of this material, are the most fertile.

Anil Kumar and P. S. Ramakrishnan’s study of energy flow through an Apatani village, part of Ramakrishnan’s long programme of research on hill agriculture in the North-East, found that the rice system had a high energy and economic efficiency compared with other farming systems of the region, and attributed this to the tight recycling of resources between forest, village and field and to the integration of fish with rice (Kumar and Ramakrishnan 1990). The point is not that the Apatani had discovered a superior technique that others failed to find, but that a valley with a reliable water supply allowed a different solution from the steep slopes of the jhum country, and that the Apatani made the most of it through generations of careful engineering and management.

docs.title: 2.14.2 Institutions and Inequality
docs.text:
Fürer-Haimendorf, who first visited the valley in 1944, was so struck by the intensity of its agriculture, the size of its villages and the elaboration of its institutions that he subtitled his monograph “a primitive civilization of the eastern Himalayas” (Fürer-Haimendorf 1962). The word “primitive” belongs to the evolutionary vocabulary of his time; the observation behind the subtitle, that the Apatani had built a complex society without a state, was sound. Land, groves and fields were owned by clans and individual households and could be inherited, bought and sold; disputes were settled not by a chief but by clan representatives (bulyañ, Fürer-Haimendorf’s buliang), who mediated and arbitrated and relied on public opinion rather than force. Rice was exchanged with neighbouring communities for cattle, especially the semi-domesticated mithun, and for other goods.

Fürer-Haimendorf was equally clear that this was not an egalitarian society. He described a division between free clans and a dependent, partly unfree class, some of whose members were descended from captives or from people bought from neighbouring groups, and he recorded the raids and kidnappings that marked relations between the Apatani and the Nyishi before the extension of Indian administration. An account that praises the ecological achievement of the valley while leaving out these facts would repeat, in reverse, the old mistake of treating Adivasi societies as all of one kind.

docs.title: 2.14.3 Pressures
docs.text: Since the 1960s the valley has changed rapidly. The towns of Old Ziro and Hapoli, the district headquarters, have grown on the valley edge; roads, schools, wage employment and Christianity, alongside a revived indigenous Donyi-Polo religion, have reshaped village life; some fields have been converted to house plots, and fewer young people farm. In 2014 the Apatani cultural landscape was placed on India’s Tentative List for World Heritage nomination. Whether that recognition helps will depend, as with the root bridges, on whether the Apatani themselves remain able to decide how the valley is farmed, built on and visited.

docs.title: 2.15 Pastoral Knowledge
docs.text:
Pastoralists, some of them Scheduled Tribes and others not, hold extensive knowledge of animals, grazing lands and seasonal movement.

  • The Toda of the Nilgiris keep herds of buffaloes that are at the centre of their religion: some herds are sacred, tended by dairymen-priests in special dairies according to elaborate ritual rules, which W. H. R. Rivers described in his classic study of 1906.

  • The Raika (Rebari) of Rajasthan are camel and sheep breeders whose knowledge of camel breeding, health and grazing has been documented by researchers working with them. The decline of camel herding, as camels lost their role in transport and as grazing lands shrank, has threatened this knowledge.

  • The Gaddi of Himachal Pradesh move their sheep and goats between high summer pastures and winter grazing in the lower hills; the Van Gujjar take their buffaloes between the Shivalik foothills and the high pastures of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh; the Bakarwal of Jammu and Kashmir follow similar routes. Their access to forests and protected areas has been repeatedly contested.

  • The Maldhari of the Banni grasslands of Kutch have bred the Banni buffalo, well adapted to heat and scarce water, which was recognised as a distinct breed by the national animal genetic resources authorities in 2010. Banni’s pastoralists have also campaigned for community rights over the grassland under the Forest Rights Act.

Pastoral knowledge includes the reading of grass and water conditions, the timing of movement, animal breeding and selection, and veterinary care (Chapter 7). It was long dismissed as backward by agricultural and forest administrations; ecologists now recognise that mobile grazing can sustain grasslands that sedentary systems degrade.

docs.title: 2.16 Bamboo Flowering and Famine
docs.text: In Mizoram and neighbouring areas, the bamboo Melocanna baccifera, which covers large parts of the hills, flowers gregariously and then dies at intervals of about half a century. The flowering produces a huge crop of seeds, on which rat populations explode; when the seeds are exhausted, the rats devour standing crops and stored grain, causing famine. Mizo tradition knew this cycle as mautām, and anticipated famine after the flowering. The mautām of 1959 led to a severe famine whose poor handling by the government contributed to the Mizo uprising of 1966 (Chapter 1). Before the next flowering, in 2006–08, the state government, drawing on both local knowledge and scientific advice, organised rat control, crop diversification and food supplies, and the effects were much less severe. The case is a clear example of community knowledge of a long ecological cycle informing public policy.

docs.title: 2.17 Adapting to Drought and Flood
docs.text:
Communities in climatically variable landscapes have built that variability into their livelihoods. The Bhil and other communities of the Aravalli hills and the margins of the Thar desert rely on drought-tolerant millets and pulses, mixed farming and livestock, water harvesting (Chapter 4) and knowledge of wild foods that can be gathered in famine years (Chapter 5).

On the Brahmaputra floodplain the Mising build houses on stilts (chāng ghar), grow rice varieties suited to flood seasons and fish in the flooded fields and channels. These adaptations are not static tradition: communities have changed their practices as embankments, deforestation upstream and changes in the river’s course have altered the floods.

docs.title: 2.17.1 Observing Climate Change
docs.text:
Farmers, herders and gatherers in many parts of India report changes in their environment: monsoons that start later and end more abruptly, heavier downpours, longer dry spells, earlier or irregular flowering of trees such as mahua and sal, declining springs in the hills, and new pests. Such reports are valuable because they come from places where scientific monitoring is thin and because they describe changes in the terms that matter for livelihoods. They need to be interpreted carefully, since memory can exaggerate or compress change, but international reviews of traditional knowledge and climate change have found that local observations often agree with instrumental records and add detail to them (Nakashima et al. 2012).

The examples in this chapter, from the Angami alders to the Doyang roost, have one thing in common: the knowledge was being used and changed by the people who held it. The next chapter turns to the places where that knowledge meets religion most directly, the sacred groves.

Key Points

  • Adivasi ecological knowledge is detailed and practical, but it is not the same as ecological virtue and changes with circumstances.

  • Shifting cultivation can be sustainable with long fallows; its problems arise mainly when fallows are shortened.

  • Forest policy has moved slowly from treating forest dwellers as a threat to recognising them as rights-holders.

  • Community conservation in places such as Khonoma and the Doyang roost shows communities changing practices through their own institutions.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Gadgil and Guha (1993): an ecological history of India, with much on forest communities.

  • Ramakrishnan (1992): the classic study of shifting cultivation in North-East India.

  • Cairns (2007): case studies of farmers’ own improvements to shifting cultivation across Asia, including the Angami alder fallows.

  • Fürer-Haimendorf (1962): the classic ethnography of the Apatani valley.

  • Berkes (1999): a general introduction to traditional ecological knowledge.

  • Guha (1989): forests, the state and peasant resistance in the Himalaya.

  • Gadgil et al. (1993): a short and influential article on indigenous knowledge and conservation.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Sacred Groves: Religion, Community and Conservation
3.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Across India, villages set aside patches of forest as the dwelling of a deity or of ancestral spirits. Within such a sacred grove, cutting trees, hunting, and sometimes even collecting dead wood or fallen fruit are forbidden or restricted, and the rules are enforced by fear of divine anger and by the village community. Some groves are a few trees around a shrine; others cover hundreds of hectares.

Sacred groves are first of all religious places. They are not, as some writing claims, “the world’s oldest conservation system” designed by far-sighted ancestors to protect biodiversity. But because they have been protected, many groves have kept old trees, rare plants, springs and wildlife that have disappeared from the surrounding landscape, and since the 1970s ecologists have drawn attention to their value for conservation (Gadgil and Vartak 1975; Ramakrishnan et al. 1998). Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna, places sacred groves in the wider history of Indian forests and sacred trees; this chapter looks at them from the side of the communities that keep them.

Most groves share four features: they are associated with a deity, spirit or ancestors, often marked by a shrine, stones or posts; cutting, hunting, collection or entry are restricted; a village, clan, lineage or temple looks after them, often through a priest; and rituals and festivals are held in them. Regional names include devrāī (Maharashtra), devarakāḍu (Karnataka), kāvu (Kerala), kōvilkāḍu (Tamil Nadu), oraṇ (Rajasthan), devvan (Himachal Pradesh), sarnā and jāherthān (Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal), and law kyntang and law lyngdoh (Meghalaya).

docs.title: 3.2 Distribution
docs.text: Sacred groves occur in almost every part of India, but they are most numerous and best studied in the Western Ghats (Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala), in the Adivasi regions of central and eastern India, in Meghalaya and elsewhere in the North-East, and in Rajasthan, where the oraṇ are large tracts of village common land dedicated to a deity. Published estimates of the total number of groves in India run from tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand; the number actually documented is much smaller, and estimates depend heavily on what is counted as a grove (Malhotra et al. 2001). Some states have conducted surveys, but there is no complete national inventory.

docs.title: 3.3 Regional Traditions
docs.text: Sacred groves were noticed by colonial foresters. Dietrich Brandis, the first Inspector General of Forests, described in his Indian Forestry (1897) the sacred groves he had seen in several provinces and the protection they gave to old trees (Brandis 1897). Some colonial officers respected them; others included them in reserved forests or allowed them to be felled.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Devrāī of Maharashtra
docs.text: The first systematic ecological studies of sacred groves in India were made by Madhav Gadgil and the botanist V. D. Vartak in the devrāī of the northern Western Ghats in Maharashtra in the 1970s. They showed that many groves preserved forest that had been cleared elsewhere, including large old trees and species rare in the region, and argued for their continued protection (Gadgil and Vartak 1975). Their work began the modern study of sacred groves in India.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Devarakāḍu of Kodagu and Kāvu of Kerala
docs.text:
In the Kodagu (Coorg) district of Karnataka there are many hundreds of devarakāḍu, dedicated to village deities and protected by Kodava and other communities. Studies have found that they retain a substantial share of the region’s native tree species in a landscape dominated by coffee plantations, though many have shrunk or been degraded.

In Kerala, the kāvu are groves associated with serpent deities (nāgas), with goddesses and with the teyyam deities of northern Kerala. Many are attached to particular households or lineages. Some preserve patches of lowland evergreen and swamp forest that have otherwise almost disappeared in the densely populated lowlands; many others have been reduced to a few trees around a shrine.

In northern Kerala many kāvu are the sites of teyyam, the ritual in which performers, after elaborate make-up and costume, become possessed by local deities, heroes and ancestors, and bless and advise the worshippers. The performers belong mostly to communities long regarded as low in the caste order, such as the Malayan, Vannan and Pulaya, who for the duration of the performance are treated as gods by the higher castes. The grove, the deity and the performance form a single tradition, and the protection of the kāvu is bound up with the continuation of the ritual.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Sarnā and Jāherthān
docs.text: In the villages of the Munda, Oraon, Ho, Santal and other communities of Jharkhand, Odisha and West Bengal, the sacred grove is the centre of village religion. The Munda and Oraon sarnā and the Santal jāherthān are typically groves of sal (Shorea robusta) and other trees, where the village priest (pāhan, nāeke) makes offerings at the great festivals, such as the Sarhul or Bāhā festival when the sal trees flower. The grove is also a symbol of the village’s identity and its claim to land. As towns such as Ranchi have expanded over former village land, many sarnā sites have been surrounded by buildings; some have been encroached upon, and others survive as small walled enclosures among houses and roads, where the festivals are still celebrated by the descendants of the village’s founders. State programmes in Jharkhand have funded boundary walls around sarnā sites and lineage burial grounds to protect them from encroachment, though some Adivasi critics argue that walls turn a living grove into a monument. For this reason, the protection of the sarnā has become central to the movement for recognition of a distinct Sarna religion (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 3.3.4 Law Kyntang of Meghalaya
docs.text:
In the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, sacred forests (law kyntang, law lyngdoh, law niam) are protected by clans, villages or himas. The best known is the sacred forest of Mawphlang near Shillong, a large patch of montane forest in a largely grassy landscape, managed by the Lyngdoh clan. Most Khasi are now Christians, and in some villages the religious basis of grove protection has weakened; but many groves continue to be protected as community forests, and some Christian villages maintain them for water supply and as heritage.

Around Mawphlang, the hima (Khasi chiefdom) and its villages have also undertaken one of India’s first community forest carbon projects, launched in the early 2010s, in which a federation of villages protects and regenerates forest and receives payments for the carbon stored. The project brings new money to forest protection, but it also raises questions about who controls decisions and benefits within the federation.

docs.title: 3.3.5 Oraṇ of Rajasthan
docs.text: In Rajasthan the oraṇ (also devbanī) are tracts of land around a shrine of a deity or a local hero, where trees may not be cut. They are not dense forests but woodland and scrub, providing grazing, water and shade in a dry landscape. Their protection is linked to the ethic of communities such as the Bishnoi (Chapter 2) and to the pastoral economy. Many oraṇ have been lost to encroachment, mining and government reallocation of “wasteland” (Gadgil and Guha 1995).

docs.title: 3.3.6 Devvan of Himachal Pradesh
docs.text: In Kullu and other districts of Himachal Pradesh, forests attached to the village deities (devtā) are protected by rules administered by the deity’s temple organisation, whose decisions are communicated through the deity’s oracle. Some rules prohibit felling entirely; others allow collection of fallen wood and leaf litter.

docs.title: 3.4 Sacred Landscapes beyond the Grove
docs.text:
Groves are part of a wider sacred geography that includes hills, rocks, springs, lakes, rivers and memorial stones.

Sacred hills. The Niyamgiri hills of the Dongria Kondh (Chapter 11) are one example. Another is the hill that Jains revere as Sammed Shikharji (Parasnath) in Jharkhand, where many Tirthaṅkaras are believed to have attained liberation, and which Santals revere as Maraṅ Buru, the seat of their great deity and the site of the regional gatherings described in Section 11.2. In 2023 a controversy over tourism and over restrictions demanded by Jain organisations led Santal organisations to assert their own claim to the hill. The same landscape can be sacred to different communities, and the claims of Adivasi religions are easily overlooked when they meet a better-organised tradition.

Sacred lakes. Khecheopalri lake in western Sikkim is sacred both to the Lepcha, the indigenous people of Sikkim, and to Buddhists; fishing and the felling of trees around it are forbidden.

Stones. Memorial stones and megaliths are a feature of many Adivasi landscapes. The Munda and Ho bury the bones of their dead under flat stones (sasan diri) in a lineage burial ground, which is evidence of the lineage’s ancestral right to village land; the Khasi and Jaintia erected monoliths in memory of their dead, of which the cluster at Nartiang in the Jaintia hills is among the most impressive; and Naga villages raise stones to commemorate feasts of merit.

These sacred places carry knowledge of history, kinship and land rights as well as religion, and their destruction by mining, dams or roads is experienced as an attack on the community itself.

docs.title: 3.5 Sacred Species and Clan Totems
docs.text:
Protection extends in many communities to particular species as well as places. Trees such as the sal, karam, mahua, banyan and pipal are honoured in ritual and often spared when land is cleared. Among the Bishnoi, protection extends to all green trees and wild animals (Chapter 2).

Many Adivasi communities of central and eastern India are divided into exogamous clans, each associated with an animal, plant or object (a totem), which members of the clan may not kill, eat or use. Oraon clan names are a familiar example. S. C. Roy recorded them with their totems, among them Ekkā (tortoise), Lakṛā (tiger), Minj (a fish), Tirkī (young mice), Tiggā (monkey), Kujūr (a creeper) and Xaxa (crow) (Roy 1915); the glosses follow his account, and usage varies between villages. The Santal are divided into twelve clans (pāris), among them Hansda, Murmu, Kisku, Hembrom, Marndi, Soren and Tudu, each with its own associations and observances; the Munda have many kili (clans) with totemic names. These clan names are now carried as surnames by millions of people.

Totemic prohibitions are sometimes presented as conservation rules. Their effect on any particular species is usually small, since only members of one clan observe each prohibition. Their importance lies elsewhere: they express a view of kinship between human groups and other living beings, and they organise marriage and social life.

docs.title: 3.6 Ecological Value
docs.text:
Many studies have found that sacred groves contain more native plant species, larger and older trees, and more species of restricted distribution than the degraded forests and farmland around them; some species in the Western Ghats have been recorded only from sacred groves. Groves protect springs and streams, provide habitat for birds, bats and insects, and serve as reservoirs from which plants can spread back into the surrounding landscape (Ramakrishnan et al. 1998; Malhotra et al. 2001).

The value of groves should not be exaggerated. Many are small, isolated and invaded by exotic weeds such as Lantana camara; protection may extend only to certain trees or certain activities; and some groves are planted or managed rather than “relics” of primeval forest. Their conservation value varies greatly, and needs to be assessed grove by grove.

docs.title: 3.7 Governance
docs.text:
Grove protection works through belief and social sanction together (Figure 3.1). The commonest rule forbids felling living trees, sometimes with exceptions for ritual needs; hunting and fire are usually forbidden too. Many groves restrict the gathering of fruit, fuelwood or leaves, and some forbid removing anything at all. Entry to the inner area may be limited to the priest or to certain times. Stories of misfortune that befell those who broke the rules are told and retold. The priest or the lineage responsible for the grove performs the rituals, and the village council punishes offenders. Where the community is united and the belief strong, protection can last for centuries; where either weakens, groves are quickly lost.

Figure 3.1. A schematic sacred grove: zones of restriction and the institutions that enforce them, as described in Section 3.7. Not every grove has every zone; some are a few trees around a shrine, and the rules differ from grove to grove and change over time.

docs.title: 3.8 Threats
docs.text: The first threat is often on paper. Many groves are recorded as government land, revenue “wasteland” or forest, and can be allotted or diverted without the community’s consent. Roads, dams, mines, quarries and the growth of towns then destroy them directly; bauxite and coal mining threaten groves in Odisha and Jharkhand. In Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka many groves have been cleared for concrete temples, so that a built shrine replaces the living grove. Conversion, migration and the weakening of village institutions can remove the basis of protection from within. And small groves surrounded by farmland suffer from weeds, drying and the other effects of isolation.

docs.title: 3.9 Legal Status
docs.text: Most sacred groves have no specific legal protection. Some lie within reserved or protected forests, where the forest department controls them; others are on revenue or private land. Three instruments can now be used. The Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act of 2002 created “community reserves” on community or private land, a category that can include groves. Under the Biological Diversity Act of 2002, state governments can declare biodiversity heritage sites in consultation with local bodies; the first, declared in Karnataka in 2007, was the Nallur tamarind grove near Bengaluru, an old grove protected by local tradition. In forest areas, the Forest Rights Act allows communities to claim community forest resource rights, including the right to protect and manage groves according to their customs (Section 11.4). Each option has its limits, and many conservationists and community organisations argue that the most important protection is secure community rights over the land.

docs.title: 3.9.1 Restoration and New Groves
docs.text: Not all change is loss. In several regions communities and organisations have restored degraded groves by removing weeds, planting native species and renewing rituals, and some villages have dedicated new groves to their deities. Schools and local biodiversity committees have used sacred groves for teaching about local plants and animals. Such efforts work best when they are led by the communities that own and worship in the groves and respect their religious character; attempts to turn groves into parks for visitors, with paths, benches and signboards, have sometimes damaged the very qualities that made them valuable.

docs.title: 3.9.2 Who Speaks for the Grove?
docs.text:
Debates about sacred groves often involve several parties with different interests: the families or clans who own or worship in a grove; the village as a whole; the forest or revenue department that holds the land on paper; conservation scientists who value it for its species; and, increasingly, tourists and religious organisations from outside. Each may describe the grove differently, as a deity’s home, a lineage’s property, a forest, a biodiversity hotspot or an attraction. Conflicts arise when one of these descriptions is used to override the others, for example when a grove is fenced for conservation and the villagers are barred from their own rituals, or when a temple trust builds over it. Lasting protection depends on recognising that the grove belongs first to the community whose deity resides in it. That principle has costs, too: a community may choose to clear or build over its own grove, and conservationists then face the question of whose judgement should prevail. The proposals most often made, from correct land records to the recognition of village managers, are gathered in Section 14.13.

Key Points

  • Sacred groves are first of all religious places, protected by belief and community sanction.

  • Many groves preserve native species and springs, but their ecological value varies and should not be exaggerated.

  • Groves are part of a wider sacred geography of hills, lakes, stones and species.

  • Most groves lack legal protection; secure community rights are the most important safeguard.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Gadgil and Vartak (1975): the founding ecological paper on Indian sacred groves.

  • Ramakrishnan et al. (1998): essays on sacred groves and sacred species.

  • Malhotra et al. (2001): a national overview of sacred groves.

  • Gadgil and Guha (1995): ecology, equity and the use of natural resources in India.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Water Harvesting and Irrigation Systems
4.1 Introduction
docs.text:
India’s rainfall comes mostly in a few months of the monsoon, and varies greatly from year to year and place to place. For thousands of years, communities have built structures to catch, store and distribute water: tanks, ponds, check dams, wells, stepwells, channels and cisterns. Many were built by villages and maintained by village institutions; others were built by kings, merchants and religious foundations. This is the chapter of the volume in which Adivasi and village folk knowledge meet most closely. It begins with the systems of hill, forest and desert communities, many of them Adivasi, and then turns to the village systems of caste society, the kuhl, phaḍ, āhar–pain and tank, which belong to the folk knowledge discussed in Chapter 10. Throughout, it attends to the social knowledge that kept water systems working. The history of irrigation in Indian agriculture as a whole, including the great tank and canal systems of the plains, is treated in Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna.

The Centre for Science and Environment’s report Dying Wisdom (1997) and Anupam Mishra’s Hindi classic Aaj Bhi Khare Hain Talab (1993) did much to draw public attention to traditional water harvesting (Agarwal and Narain 1997; Mishra 1993). Their argument, that India’s water policy had neglected small, decentralised systems in favour of large dams and tube wells, has been widely influential. This chapter shares their respect for traditional systems, but also notes their limitations: many were tied to unequal social orders, and none can by itself meet the water needs of a much larger and more urban population. Each system described below combines four kinds of knowledge: of where water flows and sinks in different rains; of earthwork, masonry, channels and sluices; of the relation between vegetation, soil and water; and of the rules by which users share water, organise repairs and settle disputes.

docs.title: 4.2 Johads of Rajasthan
docs.text:
The johaḍ is a crescent-shaped earthen embankment built across the slope of a seasonal watercourse to hold monsoon runoff. Water stands behind it for some months, recharging the groundwater that feeds wells downstream, and the bed can be cultivated as it dries. Johaḍs were once common in the Aravalli hills of eastern Rajasthan, but many had fallen into disrepair by the mid-twentieth century.

From 1985 the voluntary organisation Tarun Bharat Sangh, led by Rajendra Singh, worked with villages in Alwar district to rebuild old johaḍs and build new ones, using village labour and local knowledge of siting. By the organisation’s count, thousands of structures were built over the following years (Agarwal and Narain 1997). The organisation and several observers report that groundwater levels rose, that wells that had dried up held water again, and that seasonal rivers, among them the Arvari, flowed for longer; these reports come mainly from the organisation and its supporters, and independent hydrological measurements are few. The villages along the Arvari formed a river “parliament” (Arvarī Sansad) to make rules for the use of its water. Rajendra Singh received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 2001 and the Stockholm Water Prize in 2015. The scale of the hydrological effect, and how far the experience can be repeated in other geological settings, is debated among researchers.

docs.title: 4.3 Mountain Water: Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh
docs.text:
In Ladakh, a cold desert where most of the population belongs to Scheduled Tribes, agriculture depends almost entirely on meltwater from snow and glaciers. Villages divert streams through long channels (yura) to their fields and to small storage ponds (zing) that fill overnight and are released in the day, when the melt is strongest. Water is distributed among households by turns under the supervision of an elected water official (churpon), and the village assembly settles disputes.

Because the melt is often late in spring, when the fields most need water, Ladakhi engineers, notably Chewang Norphel, have developed “artificial glaciers” that store winter flow as ice in shaded valleys, and, since 2013, the conical “ice stupas” devised by Sonam Wangchuk, which freeze winter water into towers that melt slowly in spring. These are new inventions, but they build on the long experience of managing water in this landscape.

In Arunachal Pradesh, the Apatani of the Ziro valley divert hill streams through a network of channels into their terraced rice fields, managing the flow through the fields by bamboo pipes and earthen bunds, and raising fish in the flooded fields (Section 2.14). The channels are maintained by clan and village groups.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Springs of the Himalaya
docs.text: In the middle Himalaya, most villages depend on springs. In Kumaon and Garhwal, springs are protected by small stone-lined tanks (naulā), often roofed and decorated, and by spouts (dhārā) from which water is drawn; many are associated with shrines and rituals, and village rules forbid polluting them. In recent decades many springs have dried or become seasonal, because of changes in land use in their recharge areas, road building and changing rainfall. Programmes of “springshed” management, begun in Sikkim in the late 2000s and taken up elsewhere in the Himalaya, combine hydrogeological mapping of recharge areas with the knowledge of villagers about where their springs come from, and with trenches, ponds and vegetation to restore recharge.

docs.title: 4.4 Bamboo Drip Irrigation of Meghalaya
docs.text: In the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, farmers growing betel leaf and black pepper on steep slopes use split and hollow bamboo pipes to carry water from hill streams to their plantations. The water is led through a network of bamboo channels of decreasing size, supported on bamboo frames, and finally delivered drop by drop near the base of the plants. The system uses local materials, is built and maintained by the farmers themselves, and works on slopes where other forms of irrigation are difficult. It has attracted the attention of agricultural engineers because it shares the principle of modern drip irrigation, delivering small quantities of water to each plant, though it was developed quite independently (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

docs.title: 4.5 Zabo of Nagaland
docs.text:
The zabo system of the Chakhesang Naga, best known from Kikruma village in Phek district, combines forest, water harvesting, livestock and rice. The word is usually glossed as “impounding water”. Forest is protected on the hilltops; runoff from the slopes is collected in ponds dug on the hillside; cattle sheds placed near the ponds allow manure to be washed down with the water; and the water is led to rice terraces below, where fish may also be raised (Figure 4.1). The system joins forest protection, water harvesting and farming on slopes too steep for most other forms of irrigation (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

Figure 4.1. A schematic cross-section of the zabo system of the Chakhesang Naga of Kikruma, as described in this section. Not to scale; the number and placing of ponds, sheds and terraces vary with the site.

docs.title: 4.6 Water in the Desert: Ṭāṅkā, Kuṇḍ and Bāvaṛī
docs.text:
In the Thar desert, where rainfall is low and erratic and groundwater is often deep and saline, people collect rainwater in underground cisterns. The kuṇḍ or kuṇḍī is a circular pit, lined with lime plaster and covered with a dome, into which water runs from a prepared, sloping catchment; the ṭāṅkā is a similar cistern, attached to houses or forts. In sandy areas, kuīs or beris, narrow wells, tap the thin layer of moisture that collects above a layer of gypsum in the subsoil. Anupam Mishra’s writings on traditional water structures, including those of Rajasthan, describe the knowledge and the communities, among them specialist well-diggers and tank-builders, who made them (Mishra 1993).

Stepwells (bāvaṛī, vāv), built in western and northern India from the later first millennium CE, were mostly the works of royal and merchant patrons and are described in Volume 15; many smaller ones served villages and travellers.

In the Rann of Kutch, Maldhari herders dig shallow wells called virdā in depressions where rainwater collects; fresh water floats above the denser saline groundwater, and must be drawn carefully to avoid mixing.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Finding Water
docs.text: Rural communities in many parts of India have specialists who claim to find underground water, using a forked stick or a coconut held in the palm (dowsing), or by reading surface signs such as particular plants, termite mounds, soil colour and moisture. The surface signs can be genuine indicators of shallow groundwater, and well-diggers’ experience of local geology is valuable. Controlled tests of dowsing, however, have not shown that it locates water better than chance, and hydrogeological survey is the reliable method where wells or bore wells are expensive to dig.

docs.title: 4.7 Village Irrigation in Valleys and Plains
docs.text:
Many of the best-known village irrigation systems of India belong to settled caste villages rather than to Adivasi communities, and their history is told in Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna. They are summarised here because they show the same combination of hydrological skill and social institution. In the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh, gravity channels (kuhl) carry stream water along the contour to terraced fields; each is managed by the households it irrigates under a water master (kohli), who organises the annual repair of the intake and the rotation of water, and J. Mark Baker has shown how these institutions have adapted, and sometimes broken down, under off-farm employment and state intervention (Baker 2005). In the Tapi basin of north-western Maharashtra, diversion weirs (bandhārā) fed canals whose command was divided into crop blocks (phaḍ), each sown to a single crop in a season. In south Bihar, catchment basins (āhar) and diversion channels (pain) carried the rice crop through the end of the monsoon, until the abolition of zamīndārī left their maintenance without an organiser (Agarwal and Narain 1997). On the laterite hills of Kasaragod and Dakshina Kannada, farmers dig horizontal tunnels (suraṅga) into the hillside to draw out groundwater by gravity.

The tanks of South India (ēri in Tamil, kere in Kannada, cheruvu in Telugu), often linked in chains along a valley, were kept up by the annual collective labour of the cultivators (kuḍimarāmattu) and by village servants such as the nīrkaṭṭi, who opened the sluices and turned water from field to field. David Mosse’s study of the Ramnad region shows that these systems were never simply communal: rights to water and the duty of labour followed temple and royal authority and caste rank (Mosse 2003). Table 4.1 summarises the systems described in this chapter.

docs.title: 4.7.1 Tanks of Bundelkhand
docs.text:
In the rocky plateau of Bundelkhand in central India, the Chandela rulers (ninth to thirteenth centuries) and later the Bundela kings built large tanks by damming valleys between hills, many of which still survive, together with thousands of smaller village tanks built by local communities. Anupam Mishra described how specialised communities of tank-builders and the village institutions that cleaned and maintained the tanks were central to life in this dry region, and how their neglect in the twentieth century contributed to Bundelkhand’s chronic water crises (Mishra 1993).

Table 4.1. Some traditional water systems System Region Principle Johaḍ Eastern Rajasthan Earthen embankment holding runoff; groundwater recharge Kuhl Himachal Pradesh Gravity channel from stream to terraces (Baker 2005) Phaḍ North-western Maharashtra River weir, canals and crop blocks Ēri / kere South India Tank storing runoff for rice irrigation (Mosse 2003) Āhar–pain South Bihar Catchment basins and diversion channels Bamboo drip Meghalaya Bamboo pipes delivering water to plants Zabo Nagaland Forest, ponds, livestock and rice terraces Kuṇḍ, ṭāṅkā Thar desert Covered cisterns fed by prepared catchments Bāvaṛī Western and northern India Stepwell Virdā Kutch Shallow wells over saline groundwater Suraṅga Kasaragod, Dakshina Kannada Horizontal tunnel tapping groundwater

docs.title: 4.8 Farming below the Sea: Kuttanad
docs.text: In Kuttanad, in central Kerala, farmers have since the nineteenth century reclaimed land from the backwaters and lagoons, building earth bunds and pumping out water to create rice fields that lie below sea level. The system depends on managing the balance of fresh and salt water through the seasons, on collective maintenance of the outer bunds, and on careful timing of sowing between floods. Much of the reclamation was organised by landlords and carried out by Dalit agricultural labourers, whose knowledge and labour made it possible. The Food and Agriculture Organization recognised the Kuttanad below-sea-level farming system as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System in 2013. Kuttanad was badly affected by the floods of 2018, a reminder of the vulnerability of such systems to extreme events.

docs.title: 4.9 Floods
docs.text: On the floodplains of the Brahmaputra and the rivers of north Bihar, communities have long lived with floods rather than trying to prevent them: the stilt houses, flood-season rice and field fishing of the Mising are described in Section 2.17, and in north Bihar villagers welcomed the floods that brought silt and fertility, and built on raised ground. Embankments built since the 1950s have protected some areas but trapped water and silt in others, and have failed catastrophically during major floods. The debate between “flood control” and “living with floods” draws partly on this older knowledge.

docs.title: 4.10 Small and Large Systems Compared
docs.text:
Traditional and modern water systems are often contrasted as “small and sustainable” against “large and destructive”. The reality is more complex. Large dams and canals can store and move far more water, over far greater distances, and they made possible much of India’s agricultural growth after independence; they also displaced millions of people, many of them Adivasis (Section 12.6). Many small structures spread across a watershed spread the risk, since the failure of one affects only a small area, but they too fail in long droughts and silt up quickly without maintenance. Small structures can be built and repaired with local labour and controlled by their users, whereas large systems depend on state budgets and bureaucracies that have often failed to maintain them. Neither kind is fair by nature: large canals favoured those at the head of the system, and village tanks and wells were often closed to Dalits.

Most water specialists now argue for combining the two: protecting and restoring local storage and recharge, managing groundwater as a common resource, and using larger systems where they make sense, with the participation of those affected (Agarwal and Narain 1997; Mosse 2003).

docs.title: 4.11 Who Maintained the Water?
docs.text:
Every system described in this chapter depended on rules and institutions. Water was shared by turns, by hours or by field, usually with drinking water put first in dry years. Users gave labour for the annual cleaning and repair in proportion to the land they held or the water they received, and those who took water out of turn or failed to contribute were fined or excluded. Specialists, among them water masters, sluice-keepers and well-diggers, often came from particular castes.

Water work is also gendered. In most of rural India, women and girls fetch water for drinking and cooking, often walking long distances in the dry season; men more often control irrigation decisions and sit on the committees that manage tanks and channels. Improvements in village water supply have therefore often meant most to women, though they have rarely been consulted in planning them.

These institutions often reproduced the inequalities of village society. Dalits were frequently excluded from village wells and tanks, a practice against which B. R. Ambedkar led the Mahad satyāgraha at the Chavdar tank in 1927. Romantic accounts of “community” water systems that ignore caste exclusion give a misleading picture.

The legal framework also favoured individual extraction. Under Indian law, derived from the Indian Easements Act of 1882, the owner of land has in effect the right to draw the groundwater beneath it, without limit. When pumps became cheap, this rule allowed landowners with the means to drill deeper to capture water that had been a shared resource, while poorer farmers and those without land, including many Adivasi and Dalit households, lost access as shallow wells dried up. Reformers have proposed that groundwater be treated as a common resource managed by communities.

The decline of traditional systems in the twentieth century was due partly to the state’s takeover of irrigation, partly to the weakening of village institutions, and above all to the spread of tube wells and electric pumps, which allowed individual farmers to draw water independently of the community. The resulting depletion of groundwater across much of India has renewed interest in recharge structures such as johaḍs and tanks, and many have been built or repaired under watershed development programmes and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (2005). State programmes have also drawn on traditional names and ideas: Tamil Nadu revived the term kuḍimarāmattu for a scheme, launched in 2017, to restore tanks with the participation of their users, and Rajasthan’s water self-reliance campaign (from 2016) built and repaired thousands of village water structures.

Finally, the knowledge embodied in traditional systems is not only technical. It includes the conventions by which neighbours share a scarce resource, the rituals that mark the filling of a tank or the opening of a channel, the stories that explain why a spring must not be polluted, and the accumulated experience of which structures survive floods and which do not. Restoring the structures without this social knowledge has often failed; restoring the institutions, on fairer terms than before, has more often succeeded.

Key Points

  • India has a great variety of traditional water systems, from johaḍs and kuhls to tanks, cisterns and tunnels.

  • Every system depended on an institution for allocation and maintenance; many such institutions were also unequal and excluded Dalits.

  • Tube wells and state control contributed to the decline of collective systems; groundwater depletion has renewed interest in them.

  • Traditional systems complement but cannot replace larger-scale water management.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Agarwal and Narain (1997): a survey of traditional water harvesting systems across India.

  • Mishra (1993): the tanks of India and the communities who built them (in Hindi).

  • Mosse (2003): tank irrigation, caste and power in Tamil Nadu.

  • Baker (2005): community irrigation in the western Himalaya.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Food Knowledge, Nutrition and Fermentation
5.1 Introduction: Food as Knowledge
docs.text:
What people eat rests on knowledge accumulated over generations: which plants and animals are edible and when, which are poisonous and how they can be made safe, how food can be stored through the lean months, and how it should be shared. Adivasi food systems draw on cultivated crops, wild plants, fish, game, insects and domestic animals, and on processing techniques such as drying, smoking and fermentation. This chapter describes that knowledge and the pressures on it.

It also corrects a common romantic picture. Traditional diets are often more varied than modern ones and can be nutritionally valuable, but Adivasi communities in India today suffer high rates of undernutrition. National Family Health Surveys have repeatedly found higher levels of stunting and underweight among children of Scheduled Tribes than among other groups. The causes are loss of land and forest access, poverty, poor services and the erosion of food diversity, not the traditional foods themselves. Respecting food knowledge and addressing hunger are part of the same task (Government of India 2014).

The point was made forcefully in the 1990s, when deaths of young children from malnutrition among the Korku of Melghat in Maharashtra drew national attention, at a time when their access to the surrounding forests had been restricted by forest and wildlife regulations and their rain-fed agriculture was precarious. Malnutrition in such cases is a result of the loss of the conditions in which food knowledge could be used. That knowledge covers the species themselves and their seasons; the processing that makes them safe and keeps them through the lean months; where and how much may be gathered; and the social rules of sharing, feasting and avoidance. The sections below take these in turn.

docs.title: 5.2 Diversity on the Plate
docs.text:
Studies of Adivasi food systems in central India, the Western Ghats and the North-East commonly record a hundred or more food species used by a single community over a year: cultivated cereals, millets and pulses; leafy greens gathered from fields and forest; tubers; fruits and flowers; mushrooms; fish, crabs and snails; small game; and insects. The FAO’s study of indigenous food systems, which included a case from India, documented this diversity and its contribution to diets (Kuhnlein et al. 2009).

Wild foods are not just occasional supplements. In the months before the harvest, when stored grain runs low, greens, tubers, mushrooms and fruits gathered from the forest and from field margins can be a major part of the diet. Their importance is easily overlooked by surveys that count only cultivated crops.

docs.title: 5.2.1 Greens, Mushrooms and Honey
docs.text: Leafy greens (sāg) are among the most important gathered foods. In Jharkhand and Odisha women gather dozens of kinds of greens from fields, field bunds and forest through the year, including the leaves of crops, weeds and trees, and dry some for the lean season. Mushrooms appear with the first rains; those that grow from termite mounds (Termitomyces species) and the puffball-like rugṛā that grows under sal trees are prized and sold in local and urban markets at high prices. Wild honey, gathered by specialist communities (Chapter 2), is food, medicine and a valued item of trade.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Mahua
docs.text: The mahuā tree (Madhuca longifolia) is central to the economy and culture of central India. Its fleshy flowers, which fall in great quantities in March and April, are collected by women and children in the early morning, dried and stored. They are eaten cooked or roasted, sold, and distilled into a spirit that is important in hospitality, ritual and festivity. The seeds yield an edible fat used for cooking and lighting. Mahua is so important that the right to collect from particular trees is often a recognised family right, and the trees are protected when land is cleared (Elwin 1939).

docs.title: 5.2.3 Rice and Millets
docs.text: Rice is the staple of eastern India and the North-East, where many communities maintain numerous local varieties chosen for particular fields, seasons and uses (Chapter 2). In central and southern India and the dry west, millets have been staples for Adivasi and other poor farmers for millennia.

docs.title: 5.2.4 First Fruits
docs.text: Many communities mark the first eating of a new crop with a ritual: no one may eat the new rice, millet or fruit until it has been offered to the deities and ancestors. In western Odisha, Nuākhāī (“eating the new”) is celebrated by Adivasi and caste communities alike when the new rice is ready; families gather, the first grain is offered to the deity, and then shared. Santal, Munda and Oraon festivals similarly mark the first use of new flowers, fruits and grain. Such rituals express gratitude and kinship, and also regulate harvesting: fruit that may not be eaten before the ritual is not picked unripe.

docs.title: 5.3 Millets
docs.text:
Millets are hardy grains that grow on poor soils with little water. They were long neglected by agricultural policy, which favoured rice and wheat, and were associated with poverty. In recent years they have been revalued for their nutritional qualities and their resilience to drought. At India’s proposal the United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets. The main millets are listed in Table 5.1.

Table 5.1. Millets grown by Adivasi and other dryland farmers Species Common names Notes Eleusine coracana (finger millet) Rāgī, maṇḍuā, nācnī Rich in calcium; widely grown in hills and plateaus Pennisetum glaucum (pearl millet) Bājrā, kambu Staple of the arid west Sorghum bicolor (sorghum) Jowār, jonna Grain and fodder Setaria italica (foxtail millet) Kāṅgnī, korra, navaṇe Short season Panicum sumatrense (little millet) Kuṭkī, sāmai Grown on poor upland soils Paspalum scrobiculatum (kodo millet) Kodo, kodra Hardy; can be toxic if the grain is infected with fungus Echinochloa frumentacea (barnyard millet) Sāṃvā, jhaṅgorā Grown in the Himalaya and elsewhere Panicum miliaceum (proso millet) Cīnā, baragu Short season

Adivasi farmers often grow millets mixed with pulses and oilseeds in the same field, which spreads risk and maintains soil fertility. Cooking traditions include porridges, flatbreads, gruels fermented overnight, and millet beers. The new popularity of millets in cities has raised prices, which can benefit growers, but there is a risk that the knowledge and varieties of Adivasi farmers will be used without benefit to them.

docs.title: 5.4 Famine Foods and Detoxification
docs.text:
Communities that live with uncertain harvests know which wild foods can be eaten when crops fail. Many of these require careful preparation because they contain bitter or toxic compounds. Examples include:

  • wild yams (Dioscorea species), some of which, such as D. hispida, are poisonous unless sliced, soaked in running water or ash solution and boiled repeatedly;

  • bamboo shoots, which contain cyanogenic compounds removed by boiling, soaking or fermentation;

  • the seeds of certain trees eaten in famine, prepared by roasting and soaking;

  • mushrooms, where knowledge of which species are edible is a matter of life and death.

Wild foods

Some wild tubers, seeds and mushrooms are poisonous unless correctly identified and prepared, and some cannot be made safe at all. Deaths from eating poisonous mushrooms and improperly prepared tubers are reported in India every year. Traditional knowledge of identification and preparation is precise and local; it should not be imitated from written descriptions.

docs.title: 5.5 Fermentation
docs.text: Fermentation preserves food, changes its flavour and texture, can improve its digestibility and nutritional value, and produces drinks with important social and ritual roles. North-East India and the Himalaya have particularly rich fermentation traditions, which the microbiologist Jyoti Prakash Tamang and others have studied in detail (Tamang 2010). Table 5.2 lists some of these foods and drinks.

docs.title: 5.5.1 Rice Beer
docs.text:
Rice beer is made across eastern and north-eastern India: hãṛiyā (also called handiā) among the Santal, Munda, Oraon and Ho; zutho among the Angami Naga; apong among the Mising and Adi; judima among the Dimasa; and many others. Cooked rice is mixed with a dried starter cake (rānu, bākhar and other local names) made from rice flour and a mixture of plants, which carries the moulds and yeasts that convert starch to sugar and sugar to alcohol. Microbiological studies have identified the fungi, yeasts and bacteria in these starters (Tamang 2010). The knowledge of which plants to use and how to make and keep the starter is usually held by women.

Rice beer is food, offering and hospitality. It is offered to deities and ancestors, shared at festivals, given to guests and to people who help with work. Its regulation by excise laws has long been contentious: the state has sometimes criminalised home brewing that communities regard as part of their culture, while selling commercial liquor through licensed shops.

In the North-East, Christian churches have often discouraged or forbidden rice beer and other alcohol. Nagaland has prohibited the sale of liquor since 1989, and Mizoram has had prohibition for most of the period since the late 1990s, though both prohibitions have been widely evaded. Rice beer thus occupies a contested place, valued as heritage by some and rejected as un-Christian by others.

docs.title: 5.5.2 Mahua Spirit
docs.text:
Mahua flowers are fermented and distilled to make a spirit (mahuā dārū) which, like rice beer, is central to ritual and hospitality in central India. Colonial excise laws restricted its production in favour of licensed distilleries, a cause of resentment and of several Adivasi protests.

Alcohol is also a cause of harm in many Adivasi communities, as elsewhere: of debt, domestic violence and illness. Adivasi women’s movements in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha have campaigned against liquor shops and drunkenness. An honest account must hold together both the cultural meaning of traditional drinks and these concerns. Women’s campaigns against liquor have a long history in India beyond the Adivasi regions, notably the movement of rural women in Nellore district of Andhra Pradesh in 1992 against the government-licensed sale of arrack, which led to its prohibition in the state. Adivasi women’s campaigns have usually targeted commercial liquor shops and drunkenness rather than the household brewing of rice beer for ritual and hospitality.

docs.title: 5.5.3 Fermented Foods of the North-East and Himalaya
docs.text:
• Fermented soybean: akhunī (axone) of Nagaland, kinema of the eastern Himalaya, tungrymbai of the Khasi and hawaijar of Manipur are alkaline fermentations dominated by Bacillus bacteria, comparable to Japanese nattō (Tamang 2010).

  • Fermented bamboo shoot: mesu (Sikkim and Darjeeling), soibum (Manipur) and similar products.

  • Fermented fish: ngari and hentak of Manipur and tungtap of the Khasi hills.

  • Fermented leafy vegetables: gundruk of the Nepali-speaking communities of the eastern Himalaya.

Table 5.2. Some fermented foods and drinks of Adivasi India (Tamang 2010) Name Community / region Substrate and type Hãṛiyā Santal, Munda, Oraon, Ho Rice beer, with rānu starter Zutho Angami Naga Rice beer Apong Mising, Adi Rice beer Judima Dimasa Rice beer Mahuā dārū Central India Distilled spirit from mahua flowers Akhunī Naga Fermented soybean (alkaline) Tungrymbai Khasi Fermented soybean (alkaline) Hawaijar Manipur Fermented soybean (alkaline) Kinema Eastern Himalaya Fermented soybean (alkaline) Mesu, soibum Sikkim; Manipur Fermented bamboo shoot Ngari, hentak Manipur Fermented fish Tungtap Khasi Fermented fish Gundruk Eastern Himalaya Fermented leafy vegetables

These foods were long looked down on by outsiders because of their strong smells. They are now increasingly valued as part of regional cuisine and identity.

docs.title: 5.6 Hunting, Fishing and the Law
docs.text:
Hunting and fishing were once important sources of food for most forest communities, and remain so for some. Hunting knowledge includes the habits and signs of animals, the making of bows, arrows, traps, snares and nets, and rules about sharing the kill. Collective hunts were also ritual and political occasions, as the Santal regional hunt was (Section 11.2).

The Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972 made almost all hunting illegal. For many Adivasi communities this turned a customary practice into a crime, and forest guards have used the law to harass villagers. At the same time, the decline of many animal populations, including through commercial poaching networks that exploit local hunters, is real, and some ritual hunts now take place in landscapes where wildlife has become scarce. Conservation organisations and some Adivasi leaders have negotiated changes, such as symbolic hunts, while other communities insist on their customary rights. In Nagaland, where communities own most of the land, several villages have decided for themselves to ban or restrict hunting (Chapter 2).

Fishing in streams, ponds and flooded fields, often using traps woven from bamboo and plant-based fish poisons that stun fish in small pools, provides protein in many Adivasi diets. Large dams and the leasing of reservoirs to contractors have often taken fishing rights away from the communities displaced by them.

docs.title: 5.7 Food, Identity and Stigma
docs.text:
Food has been a marker of difference between Adivasi communities and their caste Hindu neighbours. Many Adivasis eat beef, pork, rats, insects or other foods that upper-caste Hindu norms regard as polluting, and drink rice beer and mahua spirit. Missionaries and Hindu reformers alike tried to change these habits. Some Adivasi reform movements, such as the Tana Bhagat movement among the Oraon and the Devi movement among the Bhils (Hardiman 1987), themselves called for abstinence from meat and alcohol, in part to claim higher status and resist exploitation by liquor sellers. Food choices are thus bound up with identity, status and resistance.

Today such questions appear in debates over the inclusion of eggs and meat in school meals and nutrition programmes, over restrictions on the slaughter of cattle, and over the place of traditional foods in Adivasi identity. A respectful approach recognises that communities themselves decide what they eat, and that nutritional policy should be built around the foods that people actually value.

docs.title: 5.8 Food Rules and Taboos
docs.text:
All societies have rules about food: what may be eaten, by whom, when, and with whom. Among Adivasi communities, many clans have totems (an animal or plant) that their members may not kill or eat; some foods are forbidden to women during pregnancy or menstruation; and some are reserved for particular rituals.

Some writers interpret such rules as hidden ecological or nutritional regulations, for example totemic prohibitions as conservation measures. Some rules may have such effects, but many do not, and some are harmful: restrictions on what pregnant and breastfeeding women may eat, found in many communities, can deprive them of protein and other nutrients at the time they most need them. Food rules are best understood first as expressions of social and religious identity, and only then examined for their ecological or nutritional consequences.

docs.title: 5.9 Preservation
docs.text: Before refrigeration, food had to be kept by drying, smoking, salting, fermenting or storing in cool places. Adivasi households dry greens, mushrooms, tubers, fish and meat in the sun in the season of plenty for use in the lean months. In the humid North-East, where sun-drying is difficult in the monsoon, meat and fish are smoked over the kitchen hearth on racks that are a feature of every house. Grain is stored in baskets plastered with mud and dung, or in specially built granaries, to protect it from insects and rodents.

docs.title: 5.10 The Weekly Market
docs.text: Adivasi food systems have never been self-contained. In most Adivasi regions the weekly market (hāṭ) is the place where households sell forest produce, surplus grain, vegetables, chickens and goats, and buy salt, oil, cloth, tools and, increasingly, packaged foods. In Bastar and other parts of central India the hāṭ is also a social occasion, where people from many villages meet, arrange marriages, drink rice beer and mahua, and hear news. Historically, traders at the hāṭ often bought forest produce at low prices and sold salt and cloth dear, and moneylenders used the market to bind collectors in debt; one aim of the minimum support price for forest produce (Chapter 14) is to change these terms. The hāṭ is a reminder that food knowledge includes knowledge of prices, seasons of scarcity and the negotiation of exchange, as well as knowledge of plants and cooking.

docs.title: 5.11 Threats and Revival
docs.text:
Adivasi food knowledge is under pressure from several directions. Loss of land and of access to forests removes the sources of wild foods. Agricultural policy and the public distribution system have spread rice and wheat, which has improved food security but narrowed diets, and the high-yielding varieties of the Green Revolution, which need irrigation and purchased inputs, have replaced many local ones. Stigma has led families to give up foods associated with poverty or “backwardness”, and migration takes young people away from the fields and forests where food knowledge is learned.

An example from outside the tribal areas shows what organised revival can achieve. In the Zaheerabad region of Telangana, the Deccan Development Society, working since the 1980s with groups of Dalit women farmers, has promoted the cultivation of millets and pulses in mixed fields, community seed banks, a women’s community radio station and an annual travelling festival of biodiversity. The FAO’s study of indigenous food systems included this case (Kuhnlein et al. 2009).

Against this, there are signs of revival: community seed banks, millet missions in several states (notably Odisha’s millet mission, launched in 2017), the inclusion of millets in school meals and the public distribution system, and a growing interest among Adivasi youth and urban consumers in traditional foods.

docs.title: 5.11.1 Food Policy and Adivasi Diets
docs.text:
Public food programmes now shape Adivasi diets as much as forests and fields. Under the National Food Security Act, 2013, most rural households are entitled to subsidised grain through the public distribution system, and children receive meals in schools and in the aṅganvāḍī centres of the Integrated Child Development Services. These programmes have reduced hunger, but they have supplied mainly rice and wheat, which has encouraged the shift away from millets and gathered foods. Several states have begun to include millets and locally grown pulses in the distribution system and in school meals, and to buy forest produce and millets from local farmers. The forest itself remains a source of food security in hard times: during droughts and, more recently, during the disruption of the COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020, many Adivasi households fell back on gathered foods and on grain stored in the village while wage work in the cities disappeared. That experience has strengthened the argument that secure access to forests and commons is part of food policy, not separate from it. Nutrition specialists have argued that programmes designed around the foods that communities already know and value are more likely to improve nutrition than uniform rations imposed from outside. They add a caution that applies to the whole of this chapter: traditional diets alone will not end undernutrition, which also needs income, health care, sanitation and attention to the nutrition of mothers.

Key Points

  • Adivasi diets draw on many cultivated and wild species, processed by drying, smoking and fermentation.

  • Despite this diversity, undernutrition among Adivasi children is high, because of poverty and loss of land and forest access.

  • Millets and fermented foods are being revalued, but their holders need to share in the benefits.

  • Food rules express identity; some protect resources, others, such as restrictions on pregnant women, can harm health.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Kuhnlein et al. (2009): indigenous food systems around the world, with an Indian case study.

  • Tamang (2010): the fermented foods of the Himalaya and North-East India.

  • Elwin (1939): Baiga life, including food and shifting cultivation.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Folk Astronomy, Calendars and Weather Knowledge
6.1 Introduction: Sky and Season
docs.text:
Farmers, herders and fishers everywhere watch the sky and the living world for signs of the season and the weather. In India this everyday knowledge exists alongside a learned astronomical tradition, jyotiṣa, one of the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅga) of the Veda, which developed into a mathematical astronomy and a system of calendars and almanacs (pañcāṅga); it is treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa. Folk knowledge borrows from this tradition, especially its calendar, but it also rests on direct observation of stars, moon, winds, clouds, plants and animals.

This chapter describes that knowledge. It is also cautious. Systematic studies of Adivasi astronomy are few, and much that has been written on the subject is anecdotal or invented. Claims that particular communities could predict eclipses or forecast monsoons as well as modern meteorology are not supported by evidence and are not repeated here. Four kinds of knowledge are involved: calendars that reckon months and seasons by the moon, the sun and the work of the year; the flowering, fruiting and leaf-fall of plants and the behaviour of animals as markers of season; named stars used to tell the time at night; and signs read in winds, clouds and animals as warnings of rain or drought.

docs.title: 6.2 The Nakṣatra Rain Calendar
docs.text:
The classical calendar divides the sun’s yearly path among the stars into twenty-seven nakṣatras (lunar mansions), each of about thirteen and a third degrees, so that the sun spends roughly thirteen or fourteen days in each. Across much of India, farmers name the rains of the monsoon season after the nakṣatra in which the sun stands.
