In Maharashtra the first rains of June are the Mṛg rains, followed by Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya and so on; in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh the late rains of Hasta (Hathiyā), in late September and early October, are considered vital for the rice crop. Sowing, transplanting and other work are timed by these periods, and proverbs say which crops do well or badly if a particular nakṣatra brings rain or fails to. The periods of the monsoon season are listed in Table 6.1.

Table 6.1. Monsoon nakṣatra periods in folk usage (approximate dates of the sun’s entry, sidereal reckoning) Nakṣatra Sun enters (approx.) Popular association Rohiṇī 25 May Nautapā: intense heat before the monsoon Mṛgaśiras (Mṛg) 8 June First monsoon rains in western India; sowing begins Ārdrā 22 June Main sowing of rain-fed crops Punarvasu, Puṣya 6 and 20 July Steady monsoon rains; transplanting of rice Āśleṣā, Maghā 3 and 17 August Heavy rains; weeding Pūrvā, Uttarā (Phalgunī) 30 August, 13 September Late monsoon Hasta (Hathiyā) 27 September Late rains considered vital for rice in eastern India Citrā, Svātī 10 and 24 October Retreating monsoon; rain in Svātī is proverbially rare and precious

Because the dates of these periods are fixed by the sun’s position, they fall on nearly the same dates of the Gregorian calendar every year, which makes them a practical solar calendar for agricultural work. They do not, of course, forecast whether rain will actually fall.

In north India a popular belief holds that the nine days after the sun enters Rohiṇī (late May to early June), the nautapā, should be very hot if the monsoon is to be good. In Tamil Nadu a well-known proverb, āṭip paṭṭam tēṭi vitai (“seek out the Āṭi season and sow”), advises sowing in the month of Āṭi (mid-July to mid-August).

docs.title: 6.2.1 The Almanac in the Village
docs.text: The printed pañcāṅga (almanac), produced in many regional editions, lists for each day the lunar day (tithi), the nakṣatra, festivals, auspicious times and, in many editions, forecasts of rain and harvest for the year. Village priests and astrologers consult it to fix the dates of festivals, weddings and agricultural rites. Its rainfall forecasts are astrological predictions, not meteorology. Many Adivasi communities also use it, or consult a priest who does, for festivals shared with their neighbours, while fixing their own festivals by village decision and the season.

docs.title: 6.2.2 Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī
docs.text: In the Hindi, Bhojpuri and Awadhi regions, a large body of rhyming proverbs about weather, crops and farming is attributed to the folk sages Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī, figures of uncertain date about whom many legends are told. The proverbs advise on when to sow and harvest, how to judge soil and oxen, and how to read winds, clouds and the behaviour of animals for signs of rain. Collections of these proverbs were made in the colonial period and continue to be published. They are a rich record of farmers’ observations and beliefs, of very varying reliability.

docs.title: 6.3 Adivasi Calendars
docs.text:
Adivasi communities of central and eastern India mostly use month names shared with the neighbouring Indo-Aryan calendars, but organise the year around their own festivals and work. For the Munda, Oraon, Santal and their neighbours, the year turns on a cycle such as the one shown in Table 6.2.

Table 6.2. An illustrative festival and work cycle in the Chotanagpur region Season (approx.) Festival Associated activity and signs January–February Māgh festivals End of the agricultural year; in Santal custom village officials are reappointed March–April Sarhul / Bāhā Flowering of the sal tree; worship in the sacred grove; first use of new flowers and leaves March–April – Mahua flowers collected June–July – First rains; sowing and transplanting of rice August–September Karam Branch of the karam tree worshipped; prayers for crops and kin October–November Sohrāe Harvest; cattle honoured

Such calendars are anchored as much in phenology as in astronomy: the flowering of sal and mahua, the first thunderstorms, the swarming of termites, the arrival and departure of migratory birds. They are robust because several signs confirm each other, and flexible because festivals are fixed by village decision rather than by an almanac.

docs.title: 6.3.1 The Shifting Cultivator’s Year
docs.text: In the hills of the North-East, the calendar of shifting cultivation structures the year. Plots are selected and cut in the cool dry months, left to dry, and burned shortly before the first pre-monsoon rains; sowing follows immediately, so that the ash is not washed away; weeding occupies the monsoon months; and different crops are harvested in turn from late summer to early winter. Festivals mark the main stages: among many Naga communities, for example, a festival after sowing and another after harvest. Communities judge the time for burning and sowing by the weather, by the flowering of particular trees and by the calls of particular birds, and their elders decide the date for the whole village, since burning must be coordinated to prevent fires from spreading (Ramakrishnan 1992).

docs.title: 6.4 The Night Sky
docs.text:
Many Adivasi communities name stars and star groups and use them to tell the time at night and to mark seasons. The Pleiades and the stars of Orion, conspicuous in the winter night sky, are recognised almost everywhere, as are the Great Bear, the Milky Way and the morning and evening star (Venus). Names and stories differ from community to community: star groups may be seen as animals, hunters, a plough, a cot or a group of people, and the Milky Way as a road or river.

Systematic documentation is recent and limited. The most detailed work so far comes from a team led by the astrophysicist Mayank Vahia of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and Ganesh Halkare of Amravati, who surveyed Gond villages in the borderlands of Maharashtra, Telangana (then Andhra Pradesh) and Madhya Pradesh and then the Kolam and Banjara of the same region (Vahia and Halkare 2013; Vahia et al. 2014). Their papers are the main basis of what follows. Further work of this kind, done with the communities concerned, is needed before general statements about Adivasi astronomy can be made with confidence.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The Gond Sky
docs.text:
In March 2011 Vahia and Halkare visited fifteen Gond villages between Chandrapur, Yavatmal, Adilabad, Gondia, Balaghat, Mandla, Seoni and Nagpur. To make sure that everyone was talking about the same stars, they projected images of the night sky on village walls, and in 2012 a group of twenty-three Gond villagers from three districts explained their sky to the team inside the planetarium of the Raman Science Centre at Nagpur (Vahia and Halkare 2013). Names varied from village to village, as one would expect across several Gondi dialects and a long contact with Marathi and Hindi, but a recognisable common sky emerged.

The seven bright stars of the Great Bear are a cot (katul), often “the old woman’s cot”, with the three stars of the handle seen as thieves (kalher) trying to carry it off; in one Mandla village the three were a nobleman, his wife and the village watchman. The belt of Orion is tipan or nangar, a plough, and nearby stars are seen as other implements of the threshing floor: a grain-beater, a stool on which the winnower stands, a basket. The Pleiades were variously named: as a grain-beater (kotela), as a broom, or, in one village’s story, as stones thrown by the hunter of Orion at a bird and its eggs nearby. The Milky Way is a road, sometimes “the path of the animals”. Figure 6.1 shows the cot and the plough. Venus is known as the evening star that signals the time for the evening meal (jevan sukum) and as the morning star that signals the start of the working day (pahat sukum). Comets are brooms, and shooting stars “star droppings”. Far to the south, the Southern Cross is a mahua tree, irukmara, whose appearance at about three in the morning marks the season for gathering mahua flowers; among the Gond this was recorded in only one village, but the Kolam know it widely (below).

Figure 6.1. Two star groups as seen in Gond villages of central India, after the survey of Vahia and Halkare: the four stars of the bowl of the Great Bear are a cot and the three stars of the handle are thieves trying to carry it off; the three stars of Orion’s belt are a plough (Vahia and Halkare 2013). Star positions are plotted approximately from their coordinates, with east to the left as in the sky; both panels are drawn to the same scale, and names vary from village to village (Table 6.3).

The sky is used above all for time. Villagers told the time of night by the rising of particular stars; they knew that the monsoon comes when Orion’s belt is seen at sunset and that farm work begins when a certain four-sided group of stars stands overhead before dawn; and a halo round the moon was read as a sign of rain, nearer or farther according to its size. Months run from new moon to new moon, and several villages knew that an extra month must be inserted about every three years to keep the lunar year in step with the seasons. Gond organisations now print their own calendars in Gondi, listing the community’s festivals by the lunar month; the 2007 calendar used by Vahia and Halkare listed twenty-four.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Kolam and Banjara Skies
docs.text:
The Kolam, who were shifting cultivators and foragers on the hill ridges of the same region until the mid-twentieth century, share part of the Gond sky: they too see a cot in the Great Bear, but the three thieves are a Kolam, a Gond and a chief (pradhān), a small picture of the region’s social world; and they too see a mahua tree in the Southern Cross (Vahia et al. 2014). They describe the Pleiades as one large bird with several small ones, and see in the square of stars that the researchers identified with Pegasus a great lake, samdur, that gives water to the land. They have elaborate stories of eclipses, in which gods come to collect their dues from the sun; if they take the whole sun they are satisfied, and if they take only part, people or animals must make up the shortfall.

The Banjara, whose livelihood as carriers of grain and salt by pack-bullock collapsed with the railways, have by comparison a sparse sky: the Great Bear as the cot of the dead, the Pleiades as forehead jewellery, Orion as a deer, the Milky Way as the path of the dead. For predicting the monsoon they rely much more on the halo round the moon and on terrestrial signs, such as the placing of crows’ nests, the direction of lightning and ants carrying their eggs, than on stars. Table 6.3 sets out some of the names recorded in the three communities.

Table 6.3. Some star groups as named in three communities of central India (names as transcribed by Vahia and colleagues) Star group Gond Kolam Banjara Great Bear Cot (katul) and thieves (kalher) Cot, with a Kolam, a Gond and a chief as thieves Cot of the dead (jamakhat) Orion Plough (tipan, nangar) Sowing implement (tipan); also a hunter’s belt and sword Deer (halni) Pleiades Grain-beater or broom; stones thrown at a bird One large and several small birds Forehead jewel (jhumko) Milky Way Road; path of the animals Path of the animals Path of the dead or of animals Southern Cross Mahua tree (irukmara) Mahua tree –

docs.title: 6.4.3 Reading the Studies Critically
docs.text:
These surveys are valuable because they record names, stories and uses directly from people and check the identifications against the actual sky. But their limits should be kept in view. Each rests on short visits to a small number of villages in one region, and on the memories of mainly older men; women’s knowledge of the sky, and the knowledge of Gond communities in Bastar, Odisha or the Narmada valley, are hardly represented. Some identifications are uncertain, as the authors themselves note. The authors also go beyond the evidence in places. From the story that the old woman whose cot is the Great Bear never sleeps, and from the absence of a Gond name for the pole star in most villages, they infer that Gond sky lore took shape around 1000 BCE, when the Great Bear was circumpolar for central Indian latitudes; and they describe the Gond and Kolam as genetically and culturally isolated. Neither inference is secure. A star story cannot be dated by precession unless one can show that it has not been reshaped since, and a few villages did name the pole star, one of them with a Gondi name; Gond, Kolam, Pardhan and Banjara have lived alongside one another and alongside Marathi- and Telugu-speaking peasants for centuries, as the thieves in the Kolam Great Bear themselves suggest. Their suggestion that the richness of a community’s sky lore follows the length of its settled agricultural life is an interesting hypothesis from three cases, not a finding.

The same team has since published comparable surveys of the Korku and the Pardhi of central India (Vahia et al. 2016; Halkare et al. 2019). For the Santal, Munda, Ho and other communities of eastern India no systematic modern study of sky knowledge has yet been made, and the star names and stories scattered through older ethnographies have not been brought together. The best work in this field will come from collaboration in which members of the communities themselves decide what is recorded and how it is used.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Eclipses
docs.text: Eclipses are explained in many communities by stories of a being who swallows the sun or moon; in the classical and popular Hindu tradition this is the demon Rāhu. Customs during eclipses include fasting, bathing, making noise and giving alms. The Kolam stories of gods collecting their dues, described above, are a local example; the Gond villagers surveyed by Vahia and Halkare, by contrast, had little or nothing to say about eclipses (Vahia and Halkare 2013). These are matters of belief and ritual. There is no evidence that any Adivasi community had a method for predicting eclipses; eclipse prediction in India was the work of mathematical astronomers using the siddhānta texts.

docs.title: 6.5 Weather Signs
docs.text:
Rural people throughout India read signs of coming weather:

  • winds: the direction and character of winds before and during the monsoon, such as the moist easterly purvaiyā in the Gangetic plain;

  • clouds and sky: the shape, colour and movement of clouds, a halo round the moon, the colour of the sky at sunset;

  • animals: ants carrying eggs to higher ground, the swarming of termites, the calls of particular birds, frogs croaking;

  • plants: heavy flowering or fruiting of particular trees taken as a sign of a good or bad monsoon.

Some of these signs reflect real physical connections: changes in humidity and air pressure before rain affect insects and birds, and haloes are produced by high ice clouds that often precede the arrival of a weather system. Others are probably coincidences remembered because they were sometimes right. Few such indicators have been tested systematically. UNESCO’s review of traditional knowledge for climate change assessment concludes that such knowledge is most useful for local observation of change and for adaptation, in combination with scientific forecasting (Nakashima et al. 2012).

docs.title: 6.5.1 Local and Scientific Forecasting Compared
docs.text: Modern meteorology uses satellite observations and numerical models of the atmosphere; it is good at forecasting large-scale weather a few days ahead and at issuing warnings of cyclones and heavy rain, and its seasonal monsoon forecasts are probabilistic and regional. Local knowledge, by contrast, is based on observation of a small area and its living indicators, and is expressed in qualitative terms. It may capture local features that regional forecasts miss, such as the behaviour of a particular valley or coast; it is less reliable for anything beyond the immediate future. The two are most useful together: agricultural advisories that translate scientific forecasts into local language and local terms, and that draw on farmers’ own observations, are more likely to be understood and used than either alone.

docs.title: 6.6 Disasters: Cyclones and the 2004 Tsunami
docs.text:
The coast of Odisha was struck in October 1999 by a “super cyclone” that killed many thousands of people. In October 2013 Cyclone Phailin, of comparable strength, struck the same coast; this time, after accurate forecasts by the India Meteorological Department, the state moved very large numbers of people to cyclone shelters and other safe places, and the loss of life was a small fraction of that in 1999. The improvement came from better forecasting, shelters, planning and community preparedness. Local knowledge of the coast and of which places are safe is part of community preparedness; but it was modern forecasting and evacuation that saved most lives.

The Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 devastated the Nicobar Islands and the coasts of the Andaman Islands and Tamil Nadu. Among the Andaman Islanders, the Onge, Jarawa and Great Andamanese were widely reported to have suffered few or no deaths, because they moved inland or to high ground after the earthquake. Commentators attributed this to traditions about earthquakes and the sea and to the islanders’ close observation of their environment; the islanders’ own accounts have been documented only partially. By contrast, the Nicobarese, who lived in villages on low coasts, suffered heavy losses.

docs.title: 6.7 Climate Change
docs.text:
Local observations of a changing climate (less predictable monsoons, shifts in the flowering of trees, new pests, drying springs) are discussed in Section 2.17. For the knowledge described in this chapter, change poses a particular problem: the very regularities on which folk calendars and weather signs depend are being disturbed, and knowledge calibrated to the past may become less reliable (Nakashima et al. 2012). That is one more reason to test widely used indicators with farmers, and to record calendars and star names in the communities’ own languages while those who hold them can still explain them.

Key Points

  • Folk calendars combine the classical nakṣatra system with festivals and the phenology of plants and animals.

  • Systematic studies of Adivasi astronomy are few; claims of eclipse prediction or forecasting equal to meteorology are unsupported.

  • Weather signs range from genuine physical indicators to remembered coincidences and need testing.

  • Lives in cyclones and tsunamis are saved mainly by forecasts, shelters and evacuation, with local knowledge as a complement.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Vahia and Halkare (2013): a study of Gond astronomical knowledge.

  • Vahia et al. (2014): the sky knowledge of the Banjara and Kolam, compared with that of the Gond.

  • Nakashima et al. (2012): traditional knowledge and climate change.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Folk Medicine and Healing Traditions
7.1 Introduction: Healers and Their Knowledge
docs.text:
In every village and forest hamlet of the subcontinent there have been people who knew how to deal with illness and injury: women who treated fevers and digestive complaints at home, bone-setters, midwives, herbalists, and diviners and priests who identified the hidden causes of misfortune. For many Adivasi communities, especially those far from hospitals, such healers have been, and often still are, the first and sometimes the only source of care.

This chapter describes these traditions. It treats them as knowledge systems with their own logic, and it records the respect in which healers are held. It also applies the same standard to them that should be applied to any medicine. A remedy is not shown to work because it is old, because it is used by many people, or because laboratory tests on a plant extract have found some biological activity. Only careful clinical study can establish whether a treatment is safe and effective, and very few folk remedies have been studied in that way. Nothing in this chapter is a recommendation to use any remedy, and no doses are given.

Health and Safety Note

This chapter describes traditional practices for historical and cultural understanding only. It does not recommend any treatment. Several plants mentioned here (for example Datura, Calotropis, Euphorbia latex, Acorus calamus and some wild tubers) are toxic. Snakebite, fractures, difficult childbirth, high fever, jaundice and serious infections need prompt care at a health facility; delay in seeking such care is a major cause of avoidable death. Commercially sold herbal and mineral products have repeatedly been found to contain lead, mercury or arsenic (Saper et al. 2004, 2008).

docs.title: 7.2 Folk Medicine and Āyurveda
docs.text:
All traditional healing in India is often loosely called “Āyurveda”. This is misleading. Folk medicine, as the term is used here, is the healing knowledge of rural and Adivasi communities, learned by apprenticeship and practice rather than from texts or colleges. Classical Āyurveda, as set out in the Carakasaṃhitā, the Suśrutasaṃhitā and Vāgbhaṭa’s Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, is a learned, textual system with a theory of three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha), seven bodily tissues (dhātu) and an elaborate pharmacology (Wujastyk 2003); it is treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda. Adivasi healers generally do not think in these terms. A Santal ojhā, a Gond guniyā or a Sora shaman explains illness in other ways, and uses plants of the local forest that may not appear in any Sanskrit text.

The two traditions have interacted for a very long time. As noted in Chapter 1, the Carakasaṃhitā acknowledges that herdsmen and forest dwellers know medicinal plants by sight and name (Sūtrasthāna 1.120–121), and many plants of the classical pharmacopoeia were surely learned from such people. In the other direction, Āyurvedic ideas such as “hot” and “cold” foods have spread widely in folk practice. Today many rural healers combine local plants, Āyurvedic preparations bought in the market, and biomedical drugs.

docs.title: 7.2.1 Medical Pluralism
docs.text: Anthropologists use the term medical pluralism for the coexistence of several medical systems among which people choose. The collection Asian Medical Systems, edited by Charles Leslie (1976), established the comparative study of such pluralism in South Asia and elsewhere (Leslie 1976). In an Adivasi village today a family may, for the same illness, consult a household elder, a herbalist, a diviner, a government health worker, an unqualified “doctor” who gives injections, a pharmacy and a hospital, in various orders. People are pragmatic: they judge treatments by results, cost and accessibility, and often attribute different aspects of an illness (its symptoms, its cause, its meaning) to different domains. Understanding this pattern of choice is more useful than asking whether people “believe in” traditional or modern medicine.

docs.title: 7.3 Ideas of Illness
docs.text:
In many Adivasi traditions illness can have several kinds of cause, and an important part of healing is finding out which one is at work:

  • ordinary or natural causes, such as cold, heat, bad food, injury or worms, treated with plants, diet and massage;

  • the anger of deities or spirits (boṅgā among the Santal and Munda, pen among the Gond), often because of a neglected offering or broken taboo;

  • the dead, whose wishes must be heard;

  • human malice, including sorcery and the evil eye.

Piers Vitebsky’s study of the Sora of Odisha describes how shamans, many of them women, enter trance and allow the dead to speak through them; in these “dialogues with the dead” the living and the dead negotiate over illness, grief and obligation (Vitebsky 1993). Elwin had described the Sora shamans and their wall paintings (iḍital) a generation earlier (Elwin 1955).

Such explanations attend to the social and emotional side of illness: a patient’s quarrels, losses and fears are part of the diagnosis, which biomedical consultations often leave out. But the same frameworks can do great harm. Belief that illness or death is caused by a witch (ḍāin, ṭonhī) has led, across Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Assam and elsewhere, to the accusation, expulsion, torture and murder of women, often widows or women with land. Several states have passed laws against witch-hunting, beginning with Bihar (1999) and Jharkhand (2001) (Chapter 11). An honest account of folk healing must include this.

docs.title: 7.4 Healers
docs.text:
Healers are known by many names. In eastern India the ojhā is a diviner and healer; Santals also consult the jān guru, a diviner who identifies the cause of misfortune. In Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh the guniyā and the baigā (a village priest-healer, a role often filled by members of the Baiga community for their Gond neighbours) treat illness and appease local deities. Among Bhils and Oraons the bhagat has similar functions, and in Rajasthan the bhopā is a possessed medium of a deity. Some healers specialise in particular conditions such as snakebite, fractures or children’s illnesses; many are farmers or labourers who heal part-time. The main kinds are summarised in Table 7.1.

Table 7.1. Some kinds of healers and ritual specialists (terms vary between communities) Term Region / communities Role Ojhā Eastern India; Santal, Munda, Ho and neighbours Diviner and healer; identifies spirits or sorcery behind illness Jān guru Santal Diviner consulted to find the cause of illness or death Guniyā Central India Healer using plants, charms and offerings Baigā Central India (often Baiga for Gond neighbours) Village priest of the land and healer Bhagat Oraon, Bhil and others Healer and ritual specialist; also a reformed devotee Bhopā Rajasthan, Gujarat Medium of a deity; also epic singer Shaman Sora (Saora) Woman or man who enters trance to speak with the dead (Vitebsky 1993) Amchi Ladakh, Himalaya Practitioner of Sowa-Rigpa Dāī Throughout India Birth attendant Bone-setter Throughout India Treats fractures and dislocations

Knowledge is usually learned over years from a parent, relative or teacher. The apprentice accompanies the healer to collect plants, learns their appearance in different seasons, learns preparations, and is gradually allowed to treat patients. Spells and songs (mantra in the broad sense) are often taught with the plants. Some knowledge is secret, passed on only to a chosen successor; this protects the healer’s livelihood and authority, but it also means that knowledge can die with its holder.

Healers’ knowledge of plants can be extensive: documentation projects have recorded experienced healers who use well over a hundred species. Ethnobotanical surveys, starting with the work of S. K. Jain and of P. O. Bodding among the Santal, have collected thousands of plant–use records (Bodding 1925; Jain 1991). These records are an important cultural archive. They are not, by themselves, evidence that the remedies work.

docs.title: 7.5.1 Santal
docs.text: The Norwegian missionary and scholar P. O. Bodding, who worked among the Santal for nearly half a century, published a detailed study of Santal medicine and the beliefs connected with it, based on manuscripts written for him by Santal informants (Bodding 1925). Santal healing combined plant remedies for everyday complaints with divination and offerings to the boṅgā for illness thought to have a spiritual cause. W. G. Archer’s later collection of Santal poetry shows how illness, healing and the spirit world run through Santal song (Archer 1974).

docs.title: 7.5.2 Gond and Baiga
docs.text: Among the Gond of central India and their Baiga neighbours, healing is closely tied to the village priesthood. Elwin’s The Baiga records Baiga charms, remedies and the reputation of Baiga priests as healers among other communities (Elwin 1939). Plants commonly reported in central Indian folk medicine include harṛā (Terminalia chebula), bahedā (T. bellirica), āṃvlā (Phyllanthus emblica), kālmegh (Andrographis paniculata) and bāibiḍaṅg (Embelia ribes).

docs.title: 7.5.3 Kani of the Western Ghats
docs.text:
In the 1980s scientists of the Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute (TBGRI) in Thiruvananthapuram learned from Kani guides of the Agasthyamalai hills in Kerala about a plant, ārogyappacca (Trichopus zeylanicus), which Kani men ate to keep up their energy on long walks. TBGRI developed a herbal preparation from it, licensed its manufacture to a pharmaceutical company in the mid-1990s, and agreed to share half of the licence fee and royalties with the Kani through a trust set up for the purpose. The case is often cited as an early example of benefit-sharing with a source community. It was also contested: Kani communities were divided over the arrangement, and the supply of the plant from the forest became a problem.

Another Kani healer, Lakshmikutty of Kallar in Thiruvananthapuram district, known for her knowledge of several hundred herbal preparations and for teaching it to others, received the Padma Shri in 2018; her recognition by the state is one sign of the changing status of folk healers.

docs.title: 7.5.4 North-East India
docs.text: The communities of North-East India, in one of the world’s richest botanical regions, have extensive plant medicine traditions. Khasi, Garo, Naga, Mizo and other healers use local plants for fevers, wounds, digestive and skin complaints. Much of the documentation is recent and scattered in regional journals, and many traditions have been reshaped by Christianity, which in some communities discouraged healing associated with older religious practice.

docs.title: 7.5.5 Sowa-Rigpa in the Himalaya
docs.text: In Ladakh, Lahaul and Spiti, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh and other Himalayan regions, many of whose peoples are Scheduled Tribes, the main traditional medical system is Sowa-Rigpa (“science of healing”), the Tibetan medical tradition. Unlike the oral traditions described above, it is a learned textual system, based on the Rgyud bzhi (“Four Tantras”), which draws on Indian Āyurvedic, Chinese and other sources. Its practitioners, the amchi, were traditionally trained in families or monasteries and served their villages, often without fixed payment. The Government of India recognised Sowa-Rigpa as an official system of medicine in 2010. Amchi medicine shows that “tribal” and “textual” are not opposites: Himalayan tribal communities have their own literate medical tradition.

docs.title: 7.6 Plants and the Question of Evidence
docs.text:
Table 7.2 lists some plants widely reported in Indian folk medicine. The “evidence” column is deliberately cautious.

Table 7.2. Some plants reported in folk medicine, with a note on evidence (no recommendation implied) Plant Reported traditional use Note on evidence and safety Andrographis paniculata (kālmegh) Fever, liver complaints Some clinical trials for symptoms of upper respiratory infections; not an established treatment for malaria or hepatitis Phyllanthus amarus / niruri (bhuiṃ-āṃvlā) Jaundice Early reports for hepatitis B were not confirmed by later trials Tinospora cordifolia (giloy) Fever, “strength” Case reports of liver injury associated with its use have been published Azadirachta indica (neem) Skin complaints, worms Neem oil is toxic if swallowed, especially by young children Cissus quadrangularis (hāḍjoṛ) Applied or taken for fractures Laboratory studies only; no reliable evidence that it speeds bone healing Calotropis spp. (āk) Toothache, skin complaints Latex is toxic and damages the eyes Acorus calamus (vac) Nervous complaints, cough Contains \(\beta\)-asarone, a suspected carcinogen; banned as a food additive in some countries Datura spp. Pain, asthma, external use Highly poisonous; a common cause of accidental poisoning

docs.title: 7.6.1 Lessons from Drug Discovery
docs.text:
The history of drug discovery shows both the promise and the limits of traditional medicine. Quinine, the first effective treatment for malaria, came from the bark of the South American cinchona tree, whose use was learned from Andean peoples. Artemisinin, now the basis of the most effective malaria treatments, was isolated in China in the 1970s by a team including Tu Youyou, who had searched classical Chinese medical texts for leads; she received the Nobel Prize in 2015. From India, reserpine, isolated in 1952 from Rauvolfia serpentina (sarpagandhā), a plant long used in Indian medicine for insanity and snakebite, became one of the first effective drugs for high blood pressure. In each case, however, the effective drug was a purified compound tested in clinical trials, not the traditional preparation; and the Andean and Indian communities whose knowledge pointed the way to quinine and reserpine received no share of the benefits. Most leads from traditional medicine do not produce drugs at all.

Laboratory research on plants used in folk medicine has found many with biological activity: extracts that kill microbes in a test tube, reduce inflammation in animals, or affect cells in culture. Such findings are a starting point for research, not a confirmation of traditional claims. Many promising extracts fail when tested in people, because the active compound does not reach the right place in the body in sufficient amounts, because of toxicity, or because the original observation was mistaken. At the same time, some of the most important drugs of modern medicine began with plants used in traditional medicine elsewhere in the world, and the systematic, ethical study of folk remedies, with consent and benefit-sharing, is worthwhile.

docs.title: 7.7 Bone-Setting
docs.text:
Traditional bone-setters are found throughout rural India and are widely trusted. They reduce dislocations and fractures by traction and manipulation, immobilise limbs with bamboo or wooden splints and cloth, and apply poultices of plants such as hāḍjoṛ, turmeric or castor leaves. The skill is often hereditary. For simple injuries, and where no hospital is within reach, a skilled bone-setter may help; many patients prefer them because they are near, cheap and familiar.

Bone-setting

Orthopaedic surgeons in India regularly treat serious complications of traditional bone-setting: fractures that have healed in the wrong position, stiff joints, infections, and gangrene caused by splints tied too tightly, which can lead to amputation. Open fractures, injuries to the spine, head, hip or thigh, and any injury with numbness, coldness or discolouration of the limb need hospital care.

docs.title: 7.8 Snakebite
docs.text:
Snakebite is a major cause of death in rural India. A nationally representative study, the Million Death Study, estimated that about 46,000 people died of snakebite in India in 2005, most of them farmers and their families in rural areas (Mohapatra et al. 2011). Folk responses to snakebite include incantations, cutting and sucking the wound, tight tourniquets, and plants applied or given by mouth; there are specialist snakebite healers in many villages, and shrines of snake deities where victims are taken.

Snakebite

The only proven treatment for venomous snakebite is anti-venom given in a health facility, with supportive care. Cutting the wound, sucking, tight tourniquets and herbal remedies do not help and can cause harm. Time spent with a traditional healer before reaching hospital is one of the main reasons people die. Keep the person calm and still, immobilise the bitten limb, and go to a hospital immediately (Mohapatra et al. 2011).

The Irula snake-catchers of Tamil Nadu (Chapter 2) are an instructive contrast: their knowledge of snakes is put to use in the production of anti-venom, not in competition with it.

docs.title: 7.9 Women’s Knowledge and Midwifery
docs.text:
Most everyday healing happens at home, and it is mostly done by women: treating children’s fevers, coughs and diarrhoea, preparing special foods after childbirth, and knowing which plants to gather for common complaints. Early documentation often ignored this knowledge because it focused on specialist (usually male) healers. Women’s knowledge is now more widely recognised, but it is also the most easily lost when families move to towns and buy medicines in the market.

Traditional birth attendants (dāī) attended most births in rural India until recently. Many had great experience and were trusted by the women they served. They were also, in many regions, women of low caste whose work was considered polluting and poorly paid (Jeffery et al. 1989). From the 1970s the government trained large numbers of dāīs in hygienic delivery and the recognition of danger signs, and supplied them with simple delivery kits; evaluations of these programmes found limited effects on maternal deaths, which depend above all on timely access to emergency obstetric care. From the 2000s public health policy shifted strongly towards births in health facilities, supported by cash incentives under the Janani Suraksha Yojana (launched 2005), and the role of dāīs declined. Public health researchers continue to debate how their skills and trust might be used, for example in accompanying women to facilities.

Pregnancy and childbirth

Many plants are traditionally given to hasten labour, to expel the placenta or to restore the mother after birth. Some of these act on the uterus and can be dangerous. Pregnant women should not take herbal preparations without medical advice, and danger signs in pregnancy and labour (bleeding, convulsions, prolonged labour, fever) need immediate care at a health facility.

docs.title: 7.10 Animal Healing
docs.text:
Pastoral and farming communities have extensive veterinary knowledge. The Raika (Rebari) camel and sheep herders of Rajasthan, the Toda and their buffaloes in the Nilgiris, the Gaddi shepherds of Himachal Pradesh and the Gujjar buffalo herders of the Himalayan foothills have treatments for wounds, worms, bloat, lameness and skin diseases, as well as ways of judging the health of animals from their behaviour, dung and appetite. Non-governmental organisations working with pastoralists have documented this knowledge and argued that it complements, and is sometimes more accessible than, government veterinary services. Some of the plants reported in such practice are listed in Table 7.3.

Table 7.3. Some plants reported in ethnoveterinary practice (no recommendation implied) Plant Local name Reported use and caution Butea monosperma Palāś, ḍhāk Seeds given for worms in livestock Pongamia pinnata Karañj Seed oil applied to skin diseases and wounds; toxic if swallowed Azadirachta indica Neem Leaves and oil for wounds, maggots and ticks Calotropis spp. Āk, madār Latex applied to hoof and skin conditions; highly irritant Allium sativum Garlic Given for bloat and digestive upsets Datura spp. Dhatūrā External use against parasites; poisonous to animals and people

docs.title: 7.11 Disease Deities
docs.text: In much of rural India, epidemic diseases have been understood as the presence of a deity. The goddess Śītalā was associated with smallpox in northern and eastern India, and Māriyammaṉ with smallpox and other fevers in the south; offerings, songs and restrictions on the household were the response to an outbreak. Adivasi communities have their own deities of disease and protection, often worshipped at the village boundary. The eradication of smallpox, declared in 1977 for India and in 1980 worldwide, did not end the worship of these goddesses, whose role has widened to protection against illness and misfortune in general. Such beliefs coexist, for most people, with the use of vaccines and medicines; they show that religious and medical responses to illness are not simply alternatives.

docs.title: 7.12 Ritual Healing
docs.text:
Healing in Adivasi communities often combines plants with ritual: divination, offerings, songs, drumming, trance and the participation of family and neighbours. Anthropologists have long noted the psychological and social effects of such rituals. They give illness a meaning, mobilise the support of kin and community, relieve fear, and offer a course of action. Patients may well feel better as a result, especially with conditions in which stress and anxiety play a large part.

These effects are real, but they should not be overstated. Ritual cannot cure tuberculosis, malaria or diabetes, and the authority of a healer can delay effective treatment. The best outcomes come where people can use both kinds of care, and where health workers understand and respect the explanations their patients bring.

docs.title: 7.12.1 Possession and Mental Distress
docs.text: Possession by deities, spirits or the dead is a common idiom for experiences that biomedicine would classify as mental illness, as well as for religious experience that it would not. In many Adivasi and rural communities, a person who behaves strangely, falls into fits or seems overwhelmed by grief may be taken to a diviner or to a shrine known for healing, where the spirit is identified and asked what it wants. Anthropologists and psychiatrists working in India have noted that such healing can help where distress is rooted in family conflict or social pressure, and that it offers a language in which suffering can be expressed without stigma. It cannot treat serious psychiatric illness such as psychosis, and people with such illness have suffered harm when kept at shrines for long periods. Programmes that bring mental health services into rural areas have had most success when they work alongside, rather than against, local healers and the explanations people bring.

docs.title: 7.12.2 Healers and the Law
docs.text: Indian law gives folk healers no formal recognition, but it does regulate some of what they do. The Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, prohibits advertising remedies as cures for a list of diseases, and the laws against witch-hunting (Section 7.3) punish those who accuse others of witchcraft. Maharashtra’s law against black magic and harmful superstitious practices, passed in 2013 after the murder of the rationalist campaigner Narendra Dabholkar, penalises the exploitation of sick people by those who claim supernatural powers, while leaving ordinary religious practice untouched. Such laws aim to protect patients, especially women and the mentally ill, who have sometimes been chained, beaten or starved in the name of exorcism. They also raise the question of how to distinguish harmful practices from the legitimate religious and healing traditions of communities.

docs.title: 7.13 Adivasi Health Today
docs.text:
Discussion of traditional healing must be set against the health situation of Adivasi communities. The High Level Committee on tribal communities (2014) reported that Scheduled Tribes had higher infant and child mortality, higher rates of undernutrition and anaemia, and a heavier burden of malaria and tuberculosis than other social groups, and that health services in tribal areas were thinly staffed and often far away (Government of India 2014). Forested tribal districts of Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and the North-East account for a large share of India’s malaria cases. Sickle cell disease, an inherited blood disorder, is common in many communities of central, western and southern India; in 2023 the central government launched a national mission to screen for and manage it.

Some of the most effective responses have combined modern medicine with respect for local culture. In Gadchiroli, the organisation SEARCH, founded in 1986 by the physicians Abhay and Rani Bang, trained village women to care for newborn babies at home, including recognising and treating infections; a field trial published in 1999 showed a large fall in newborn deaths, and the approach was later adopted in national programmes (Bang et al. 1999). Its hospital for the Gond and other Adivasi patients of the district was built to resemble a village, with space for families to stay and for patients’ own beliefs to be respected. Other voluntary organisations in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha and the Nilgiris have built similar community health programmes, often employing Adivasi health workers who speak patients’ languages.

docs.title: 7.14 The Trade in Medicinal Plants
docs.text: Most of the medicinal plants used by India’s herbal medicine industry are still collected from the wild, very largely by Adivasi and other forest-dwelling collectors, who are paid little and have no share in the value added later. Some species have been overharvested to the point of scarcity. The National Medicinal Plants Board, set up in 2000, promotes cultivation and conservation, and the Forest Rights Act and PESA give communities ownership of minor forest produce, including medicinal plants. Making that ownership effective, with fair prices and sustainable harvesting rules, would do more to sustain folk medical knowledge than documentation alone.

docs.title: 7.15 Threats and Protection
docs.text:
Folk medical knowledge is threatened by loss of forests and access to them; by the disappearance of apprenticeship as young people move away; by the low status of healers; and by the attraction of quick biomedical remedies. It is also open to appropriation: knowledge recorded by researchers may be used commercially without the knowledge holders’ consent.

India’s Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL), established in 2001 by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research and the government department now called the Ministry of AYUSH, translates formulations from classical texts of Āyurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Yoga into formats that patent examiners can search, in order to prevent patents on known knowledge. It has had notable successes. But it covers only codified, textual knowledge; oral folk and tribal knowledge is largely outside it. The legal and ethical questions this raises are discussed in Chapters 12 and 13.

docs.title: 7.15.1 Quality and Contamination
docs.text: As folk and classical remedies are increasingly sold as packaged products, questions of quality arise that did not exist when a healer gathered fresh plants for a single patient. Two studies published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that about one in five of the Āyurvedic products tested, bought in shops in the Boston area and over the internet, contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic, in some cases at levels that could cause poisoning (Saper et al. 2004, 2008). Some contamination comes from the deliberate use of metals and minerals in certain preparations, some from poor manufacturing. Herbal products may also be adulterated with undeclared pharmaceutical drugs, or made from wrongly identified plants. These are problems of commercialised medicine rather than of village healing, but they show that “natural” is not the same as “safe”.

docs.title: 7.15.2 What Can Be Said with Confidence
docs.text:
Summing up the evidence reviewed in this chapter, a few statements can be made with confidence. First, folk healers hold a large body of knowledge about plants, the body and the social side of illness, and this knowledge is a significant cultural and scientific resource that is being lost. Second, very few folk remedies have been shown in clinical trials to be effective, and some are harmful; claims that particular remedies cure particular diseases should be treated with caution until they are tested. Third, healers often play an important part in the care of their communities, especially where health services are distant, and they can help or hinder access to effective treatment. Fourth, the communities who hold this knowledge have a right to decide how it is recorded and used, and to share in any benefits. Policies that take all four statements seriously are most likely to serve Adivasi health; the measures most often proposed are gathered in Section 14.13.

Key Points

  • Folk healing combines plants, ritual and social explanation of illness; it is distinct from classical Āyurveda.

  • Very few folk remedies have been tested clinically; laboratory activity is not proof of effectiveness, and several plants are toxic.

  • Snakebite, fractures, childbirth and serious infections need prompt care at a health facility.

  • Witchcraft accusations are the darkest side of beliefs about illness, and several states have laws against witch-hunting.

  • Adivasi health indicators are poor; respect for traditional knowledge is no substitute for good public health services.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Wujastyk (2003): translations from the classical Sanskrit medical texts.

  • Jain (1991): a reference work on plants in Indian folk medicine.

  • Vitebsky (1993): Sora shamanism and healing.

  • Bodding (1925): Santal medicine and the beliefs connected with it.

  • Mohapatra et al. (2011): the scale of snakebite deaths in India.

  • Jeffery et al. (1989): childbirth and the work of village midwives in north India.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Oral Literature, Myth and Narrative Knowledge
8.1 Oral Tradition as Knowledge
docs.text:
One Sanskrit word for literature, vāṅmaya, means “made of speech”. The Vedas themselves were transmitted orally for many centuries before they were written down. Oral tradition is not a defective form of writing; it is another way of composing, storing and transmitting knowledge, with its own techniques and its own weaknesses.

Adivasi and folk oral traditions in India include myths of the origin of the world, of people, clans and crops; epics and ballads of heroes and deities; songs for every season, task and stage of life; laments, riddles and proverbs; and the genealogies kept by bards. They carry history, law, religious knowledge and ecological observation. A. K. Ramanujan, Stuart Blackburn and other folklorists have shown that Indian folk traditions are not crude versions of the classical texts but a parallel world of literature with its own aesthetics and its own answers to the classical stories (Blackburn and Ramanujan 1986; Ramanujan 1991a).

Oral traditions keep knowledge by several means. Metre, rhythm and melody aid memory and make changes noticeable. Formulae and set scenes allow a performer to recompose a long narrative in performance. Bards, priests and genealogists are trained over years, and audiences who know the tradition correct or challenge them. Ritual and seasonal settings give each performance its meaning. Oral traditions also change: each performance adapts the tradition to its audience, and stories travel between communities and languages.

docs.title: 8.2 Genres
docs.text:
Myths are foundational narratives: how the earth was made, where people and clans came from, how humans obtained fire, grain and iron, why there is death. They state how the world is ordered and what obligations people have to deities, ancestors, animals and one another.

Legends and histories recount the deeds of ancestors, migrations, the founding of villages, wars and encounters with kings and colonial officials. For communities without written records, these narratives serve as chronicle and as evidence of land rights.

Folktales (stories told for entertainment and instruction) rehearse cleverness and folly, greed and generosity, and often turn the social order upside down: the poor youngest son outwits the king, the animal outwits the hunter.

Songs accompany dances, festivals, agricultural work, marriages and funerals. Much of the finest Adivasi poetry, such as the Santal songs translated by W. G. Archer and the Gond songs collected by Elwin and Shamrao Hivale, is lyric song (Archer 1974; Elwin and Hivale 1935).

Proverbs and riddles compress observation and judgement into memorable form. Riddles in particular test and teach knowledge of plants, animals and household objects, and riddling contests are a common entertainment at weddings and festivals.

docs.title: 8.2.1 How Proverbs and Riddles Work
docs.text:
Proverbs are short, fixed sayings used in conversation to sum up a situation, give advice or settle an argument. Their authority comes from being traditional: a speaker who quotes a proverb appeals to the community’s accumulated judgement rather than to his or her own opinion. In village councils, a well-chosen proverb can carry an argument. Many proverbs comment on farming, weather and the behaviour of animals; others on kinship, marriage, hospitality, greed and the relations between the weak and the powerful.

Riddles work differently. They describe something familiar in a strange way (an animal as a person, a household object as a living being) and challenge the listener to find the answer. They train attention to the shape, sound and behaviour of things, and they are a favourite form of play at evening gatherings and weddings. Collections of proverbs and riddles in many Adivasi languages have been published by missionaries, folklorists and, increasingly, by Adivasi scholars; the most reliable give the original text, a literal translation and an explanation of when the saying is used.

docs.title: 8.3 The Gond Tradition: Pardhans and Lingo
8.3.1 The Pardhans
docs.text: Among the Gond of central India, the hereditary bards are the Pardhans, a related community who sing the Gond myths, the stories of the clans and their deities, and clan genealogies to the accompaniment of the bowed fiddle bānā. In return they receive gifts from their Gond patrons. Shamrao Hivale’s study of the Pardhans of the upper Narmada valley (1946) remains the main account of this institution (Hivale 1946). The Pardhans’ role as keepers of Gond stories also explains why modern Gond painting emerged from Pardhan artists (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 8.3.2 Lingo
docs.text:
The most famous Gond narrative concerns Lingo, the culture hero. The first written record of it was made by the missionary Stephen Hislop in central India before 1863 and published posthumously (Hislop 1866); many versions have been recorded since (Elwin 1949). In the versions most often cited, the Gond gods (or the first Gond ancestors) have been imprisoned in a cave by the great god; Lingo, born miraculously, frees them, teaches them agriculture and music, and organises them into the exogamous clan groups, each group worshipping a set number of gods, that structure Gond marriage and ritual to this day. Among the Muria of Bastar, Lingo is also the founder of the ghoṭul, the youth dormitory (Elwin 1947).

The Lingo narrative is therefore above all a charter of Gond social organisation: it explains why clans exist, how they are grouped, and whom one may marry. It has also become a focus of Gond cultural and political revival, in which Lingo is honoured as the founder of a distinct Gond religion (Koyā Punem). Comparisons with heroes of other mythologies such as Orpheus can be suggestive, but they say more about the comparer than about the Gond.

docs.title: 8.3.3 Creation Narratives
docs.text: Gond, Baiga and other central Indian creation narratives often begin with a world of water, from which earth is brought up, sometimes by a crow or crab or earthworm, and made firm. Elwin’s collection Myths of Middle India gathers many such narratives from across the region (Elwin 1949). They frequently explain the origin of particular crops, of iron-working, of death, and of the relations between Adivasi communities and their caste Hindu neighbours.

docs.title: 8.4 Santal Oral Literature
docs.text: The Santal have one of the richest recorded oral literatures in India. In the 1870s and 1880s the Santal guru Kolean narrated the traditions of the Santal ancestors to the Norwegian missionary L. O. Skrefsrud, who published them in Santali in 1887; P. O. Bodding later edited and translated much Santal folklore (Bodding 1925). Archer’s The Hill of Flutes presents Santal poetry in its social setting (Archer 1974).

docs.title: 8.4.1 The Santal World
docs.text: In Santal religion the supreme being is Ṭhākur Jīu; the most important boṅgā (deities and spirits) include Maraṅ Buru (“the great mountain”) and Jāher Erā (“the lady of the sacred grove”), worshipped in the village grove (jāherthān) by the village priest, the nāeke. In the Santal account of creation, Ṭhākur Jīu creates a pair of birds, Hãs and Hãsil, from whose eggs the first human pair, Pilcu Hāṛām and Pilcu Buḍhī, are born; their descendants become the Santal clans.

docs.title: 8.4.2 Festivals and Songs
docs.text: The great Santal festivals are Sohrāe, the harvest festival in which cattle are honoured, and Bāhā, the flower festival of spring, when the sal trees blossom. Each has its own songs and dances. Santal song is overwhelmingly about love, marriage, separation and the beauty of the landscape; it also contains a record of history, including the hul of 1855.

docs.title: 8.4.3 Forms of Santal Song
docs.text: Santal song is organised by occasion and dance. There are songs for the great festivals, sung by men and women in separate or answering groups; songs for weddings, which include teasing exchanges between the families; songs for the dances of the young people, which change with the season; and songs for the hunt. Most are short lyrics of a few lines, sung repeatedly to a tune that fits a particular dance step, with drums and flutes. Their poetry works through images drawn from the landscape (flowering trees, rivers, birds, the moon) and through hints and allusions that listeners understand. Archer’s translations, made with Santal collaborators, give a sense of their range: love, longing, jealousy, the pain of a daughter leaving home at marriage, and occasionally the shock of encounters with outsiders (Archer 1974).

docs.title: 8.4.4 A Script of Their Own
docs.text: The Santali language was written in the Bengali, Odia, Devanagari and Roman scripts before Pandit Raghunath Murmu devised the Ol Chiki script, usually dated to 1925. Ol Chiki became a powerful symbol of Santal identity. In 2003 the 92nd Amendment to the Constitution added Santali (together with Bodo, Dogri and Maithili) to the Eighth Schedule of recognised languages.

docs.title: 8.4.5 Adivasi Scripts
docs.text:
Santali’s Ol Chiki is one of several scripts created in the twentieth century by Adivasi reformers who wished their languages to have a script of their own rather than one borrowed from a dominant neighbour. Several have since been encoded in the international Unicode standard, which allows them to be used on computers and phones. The main ones are listed in Table 8.1.

Table 8.1. Some scripts devised for Adivasi languages Script Language Creator / origin Notes Ol Chiki Santali Raghunath Murmu (usually dated 1925) Unicode 2008; widely used in education and publishing Sorang Sompeng Sora Mangei Gomango (1936) Unicode 2012 Warang Citi Ho Lako Bodra (mid-twentieth century) Unicode 2014 Masaram Gondi Gondi Munshi Mangal Singh Masaram (1918) Unicode 2017 Gunjala Gondi Gondi Manuscripts found at Gunjala village, Telangana Unicode 2018 Tolong Siki Kurukh Narayan Oraon (late twentieth century) Used in Kurukh publications

Other Adivasi languages are written in the scripts of the regional languages (Devanagari, Bengali, Odia, Telugu) or, especially in the North-East, in the Roman script introduced by missionaries. The choice of script is often a political as well as a practical question.

docs.title: 8.5 Munda and Ho Traditions
docs.text:
The Munda tradition recounts how Siṅboṅgā, the supreme deity associated with the sun, created the world and the first human beings. A central episode tells of the Asur, a people of iron-smelters whose furnaces burned day and night and scorched the earth; Siṅboṅgā, coming among them in disguise, tricks and destroys them. The narrative is recited at an important Munda ritual and has been read by scholars as a memory of the coming of iron-working and of conflict over it (Roy 1912). The Asur are also a living community of Jharkhand, one of the Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups, whose own traditions of iron-smelting survived into the twentieth century.

Munda tradition also preserves the memory of how the first lineages cleared the forest and founded villages. These clearing rights (khuṇṭkaṭṭi) were recognised in the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act of 1908 and remain central to Munda land claims (Roy 1912; Singh 1966).

docs.title: 8.6 Epics of Western India
docs.text:
Western India has a rich tradition of oral epics, some sung by and for Adivasi communities, others shared between tribal and caste communities.

Bhil versions of the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa. Bhil singers in Gujarat and Rajasthan perform their own versions of the great epics, in which the familiar characters take part in very different stories, often centred on women and on the gods of the Bhil world. The Gujarati folklorist Bhagwandas Patel recorded and published several of them; the best documented, the Bhārath of the Dungri Bhils, is described in Section 8.7. These versions are not corruptions of Vālmīki or Vyāsa but independent tellings, of the kind Ramanujan described in his essay on the “three hundred Rāmāyaṇas” (Ramanujan 1991b).

Ramanujan’s essay, which showed how the story of Rāma has been told in many different ways across languages, religions and communities, including Jain, Buddhist and folk versions, was itself the subject of controversy when it was removed from a Delhi University syllabus in 2011 after protests that it offended religious sentiment. The controversy showed that the existence of many tellings, which is a commonplace for folklorists and for the communities who sing them, can be contested in public life.

Pābūjī. The epic of Pābūjī, a Rajput hero who died defending the cattle of a woman to whom he had given his word, is sung in Rajasthan by bhopā priest-singers, often of the Nayak community, in front of a long painted scroll (phaḍ) that serves as a portable temple. Pābūjī is especially worshipped by the Raika camel-herders, who credit him with bringing camels to Rajasthan. John D. Smith’s edition and translation is the standard study (Smith 1991).

Devnārāyaṇ and Tejājī. The epic of Devnārāyaṇ, a hero-god of the Gujar herders, is sung by Gujar bhopās before a painted phaḍ even longer than Pābūjī’s; the scrolls of both epics are painted by Joshi families of Shahpura in Bhilwara district; Tejājī is a folk deity of the Jat cultivators of Rajasthan, worshipped above all as a protector against snakebite. Neither is a Bhil epic, but both show how western Indian epic traditions are tied to particular communities and livelihoods. Table 8.2 summarises the narrative traditions discussed in this chapter.

Table 8.2. Some oral narrative traditions discussed in this chapter Tradition Community and performers Content Lingo narratives Gond; sung by Pardhan bards Freeing of the gods, origin of clans and ghoṭul (Hislop 1866; Elwin 1949) Santal traditions Santal; recorded from Kolean guru Creation, clans, migrations, festivals Asur narrative Munda Destruction of the iron-smelting Asur by Siṅboṅgā (Roy 1912) Birsa songs Munda and neighbours The ulgulān of 1899–1900 (Singh 1966) Bhil Bhārath and Rāmāyaṇ Bhil; Gujarat and Rajasthan Independent versions of the epics (Patel 2012) Pābūjī Rajasthan; Nayak bhopās, Raika devotees Rajput hero, camels, a vow kept (Smith 1991) Devnārāyaṇ Gujar Hero-god of herders Candainī Chhattisgarh Love of Lorik and Candā (Flueckiger 1996) Siri Tulu-speaking coastal Karnataka; women devotees A heroine deified; possession at Siri festivals (Claus 1975; Honko 1998)

docs.title: 8.6.1 Performing the Epic: Paṇḍvānī and Gavrī
docs.text:
Two performance traditions of central and western India show how Adivasi performers have made the great epics their own. In Chhattisgarh, Paṇḍvānī is the solo narration, in song and speech, of episodes from the Mahābhārata centred on Bhīma, accompanied by a small group of musicians. Its best-known exponent, Teejan Bai, from the Pardhi community, broke the convention that women should perform only in the seated style and became famous for her vigorous standing style; she received the Padma Vibhushan in 2019.

Paṇḍvānī is usually described as a Chhattisgarhi folk form, but its roots lie partly in Adivasi tradition. The Pardhans, bards of the Gond (Section 8.3), and the Devār, a community of itinerant singers, sang Pāṇḍava stories drawn from oral lore, and among many Gond communities Bhīma is not simply a hero of the Mahābhārata but a deity, Bhīmsen or Bhīmal Pen, who is invoked in many places for rain. In these tellings Bhīma, the strong eater and fighter of the Sanskrit epic, becomes a figure of Adivasi power. Performers today distinguish two styles. In the vedamatī (“according to the text”) style the narrator, usually seated, sings and expounds a written Hindi Mahābhārata, the seventeenth-century version in dohā and caupāī verse attributed to Sabal Singh Chauhan; the style is associated with Jhaduram Devangan, a weaver who learnt the text by heart and made his name as a performer from the 1940s. In the kāpālik style the narrator draws on memory and the oral tradition, improvises, and acts out the characters on a moving stage; Teejan Bai is its most famous exponent. Students of the form have pointed out that the two labels are not neutral: once the text-based style was called “vedic”, the older oral lore came to be described as merely imaginative, a small instance of the way written and Sanskritic versions have gained authority over oral and Adivasi ones. The same tension runs through the study of the Bhil epics described below.

In southern Rajasthan, Bhil men perform the Gavrī, a ritual dance-drama in honour of the goddess, during the monsoon month of Bhādo: for about forty days troupes travel from village to village performing episodes in which deities, demons, kings, traders and tricksters appear, with the performers observing strict ritual restrictions throughout.

docs.title: 8.7 The Bhil Bhārath
docs.text: The fullest record of an Adivasi Mahābhārata is the Bhārath of the Dungri (“hill”) Bhils, who live in the Aravalli hills on both sides of the Gujarat–Rajasthan border, around Khedbrahma and Danta in north Gujarat and in the adjoining hills of southern Rajasthan. Bhagwandas Patel (b. 1943), a schoolteacher who spent several decades recording the oral literature of north Gujarat’s Adivasis, recorded the epic between 1984 and 1987 on some four hundred audio cassettes. Most episodes were taken down during actual performances; some were recorded afterwards at the singer’s convenience; and details missing from a particular performance were added after discussion with several singers. Patel published the result in Gujarati as Bhīlonuṃ Bhārath (1997); a Hindi version followed, and an English translation by Nila Shah appeared in 2012 (Patel 2012).

docs.title: 8.7.1 Editing an Oral Epic
docs.text: The way the text was made matters for how it can be read. It is not the transcript of a single performance, like the Siri epic Lauri Honko recorded from Gopala Naika (Section 8.8), but a composite established by the editor from several performances and singers. Reviewers of the English translation have noted this, and also that the translation does not print the Bhili text alongside it, so that readers without access to the Gujarati edition cannot check the wording. Folklorists are generally cautious about composite texts because they can give a single, fixed form to something that exists only in variable performances. Against this, Patel’s edition preserves a narrative that might otherwise not have been written down at all, and it was made in consultation with its singers. Like Smith’s edition of Pābūjī (Smith 1991), it is best read as one carefully made version of a living tradition, not as the tradition itself.

docs.title: 8.7.2 Performance
docs.text: According to Patel and those who have written about his work, the Bhārath is sung by specialist singers in a mixture of verse and prose, with instrumental accompaniment, and its singing is surrounded by ritual: performers observe restrictions of food and conduct before and during a recital, and episodes are sung on particular festivals and ritual occasions, including weddings and the rites that follow a death. The epic is therefore not entertainment that happens to use a famous story; for its singers and listeners it is sacred narrative, and parts of it are performed as worship. In this it resembles the community epics of Rajasthan and the South discussed in Section 8.8, and the Bhil Gavrī described above.

docs.title: 8.7.3 A Different Story
docs.text:
Readers who know the Sanskrit Mahābhārata, or its many retellings in the regional languages, will recognise the names and little else. The summary that follows draws on published accounts of the epic, which differ in detail. The Bhārath opens with a long chain of earlier births and curses, through which Śantanu and Gaṅgā come to be married, and Gaṅgā’s condition that her children be thrown into the river is set within a world of gurus, sages and rebirths quite unlike the Sanskrit frame. Kuntī and Gāndhārī are not princesses born to kings but are made by sages; the Pāṇḍavas are born to Kuntī from the gods in a sequence that differs from the Sanskrit account. Some of the episodes on which the Sanskrit epic turns are absent: there is no attempt to disrobe Draupadī, and there is no Bhagavadgītā, although Kṛṣṇa is a major character. The quarrel between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas is presented as a dispute over the division of land.

New episodes take their place. The serpent king Vāsuki, who in the Sanskrit epic is a victim of Janamejaya’s snake sacrifice, is in the Bhil epic a powerful and often triumphant figure of the underworld (pātāḷ). In one well-known episode Draupadī’s golden hair, too heavy for the earth to bear, falls into the underworld onto the sleeping Vāsuki, who comes to Hastināpur in search of its owner and becomes her lover while Arjuna, tied to the bedpost, is helpless to prevent it. Arjuna himself travels to the underworld and marries Vāsuki’s daughter. Throughout, Kuntī and Draupadī hold authority in the household and the kingdom: the Pāṇḍavas defer to their decisions, and Draupadī rebukes them in council. Several Gujarati and Indian scholars have accordingly read the Bhārath as a women’s epic. The reading has force, but it should not be pressed too far: an epic in which goddesses and queens command is not a straightforward record of the position of ordinary Bhil women, any more than the Sanskrit epic is of high-caste women’s lives.

docs.title: 8.7.4 What Kind of Text Is It?
docs.text: G. N. Devy, who founded the Bhasha Research and Publication Centre, which co-published the English translation, and its Adivasi Academy at Tejgadh in eastern Gujarat, has argued in his essays that the Bhil Bhārath is not a “vulgarisation” or folk adaptation of the Sanskrit epic, and has suggested that it may preserve an independent, even an older, line of the story; his wider case for hearing Adivasi literatures on their own terms is made in Devy (2006). The first point is well made and is the view of most folklorists: like the Bhil Rāmāyaṇa, the Gond Lingo narratives and the community epics of other regions, the Bhārath is a telling in its own right, organised around Bhil gods, Bhil ideas of kinship and land, and Bhil ritual, and it should not be measured by its distance from Vyāsa (Ramanujan 1991b). The second point is a different kind of claim. The oral Bhārath was recorded in the 1980s, and there is no means of dating its episodes; it could as well contain recent elements as ancient ones, and the absence of an episode such as the Gītā proves nothing about the age of the rest. It is safer to say that the Bhil epic shows how a story known across India has been taken over by a community and made to carry that community’s own concerns.

docs.title: 8.7.5 Patel’s Wider Record
docs.text: The Bhārath is one of several long narratives Patel recorded from the Dungri Bhils. His Bhil Rāmāyaṇa, Rōm Sītmānī Vārtā (1995), is described as the first Adivasi version of the Rāma story to be published as a book, and he also recorded heroic narratives such as the Rāṭhoḍ Vārtā, which Nila Shah has also translated into English. Together with the Rajasthani epics of Pābūjī and Devnārāyaṇ and the Gavrī of the Mewar Bhils, they show that the Aravalli region has one of the richest concentrations of oral epic in India, shared, contested and reshaped across lines of tribe and caste. Most of this material still exists in print only in Gujarati or Hindi; translation into English and, more importantly, publication in Bhili for Bhil readers remain unfinished tasks.

docs.title: 8.8 Community Epics across India
docs.text:
Pābūjī and Devnārāyaṇ belong to a much larger family. In almost every region of India, long epics in the regional languages are sung by professional bards, often over many nights, for particular castes and communities, in honour of heroes and heroines whom those communities worship as deities. The collection Oral Epics in India, edited by Stuart Blackburn, Peter Claus, Joyce Flueckiger and Susan Wadley, established the comparative study of this tradition (Blackburn et al. 1989). Its central observation is that each epic belongs to a community: it tells that community’s own story and values, is sponsored by its members, and is often performed as worship rather than as entertainment. The editors proposed a rough grouping into martial epics, whose heroes fight and die for honour, land or cattle (Pābūjī, the Ālhā of Bundelkhand and the Telugu epic of Palnāḍu are examples); sacrificial epics, more common in the south, in which the violent death of a hero or heroine leads to deification; and romantic epics centred on love and marriage, such as the story of Lorik and Candā (the Candainī) in Chhattisgarh and the Dhola of western Uttar Pradesh. The music and staging of several of these traditions are described in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya.

Two studies show how much such epics carry besides story. In the Tulu-speaking region of coastal Karnataka, the deeds of the spirit-deities (bhūta) and of the heroine Siri are sung in long oral narratives (pāḍdana). According to the epic, Siri leaves an unfaithful husband and after her death becomes a goddess; at the annual Siri festivals large numbers of women are possessed by Siri and her companions and speak with their voices. Peter Claus’s work on the Siri tradition showed how closely narrative and ritual interpret each other (Claus 1975), and the Finnish folklorist Lauri Honko later recorded and published a complete performance by a single singer, Gopala Naika, together with a study of how an oral epic becomes a written text (Honko 1998). In Chhattisgarh, Joyce Flueckiger found that the region’s genres are divided by gender as well as by caste: women’s songs such as the suā nācā (parrot-dance songs) and men’s performances of the Candainī belong to different occasions and give different views of the same social world (Flueckiger 1996).

These epics complicate the line between “tribal” and “caste” tradition. Many are sung by herders, bards and other once-mobile or low-ranked communities; their heroes are local deities rather than the gods of the Purāṇas, although Purāṇic gods often appear in them; and, like the Bhil epics and the Lingo narratives, they have often been dismissed as “folk versions” of a classical original that they do not in fact follow.

docs.title: 8.9 Song in Central India
docs.text:
Song is the most abundant form of Adivasi oral literature. In the 1930s and 1940s Elwin and Shamrao Hivale collected thousands of songs from the Gond, Baiga, Pardhan and their neighbours in central India, published in volumes such as Songs of the Forest (1935) and Folk-Songs of Chhattisgarh (1946) (Elwin and Hivale 1935; Elwin 1946). They include songs for the Karam festival, for weddings and for the ghoṭul; the dadariyā, short songs of love and teasing exchanged between young men and women in Chhattisgarh; songs of work, sowing and harvest; and laments. Their themes are love and desire, the beauty of the forest and the hardship of poverty, quarrels with officials and moneylenders, and the comedy of village life.

These songs complicate the image of Adivasi culture as solemn and sacred. They are frequently witty, sensual and irreverent, and they comment on social change: the arrival of the railway, the forest guard, the school and the market. Like Santal songs (Archer 1974), they are best read as literature, not merely as ethnographic data.

docs.title: 8.9.1 Women’s Song
docs.text: Many song genres belong especially to women: lullabies; songs sung while husking or grinding grain; wedding songs, including the songs with which women of the bride’s and groom’s families tease each other; laments at a daughter’s departure after marriage and at funerals. These songs have often been collected less carefully than men’s epics, yet they contain some of the most direct expressions of women’s experience: the hardship of work, the loneliness of the married daughter in a strange village, criticism of husbands and in-laws, and humour at the expense of men. Recent collections by women folklorists and Adivasi women writers have given them more attention. The most influential study of such songs in a caste village is Gloria Goodwin Raheja and Ann Grodzins Gold’s Listen to the Heron’s Words, on women’s songs, stories and proverbs in Rajasthan and western Uttar Pradesh. The authors argue that in their songs women do not simply accept the ideals of kinship and modesty that male and textual sources describe; they comment on them, mock them and put forward other views of marriage, sexuality and the obligations of kin (Raheja and Gold 1994). Joyce Flueckiger’s study of Chhattisgarh, mentioned above, makes a similar point about the division of genres by gender (Flueckiger 1996). Women’s songs of village India more generally are discussed in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 8.10 Oral Traditions of the North-East
docs.text:
The peoples of North-East India have rich traditions of origin and migration narratives, many of which have become central to modern ethnic identity.

  • Ao Naga: Ao tradition holds that the first ancestors emerged from the earth at Lungterok (“six stones”) near Chungliyimti, from which the Ao clans descend.

  • Khasi: according to Khasi tradition, sixteen families once lived in heaven and travelled freely between heaven and earth by a golden ladder on the peak of Sohpetbneng; seven families were on earth when the link was cut, and from them descend the Hynniewtrep (“seven huts”), the Khasi–Jaintia people. The story underlies Khasi ideas of right conduct and of the covenant between humans and God.

  • Mizo: many Mizo and related Chin and Kuki communities trace their origin to Chhinlung, a place where the ancestors emerged from beneath a great rock; the name has become a symbol of the unity of these peoples.

Christian missionaries wrote down many North-Eastern languages for the first time, in the Roman script, and the first printed literatures were largely religious. Since the mid-twentieth century, writers in these languages and in English have drawn on oral narratives to create modern literatures (Section 8.14).

docs.title: 8.11 Songs of Resistance and Memory
docs.text:
Adivasi oral traditions preserve the memory of struggles that official histories long ignored. Birsa Munda (c. 1875–1900), who led the ulgulān (great tumult) of 1899–1900 against landlords, missionaries and the colonial state, and who died in Ranchi jail, is remembered in songs across Jharkhand as Birsā Bhagavān and dhartī ābā (“father of the earth”) (Singh 1966). The Santal hul, the Bhumkal of Bastar and many local revolts are similarly remembered.
