These songs are not simply records of fact; they interpret events, and they have been revived and reworked in every subsequent movement for Adivasi rights.

Song remains a medium of protest today. Movements against dams, mines and displacement in Jharkhand, Odisha, the Narmada valley and elsewhere have produced new songs in Adivasi languages and in Hindi, sung at rallies and meetings and spread by cassettes and now mobile phones. They draw on older forms and tunes while addressing new subjects such as companies, police and the law.

docs.title: 8.11.1 Outlaw Heroes
docs.text: Some heroes of Adivasi song are remembered by the state as criminals. Tantya Bhil, who in the 1870s and 1880s raided the rich in the Nimar region of central India and was said to share his spoils with the poor, was captured and hanged at Jabalpur in 1889. The colonial press called him a dacoit; Bhil and other songs and stories in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra remember him as a protector of the poor, and he is now commemorated as a freedom fighter. The contrast between the official record and the oral tradition is typical, and shows why oral history matters for writing the history of communities who left few documents of their own.

docs.title: 8.11.2 Memory and Commemoration
docs.text: Oral memory has increasingly been joined by public commemoration. The anniversary of the Santal hul, 30 June, is observed as Hul Diwas across the Santal region; Jharkhand was created as a state on 15 November 2000, the anniversary of Birsa Munda’s birth; and since 2021 the central government has marked 15 November as Janjātīya Gaurav Divas (Tribal Pride Day). Statues, museums and school textbooks now present Adivasi leaders such as Birsa Munda, Sidhu and Kanhu, Tilka Manjhi, Rani Gaidinliu and Komaram Bheem as heroes of the freedom struggle. Historians note that such official commemoration can also simplify or redirect the meaning of the struggles: Birsa Munda’s movement was directed against landlords and missionaries as well as the British, and was also a religious movement of reform (Singh 1966).

docs.title: 8.12 Translation
docs.text: Most readers encounter Adivasi oral literature in translation, and translation raises its own problems. Early collectors often translated freely, omitting what they found obscene or obscure, adding explanations, or recasting songs in the style of English ballads. Many recorded texts were translated not directly but through an intermediary language such as Hindi. Puns, allusions, metres and the music of performance are almost impossible to carry over. Modern collections increasingly print the original-language text alongside the translation, involve speakers of the language as co-translators, and give information about the performer and the occasion, so that readers can see how a text was produced. Readers should treat older translations, including those cited in this volume, as valuable but partial representations.

docs.title: 8.13 Performance, Memory and Change
docs.text:
Oral narratives are performed in particular settings: myths at rituals, epics on festival nights, work songs in the fields, laments at funerals. In many communities certain stories may be told only at certain times of year or of day, or only by certain people. The setting is part of the meaning.

Performers combine memory and improvisation, recomposing a known story with formulae and set scenes (Section 8.1). Stuart Blackburn’s study of the Tamil bow-song tradition showed how performance itself turns the dead into deities (Blackburn 1988).

Scholarly Note: Walter Ong and “Orality”

Walter Ong’s Orality and Literacy (1982) contrasted the thought and expression of “primary oral” cultures, which he described as additive, aggregative, conservative and participatory, with those of literate cultures (Ong 1982). His book was influential, but many scholars of South Asia have criticised its sharp opposition: in India oral and written transmission have coexisted and interacted for millennia, and Adivasi communities have long lived alongside writing, even when they did not use it themselves. Oral traditions are not survivals from a pre-literate stage but a living alternative.

docs.title: 8.14 From Orality to Print: Adivasi Writing
docs.text: The twentieth and twenty-first centuries have seen a growing body of literature written by Adivasi authors, in their own languages and in Hindi, Bengali, Odia, Marathi, Malayalam, English and other languages. It draws on oral tradition and also challenges outsiders’ images of Adivasi life. Its history is not simply one of a move from speech to writing. For a long time Adivasi words reached print through missionaries, officials and ethnographers who chose what to record and how to present it; the more recent history is of Adivasi authors, editors and publishers taking those decisions themselves. Modern Indian literature in general is treated in Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā, which notes these literatures and refers to this volume for them.

docs.title: 8.14.1 The First Adivasi-Authored Texts
docs.text:
The earliest extended texts composed by Adivasis in their own languages were dictated or written for, or in collaboration with, missionaries. The traditions narrated by the Santal guru Kolean (Section 8.4) were published by Skrefsrud in Santali in 1887 and translated into English by Bodding in 1942 as Traditions and Institutions of the Santals (Bodding 1942). The work gives an account of the creation of the first pair, the wanderings of the ancestors through a sequence of named countries, the formation of the clans, and the rules of village life, marriage, the hunt and the council. It is mediated twice, by the missionary who recorded it and by the translator, and Kolean was speaking to an outsider; but it is a Santal account of the Santal past, organised by Santal categories, and it has been read by Santals themselves as a foundational text.

A few years later, in 1894, the Santal writer Ramdas Tudu “Reska” published, in the Bengali script, a book on the Santal religion and its customs usually known as the Kherwāl Bansa Dharam Puthi. It was written by a Santal for Santal and other readers, without a missionary’s frame, and it is often cited as the beginning of Santal authorship. Raghunath Murmu (1905–1982), whose Ol Chiki script is discussed above, saw the script as one part of a wider programme: he wrote primers, a grammar and plays, among them Bidu Candan, for performance in Santal villages, so that the new script would be used for a literature that people actually read and watched. Comparable work was done for Ho by Lako Bodra and for Kurukh by Narayan Oraon (Table 8.1).

docs.title: 8.14.2 Santali after Recognition
docs.text: The inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule in 2003 brought institutional support: the Sahitya Akademi, India’s national academy of letters, began to give its annual awards to books in Santali, and Santali has been taught in some schools and universities in Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha. Recognition also exposed an old difficulty. Santali literature is published in several scripts: Ol Chiki, which most Santal cultural organisations promote as the language’s own script, but also Bengali, Odia, Devanagari and the Roman script used by the missions. A reader schooled in one state may not be able to read a Santal writer from the next, and the choice of script for school textbooks and examinations has been a recurring political issue. Recognition of a language begins the decisions about it rather than ending them (Chapter 13, Section 13.10).

docs.title: 8.14.3 Writing in Hindi and the Idea of Ādivāsī Sāhitya
docs.text:
Much of the most widely read Adivasi writing is in Hindi, the language of schooling across central India. Ram Dayal Munda (1939–2011), scholar, musician and cultural leader from Jharkhand, worked to revive Munda music and dance and to build institutions for the study of tribal languages; he wrote songs and poems in Mundari, Nagpuri and Hindi. The Kharia writer Rose Kerketta (1940–2025) wrote stories and essays in Hindi and Kharia, many of them about women’s lives in the villages of Chotanagpur. The Santal poet Nirmala Putul, from Dumka, writes in Santali, and her poems are widely read in Hindi; her collection Nagāṛe kī Tarah Bajte Śabd (2004) addresses the place of Adivasi women both in their own communities and in the eyes of outsiders (Putul 2004). Jacinta Kerketta, an Oraon poet born in West Singhbhum in 1983, has published several collections of poems on Adivasi life, displacement, mining and resistance, beginning with Aṅgor (2016) (Kerketta 2016) and Jaḍoṁ kī Zamīn (2018); she writes in Hindi, and her work has been widely translated. The Munda poet Anuj Lugun belongs to the same generation.

This writing has been accompanied by a critical argument about what “Adivasi literature” (ādivāsī sāhitya) is. For most of the twentieth century Adivasi life entered Hindi and Bengali literature through non-Adivasi writers, some of them deeply committed: Mahasweta Devi’s Bengali novel on Birsa Munda, Araṇyer Adhikār (1977), and Ranendra’s Hindi novel Global Gāṁv ke Devtā (2009), on the Asur iron-smelters of the Netarhat plateau (Ranendra 2009), are examples. Adivasi critics, among them the Kharia writer and editor Vandana Tete and others associated with the Ranchi-based publishing and cultural organisations of the 2000s, argued that such books, however sympathetic, write about Adivasis rather than from within Adivasi experience. They proposed that Adivasi literature should be defined not only by the author’s identity but by a worldview: a sense of the collective rather than the individual hero, of land, forest and animals as kin rather than scenery, of continuity with oral song and story, and of a history of dispossession told by those who suffered it. A statement on Adivasi literature adopted at a gathering in Ranchi in 2014 set out such principles. Critics within the movement have warned that any fixed definition can itself become a cage, excluding writers whose subjects are urban, personal or experimental; the debate parallels earlier arguments about Dalit literature.

docs.title: 8.14.4 Other Languages
docs.text: In Marathi, an Adivasi literary movement grew from the 1980s, partly in dialogue with the Dalit literature of Maharashtra. Poets such as the Bhil activist Waharu Sonawane and Bhujang Meshram wrote of forest, migration, debt and the police, and Adivasi literary conferences (ādivāsī sāhitya sammelan) have been held regularly. In Gujarat, G. N. Devy’s Bhasha Research and Publication Centre at Vadodara (founded 1996) published a periodical in several tribal languages and set up an Adivasi Academy at Tejgadh, and Devy’s anthology Painted Words (2002) brought together translated oral and written texts from many Adivasi languages for a national readership (Devy 2002). In Malayalam, Narayan (1940–2022), of the Malayarayar community of the Idukki hills, wrote Kocharethi (1998), the first Malayalam novel by an Adivasi writer. It follows a Malayarayar family through the first half of the twentieth century, as forest land passes to settlers and moneylenders and as new religions and schooling reach the hills; it won the Kerala Sahitya Akademi award, and its English translation (2011) found a wide readership (Narayan 2011). In the North-East, where Roman-script writing in Khasi, Mizo, Ao and other languages goes back to the missions, writers such as Temsula Ao (Ao Naga), Easterine Kire (Angami) and Mamang Dai (Adi, Arunachal Pradesh) have written fiction and poetry in English rooted in the oral histories of their peoples (Ao 2006; Dai 2006) (Volume 8, Kāvya Kalpalatā).

docs.title: 8.14.5 English, Publishing and Controversy
docs.text:
Writing in English reaches the largest national and international audience, and has raised in the sharpest form the question of who may represent a community. Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar, a Santal writer and physician from Jharkhand, is the author of the novel The Mysterious Ailment of Rupi Baskey (2014), which won the Sahitya Akademi’s Yuva Puraskar for young writers, and the story collection The Adivasi Will Not Dance (2015) (Shekhar 2015). In the title story, a Santal musician refuses to perform for the President of India at the inauguration of a power plant that will displace his people. In 2017 the Jharkhand government banned the collection and suspended the author from his government post, after protests that one story portrayed Santal women in a degrading way; the ban was later withdrawn. Writers and critics, Adivasi and non-Adivasi, divided over the case: some saw a community defending its dignity against an insider’s frankness, others a state using community sentiment to silence a writer who had criticised mining and displacement.

Adivasi writers have also sought control over publication. In 2012 the Santal writer and publisher Ruby Hembrom founded adivaani in Kolkata, an Adivasi-run press publishing in English, with the declared aim of letting Adivasis document and present their own histories, cultures and literatures; its books have included bilingual editions of Jacinta Kerketta’s poems. Such ventures are small, but they mark a change from the period, described earlier in this chapter, when almost every printed record of Adivasi words was edited by someone else.

docs.title: 8.15 Endangered Traditions
docs.text:
Oral traditions depend on languages and on people willing to learn them. Among the most endangered are those of the Great Andamanese, whose languages are now remembered by only a few people; the last fluent speaker of the Bo language, Boa Sr., died in 2010. The Nihali language isolate of central India has only a small number of speakers. Many Adivasi languages with large numbers of speakers are also losing ground as children are schooled in the regional language or English and as families migrate (Chapter 13).

The loss of a tradition is not always simply decline. Communities also abandon stories and rituals they no longer believe in, or that they find demeaning, and create new ones. Documentation should respect communities’ own choices about what to keep, and for oral traditions it should record the performance, music and setting as well as the words; the general principles are set out in Chapter 13.

Key Points

  • Adivasi oral traditions include myth, epic, song, proverb, riddle and genealogy, performed by specialists and communities.

  • The Gond Lingo narrative is above all a charter of clan organisation, recorded first by Hislop and sung by Pardhan bards.

  • Santal, Munda, Bhil and North-Eastern traditions show the variety of Adivasi literature and its links to land and history.

  • Regional epics such as Pābūjī, Siri and the Candainī belong to particular communities, which sponsor them and often worship their heroes.

  • Adivasi writers and new scripts such as Ol Chiki have carried oral traditions into print and digital media; Adivasi critics now debate what makes a literature Adivasi, and Adivasi-run presses publish their own authors.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Elwin (1949): myths from many communities of central India.

  • Archer (1974): Santal poetry and its social setting.

  • Ramanujan (1991a): an anthology of Indian folktales with an influential introduction.

  • Blackburn and Ramanujan (1986): essays on Indian folklore.

  • Smith (1991): a Rajasthani oral epic, edited and translated.

  • Blackburn et al. (1989): the regional oral epics of India and the communities that sing them.

  • Patel (2012): the Mahābhārata of the Dungri Bhils, recorded and edited by Bhagwandas Patel, in English translation.

  • Ramanujan (1991b): the essay on the many tellings of the Rāma story.

  • Singh (1966): Birsa Munda and his movement.

  • Bodding (1942): the Santal traditions narrated by Kolean, in English translation.

  • Devy (2002): an anthology of oral and written Adivasi literature in translation.

  • Kerketta (2016), Putul (2004), Ao (2006) and Dai (2006): poetry and fiction by Adivasi writers from Jharkhand, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh.

  • Honko (1998): the making of a written text from a Tulu oral epic.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Folk Arts: Painting, Craft, Dance and Visual Knowledge
9.1 Introduction: Art, Ritual and Meaning
docs.text:
The white-on-earth paintings of the Warli, the crowded and brilliant panels of Mithila, the dotted and patterned animals of Pardhan Gond painters, the ritual wall paintings of the Saura and the horse-filled Pithora murals of the Rathwa and Bhilala are among the best-known visual traditions of India. Most began as ritual art: paintings made on house walls or floors for weddings, harvests, vows and the honouring of deities and ancestors. In the twentieth century many of them moved onto paper and canvas, entered markets and museums, and produced named artists of national and international reputation.

This chapter looks at these traditions both as ritual and as art. Crafts and textiles as a whole are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru, and folk and tribal music, dance and theatre in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya. It avoids two misreadings: that the images are “mere decoration”, and that every line encodes a hidden cosmological message. Painters work within shared conventions, and those conventions carry religious and social meaning; but they are also individual artists who innovate, sign their work and earn their living by it.

docs.title: 9.2 Warli Painting
docs.text: The Warli live in the hills of the northern Konkan and the Sahyadri in Maharashtra’s Thane and Palghar districts and in neighbouring Gujarat. Their traditional painting is done by women on the mud-plastered walls of the house, in white rice paste on a ground of earth or red ochre, using circles, triangles and lines: two triangles joined at the tip make a human figure.

docs.title: 9.2.1 The Chauk
docs.text: The central ritual painting is the chauk, a square frame painted for a wedding. Inside it is Pālaghaṭā, the goddess of fertility; around it are scenes of village life, dancing, farming, hunting and animals. The painting creates a sacred space for the marriage and invokes the goddess’s blessing on the couple and their household.

docs.title: 9.2.2 Scenes of Life
docs.text: Around the ritual core, Warli paintings depict the tārpā dance, in which a chain of dancers follows the player of the tārpā wind instrument; sowing, harvest and threshing; hunting and fishing; trees full of birds; and the village with its houses and animals. The images record the rhythms of the agricultural year and of community life. Yashodhara Dalmia’s study remains the fullest account of the ritual setting of these paintings (Dalmia 1988).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Jivya Soma Mashe and the New Warli Painting
docs.text: From the early 1970s, after Warli painting was noticed by officials of the government’s handicrafts programmes, artists began to paint on paper and cloth for sale. The most celebrated was Jivya Soma Mashe (1934–2018) of Ganjad in Dahanu taluka (then in Thane, now in Palghar district), a man working in what had been a women’s tradition, who developed a dense and dynamic personal style. He was awarded the Padma Shri in 2011. Warli motifs are now used widely in textiles, advertising and decoration, often without any benefit to Warli artists. This raises questions of recognition and intellectual property, which are discussed below.

docs.title: 9.3 Mithila Painting
docs.text: Mithila (Madhubani) painting of northern Bihar is a caste-society tradition rather than an Adivasi one, and its history as a craft (the wall paintings of the nuptial chamber, kohbar, seen by W. G. Archer after the earthquake of 1934, and the move to paper during the drought of the late 1960s) is told in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru. It belongs here for what it shows about caste and style. Brahmin women developed the brightly coloured bharnī (filled) style with mythological subjects, and Kayastha women the fine-line kachnī style; from the 1970s women of the Dusadh and other Dalit communities created their own styles, drawing on tattoo designs (godnā) and on the epic of their hero Raja Salhesh. The painter Jagdamba Devi received the Padma Shri in 1975, and Sita Devi, Ganga Devi, Mahasundari Devi and Baua Devi later became widely known. The Dalit painters’ achievement challenged the assumption that the tradition belonged only to upper-caste households, and shows how folk art changes with the social position of those who make it.

docs.title: 9.4 Pardhan Gond Painting
docs.text:
Modern Gond painting begins with Jangarh Singh Shyam (c. 1962–2001), a Pardhan Gond from Patangarh in Mandla (now Dindori) district of Madhya Pradesh. In the early 1980s he was discovered by a team led by the artist J. Swaminathan, who was collecting tribal and folk art for the new Bharat Bhavan arts centre in Bhopal. Jangarh moved to Bhopal and, working first with poster colours and then with acrylics on paper and canvas, created a powerful new idiom from the motifs of Gond wall painting, tattoo and the stories the Pardhans sang. His work was exhibited in India and abroad, including at the Centre Pompidou in Paris in 1989. He died in 2001 in Japan, where he had gone to work at a museum.

Jangarh’s style, sometimes called Jangarh kalam, was taken up by relatives and others from Patangarh and neighbouring villages, among them his wife Nankusia Shyam, Bhajju Shyam, Venkat Raman Singh Shyam, Ram Singh Urveti and Durga Bai Vyam. Characteristic features are large flat forms of animals, trees and deities filled with dense patterns of dots, dashes and lines, each artist developing a personal pattern as a kind of signature.

Pardhan Gond artists have taken their art in new directions. Bhajju Shyam’s The London Jungle Book (2004) depicts London as seen by a Gond artist on his first journey abroad (Shyam et al. 2004). Durga Bai Vyam and Subhash Vyam illustrated Bhimayana (2011), a graphic biography of B. R. Ambedkar that turned Gond painting to the depiction of caste discrimination (Natarajan and Anand 2011).

docs.title: 9.5 Saura Wall Paintings
docs.text: The Sora (Saura) of the hills of southern Odisha paint ritual pictures called iḍital on the walls of their houses. They are made at the request of a shaman, usually to honour or placate a deity or one of the dead, and depict figures of people, horses, elephants, trees, the sun and moon, and scenes of ritual within a framed space. Elwin described them as “icons” and recorded many in his study of Saora religion (Elwin 1955, 1951); Piers Vitebsky places them in the context of the Sora’s continuing conversation with their dead (Vitebsky 1993). The paintings are addressed as much to the spirit world as to human viewers.

docs.title: 9.6 Pithora and Bhil Painting
docs.text:
The Pithora paintings of the Rathwa, Bhilala and related communities of eastern Gujarat and western Madhya Pradesh are large, brightly coloured murals painted on the inner walls of houses in fulfilment of a vow to the deity Baba Pithora, for example after recovery from illness or the birth of a child. They are painted by specialist painters (lakhārā) and consecrated by the priest (baḍvā), who reads the painting and recites the associated narrative. Horses, the mounts of the gods, dominate the composition, together with deities, animals, people and, increasingly, modern objects such as aeroplanes and motorcycles.

Bhil painters have also developed new styles on paper and canvas. Bhuri Bai, a Bhil artist from Jhabua district who began painting at Bharat Bhavan in the 1980s, became one of the best-known Adivasi artists in India and received the Padma Shri in 2021.

docs.title: 9.7 Other Wall-Painting Traditions
docs.text: In the Hazaribagh region of Jharkhand, women of several communities paint the mud walls of their houses with sohrāī paintings at the harvest festival and with khovar paintings, made by scratching through layers of coloured earth, for weddings. In Odisha and Chhattisgarh, house walls are decorated with relief and painting at festivals. These traditions are mostly anonymous, ephemeral (renewed each year) and made by women; they have only recently been studied and marketed.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Painted Scrolls for the Santal
docs.text: In the Santal country of Jharkhand and West Bengal, a community of travelling scroll painters known as jādu paṭuā made painted scrolls for Santal patrons, illustrating the Santal account of creation, the origin of the clans and the fate of the soul after death. Their most striking practice, described by twentieth-century observers, was the “eye-giving” picture (cakṣudān paṭ) of a person who had recently died: the painter brought the bereaved family a picture of the dead person without pupils in the eyes and, on receiving a payment, painted them in, which was believed to allow the soul to find its way. The jādu paṭuā were not Santals, and their art shows the close exchanges between Adivasi patrons and caste specialists in eastern India.

docs.title: 9.8 Metal, Clay and Body: Craft Traditions
9.8.1 Iron-Smelting: Asur and Agaria
docs.text:
Iron-working is an old craft of forest India, and two Adivasi communities of central and eastern India were known above all as smelters: the Asur of the Netarhat plateau and neighbouring hills of Jharkhand, and the Agaria of the Maikal hills and adjoining regions of central India. Elwin’s monograph on the Agaria, written when smelting was still practised, describes the craft and the myths attached to it (Elwin 1942).

The smelters dug iron ore from surface deposits, roasted and broke it, and smelted it with charcoal in small clay furnaces, the draught supplied by bellows worked by hand or foot. The product was a spongy bloom of iron mixed with slag, which was reheated and hammered to drive out the slag before it could be forged into tools. The work required knowledge of which ores and which woods to use, how to build and line a furnace, how to control the draught and how long to fire. Smelting was household work, in which gathering ore and charcoal and working the bellows were shared among its members. The process belongs to the general family of bloomery smelting whose history in the subcontinent, and the archaeometallurgical evidence for it, are discussed in Volume 14, Rasāyana.

The craft carried meaning as well as technique. Among the Agaria, Elwin recorded myths in which the first smelters’ furnaces scorch the earth until a deity destroys them, a story close to the Munda narrative of the Asur and Siṅboṅgā (Section 8.5); the furnace and the bellows were treated with ritual care. The smelters also had a recognised place in the village economy, exchanging iron and tools with cultivators for grain.

Bloomery smelting declined from the late nineteenth century. Cheap imported and factory iron undercut village iron; colonial forest law restricted the cutting of trees for charcoal; and in parts of central India furnaces were taxed (Elwin 1942). By the mid-twentieth century most Agaria and Asur families had turned to cultivation, labour or blacksmithing with bought iron. The Asur are now listed as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, and their history has been taken up in Hindi fiction (Section 8.14). A technical knowledge can thus disappear within two generations once its raw materials and its market are taken away, even while the community that held it survives.

docs.title: 9.8.2 Iron and Bamboo Today
docs.text: In Bastar, blacksmiths forge wrought-iron lamps, figures of deities, horsemen and animals, which, like Dhokra brass, are now made largely for sale. In North-East India, bamboo and cane are the basic materials of daily life: houses, floors, baskets, mats, fish traps, containers, hats and furniture are made from them, and the knowledge of selecting, splitting, weaving and treating bamboo is shared by men and women in every village.

docs.title: 9.8.3 Dhokra, Terracotta and Pottery
docs.text: Dhokra, the lost-wax brass casting of itinerant and settled craft communities in Bastar, Odisha, Jharkhand and West Bengal, made figures of deities, animals, lamps and measuring bowls for Adivasi patrons and their shrines before it found a wider market; its technique is described in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru. In Bastar, potters (kumhār) make the terracotta horses, elephants and other figures that Gond, Halba and other communities offer at the shrines of village and clan deities, where large groups of such horses accumulate over the years. The hand-built black stone-and-clay pots of the Tangkhul Naga village of Longpi in Manipur are another case of a community craft that has found new buyers far from home.

docs.title: 9.8.4 Weaving
docs.text: Textiles carry social information, and weaving traditions of Adivasi India are particularly rich in the North-East. Among the Naga peoples each community, and often each village, has its own repertoire of shawl designs, worn by men and women according to age, status and achievement; some designs were reserved for men who had distinguished themselves in war or had given the great “feasts of merit”, such as the Ao warrior’s shawl (tsungkotepsu). Weaving on the back-strap loin loom has traditionally been women’s work. Bodo women weave the dokhonā, the wrapped garment of Bodo women, on looms kept in almost every household; Mizo women weave the puan, whose patterns identify occasions and sometimes communities. In the Nilgiris, Toda women embroider the white cotton cloak (puthkuli) worn by men and women with bands of red and black geometric patterns, worked by counting threads rather than following a drawn design; the cloak is worn on ritual occasions and at funerals. In central and eastern India, most cloth worn by Adivasis was traditionally woven for them by specialist weaving castes. At Kotpad in the Koraput district of Odisha, weavers of the Mirgan community weave cotton saris and shawls dyed with the red of the āl tree (Morinda) root, worn especially by Adivasi women of the region; the cloth has received Geographical Indication registration. As with painting, weaving has moved between the household, the local market and national and international markets, with mixed results for the weavers.

docs.title: 9.8.5 Tattoo
docs.text: Tattooing (godnā) was widespread among women of central Indian communities such as the Baiga, Gond and Korku, as well as among many castes. Tattoos were applied in stages from girlhood to marriage by specialist women, using needles and lampblack or plant pigments. Elwin recorded Baiga beliefs about tattoos, among them the widespread belief that tattoos, unlike ornaments, go with a woman after death (Elwin 1939). Among some North-East communities, facial and body tattoos marked clan, status and achievement; among the Konyak Naga, facial tattoos were associated with head-hunting and are now borne only by the oldest generation. Among the Apatani of Arunachal Pradesh, women once wore large nose plugs and facial tattoos; the practice was abandoned from the 1970s, and today only older women bear these marks. Tattooing in these forms has largely ceased, partly because of missionary and reformist disapproval and partly because younger women prefer not to be marked.

docs.title: 9.9 The House and the Village
docs.text:
Architecture is among the most visible forms of Adivasi knowledge. Houses are built from local materials (mud, wood, bamboo, thatch, stone) by the household and its neighbours, using techniques suited to the climate and to the community’s way of life.

  • Santal houses have thick mud walls, often painted in bands of white, black and red earth and sometimes decorated with relief designs, set around a clean courtyard; the walls are renewed before the major festivals.

  • Toda houses, grouped in small hamlets (mund), were half-barrel-shaped huts of bamboo and thatch, with a very small entrance through which one had to crawl, and the Toda dairy-temples had a similar form; Rivers described them in his study of 1906 (Rivers 1906).

  • Naga villages were traditionally built on hilltops for defence, around large houses and the morung or men’s house (Section 11.12).

  • Khasi houses were traditionally oval in plan, with stone plinths and thatched roofs suited to the heavy rainfall of the hills (Gurdon 1907).

  • Apatani villages are dense clusters of houses on stilts, surrounded by the terraced fields and bamboo groves of the valley (Fürer-Haimendorf 1962).

Wood carving was highly developed among the Naga (Hutton 1921; Mills 1926). The posts, beams and façades of morungs and chiefs’ houses, especially among the Konyak, were carved with figures of hornbills, mithun heads, tigers, human figures and heads, which recorded the status, feasts and exploits of the village and its men. Log drums, house posts and grave effigies were carved by specialists. With the end of head-hunting and the spread of Christianity, much carving lost its ritual meaning, and many fine pieces were removed to museums; carving continues today for churches, public buildings and the market.

Government housing programmes have often replaced these houses with concrete structures that are hotter in summer, colder in winter and require purchased materials. Architects and community organisations have argued for housing designs that build on local materials and knowledge, and the Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya in Bhopal preserves full-scale examples of Adivasi houses from many regions, built by members of the communities.

docs.title: 9.10.1 Chhau
docs.text: Chhau is a dance tradition of eastern India with three main styles: Purulia (West Bengal) and Seraikela (Jharkhand), in which dancers wear masks, and Mayurbhanj (Odisha), which is performed without masks. It combines martial movements with stories from the epics and Purāṇas, and was inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. The masks, especially the large papier-mâché and clay masks of Purulia, are made by specialist mask-makers in villages such as Charida.

docs.title: 9.10.2 Dance in Adivasi Life
docs.text:
Dance is part of almost every festival, ritual and celebration in Adivasi life, and is usually communal rather than a performance by specialists for an audience. Some examples (see also Table 9.1):

  • Karam (Karmā): danced across Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha by Oraon, Munda, Gond, Baiga and many others around a branch of the karam tree planted in the village during the monsoon month of Bhādo, with prayers for good crops and the welfare of brothers and sisters.

  • Gaur dance: danced by the Maria of Bastar, whom Grigson called “Bison-horn Maria” after their headdresses of gaur (Indian bison) horns, feathers and cowries (Grigson 1938).

  • Bihu: the festivals of Assam (Rongāli or Bohāg Bihu in April, Kongāli or Kāti Bihu in October, Bhogāli or Māgh Bihu in January) are shared by Assamese and many tribal communities, such as the Bodo, whose spring festival is Bwisāgu, and the Mising, whose spring agricultural festival is Ali-Āye-Ligaṅ.

  • Cheraw: the Mizo bamboo dance, in which dancers step in and out of bamboo poles clapped together in rhythm.

Table 9.1. Some Adivasi and folk dances Dance Communities / region Occasion Karam Oraon, Munda, Gond and others; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha Karam festival in the monsoon Tārpā dance Warli, Kokna; Maharashtra Harvest and festivals Gaur dance Maria Gond; Bastar Festivals and weddings (Grigson 1938) Sohrāe and Bāhā dances Santal Harvest and spring festivals Chhau Purulia, Seraikela, Mayurbhanj Spring festival (Caitra Parva) Bihu Assamese, Bodo, Mising and others Seasonal festivals Cheraw Mizo Festivals

docs.title: 9.11 Music and Instruments
docs.text:
Music accompanies festival dance, ritual, work and courtship in Adivasi life, and its instruments and repertoires are independent of the classical saṅgīta codified in texts such as the Nāṭyaśāstra and the Saṅgītaratnākara; folk and tribal music as a whole is surveyed in Volume 9, Saṅgīta–Nāṭya. Drums are central. In Jharkhand and neighbouring regions the māndar, a double-headed clay-bodied drum, accompanies the dances of the Oraon, Munda and others; Santal music uses the large kettledrum tamak’ and the barrel drum tumdak’. In Nagaland the great log drums carved from single tree trunks, found in Konyak, Ao and other villages, were used to summon and signal as well as for music. The Warli tārpā leads a chain of dancers who follow the player’s movements, a scene often painted on Warli walls, and the Pardhans sing the Gond narratives and clan genealogies to the bānā (Chapter 8). Table 9.2 lists some of these instruments.

Table 9.2. Some instruments of Adivasi and folk music Instrument Community / region Description Māndar Oraon, Munda and others; Jharkhand Double-headed drum, clay body Tamak’, tumdak’ Santal Large kettledrum; barrel drum Bānā Pardhan Gond; central India Bowed fiddle used for Gond epic and genealogy (Hivale 1946) Tārpā Warli and Kokna; Maharashtra Wind instrument of gourd and bamboo leading the dance Dhodro banam Santal Bowed lute Pepā Assam Buffalo-horn pipe, played in Bihu Rāvaṇhatthā Rajasthan (Bhopa performers) Bowed fiddle accompanying the Pābūjī epic (Smith 1991) Log drum Konyak, Ao and other Naga villages Hollowed tree trunk, struck with beaters

docs.title: 9.12 Music and Performance Today
docs.text: Adivasi music and dance are not only village traditions. In Jharkhand, songs in Nagpuri, Kurukh, Mundari and Santali circulate on cassettes, discs and now online video, and a Santali film and music industry has developed. In Nagaland, the state government’s Hornbill Festival, held each December since 2000 and since 2003 at the Naga Heritage Village at Kisama near Kohima, presents the dances, songs, games and crafts of the Naga communities to visitors. Musicians such as the Tetseo Sisters, who perform the polyphonic songs (li) of the Chakhesang Naga, and many rock, hip-hop and folk-fusion groups across the North-East combine traditional songs with new forms. Festivals of this kind have been criticised for turning culture into spectacle, but they have also given young people new reasons to learn the songs and dances of their communities.

docs.title: 9.13 Artists, Markets and Rights
docs.text:
The movement of ritual art into markets has transformed it. It has given artists, many of them women and many from communities with few other sources of cash income, a livelihood and public recognition; it has also produced new styles, subjects and individual careers. At the same time it raises difficult questions:

  • Authorship: art that was once anonymous and communal is now signed. Who owns a tradition: the community, the families who practise it, or the individual artist?

  • Copying: designs are copied by machine printing and by non-community painters and sold as “Warli” or “Gond” art, often more cheaply than the work of the artists themselves.

  • Middlemen and prices: the gap between what artists are paid and the price of their work in city galleries remains large.

  • Context: a painting made for a wedding wall and one made for a gallery are different objects, and both are genuine work of the tradition; but the ritual knowledge behind the first may not survive if only the second is valued.

Institutions have played an important part in this history. Bharat Bhavan in Bhopal, opened in 1982, displayed Adivasi and folk art alongside modern Indian art in its museum, Roopankar, treating Jangarh Singh Shyam, Bhuri Bai and others as contemporary artists rather than as anonymous craftspeople. The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya, also in Bhopal, invited Adivasi builders and artists from across India to construct houses, shrines and installations in its open-air exhibitions. Non-governmental organisations, publishers such as Tara Books in Chennai, and galleries in India and abroad have helped artists to reach new audiences, sometimes with fair terms and sometimes not.

Geographical Indication registration, which protects the name of a product associated with a place, has been obtained for several folk arts, including Madhubani painting. It can help against misleading labelling, but it does not by itself secure fair prices or protect individual artists (Chapter 12).

The most useful way to understand these arts is through the work and words of the artists themselves: in exhibitions, in books such as The London Jungle Book, and in the growing number of interviews and memoirs in which painters describe how they learned, what their images mean to them, and how their art has changed.

Key Points

  • Warli, Mithila, Pardhan Gond, Saura and Pithora painting began as ritual art and became contemporary art with named artists.

  • Caste and gender shape who makes art and how it is valued, as the Dalit painters of Mithila show.

  • Craft traditions such as Dhokra casting, pottery, weaving and tattoo, and the drums and pipes of Adivasi music, carry technical and social knowledge.

  • Markets have brought income and recognition but also copying, unfair prices and loss of ritual context.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Elwin (1951): an early study of tribal art in central India.

  • Shyam et al. (2004): a Pardhan Gond artist’s vision of London.

  • Grigson (1938): the Maria of Bastar, including their dances.

  • Dalmia (1988): Warli painting and its ritual setting.

  • Elwin (1942): the Agaria iron-smelters and their myths.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Village and Folk Knowledge beyond the Adivasi World
10.1 Folk Knowledge in a Caste Society
docs.text:
Most of the people who farm, herd, fish and make things in rural India are not Adivasis. They live in villages organised by caste, and their knowledge, like that of Adivasi communities, is held mainly in practice and in speech. It is the “folk” half of this volume’s title (Section 1.2). Earlier chapters have already met parts of it: the water systems of caste villages (Chapter 4), the rain calendar and the proverbs of Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī (Chapter 6), the bone-setters, midwives and disease goddesses of village medicine (Chapter 7), the community epics of Rajasthan and the south (Chapter 8) and Mithila painting (Chapter 9). This chapter looks at this knowledge as a whole, through the people who hold it: cultivators, herders, fishers, artisans, Dalit specialists, priests of the village goddess, bards and the women who sing at the grindstone and in the fields.

Two features set it apart from the Adivasi knowledge described elsewhere in this book. The first is caste. In a caste village, knowledge is distributed by birth: the potter’s son learns the wheel, the barber’s son the razor and the rites at which barbers serve, the drummer’s son the drum. Hereditary transmission kept skills alive across generations, but it also fenced them in. Some kinds of knowledge were reserved for some castes, and others, such as the handling of hides or the dead, were imposed on the lowest castes and despised with them. Any account of village knowledge that praises the skill and ignores the fence repeats the error that Chapter 4 found in romantic accounts of village tanks.

The second is the closeness of village knowledge to the textual tradition. Village priests use the pañcāṅga; farmers name the rains after the nakṣatras; the epics of Rāma and the Pāṇḍavas are sung in village versions. Folklorists have shown that this closeness does not make village knowledge a copy of the texts. A. K. Ramanujan, Stuart Blackburn and their colleagues described the relation as a conversation in which oral and written traditions borrow from, answer and sometimes mock each other (Blackburn and Ramanujan 1986). The encyclopedia of South Asian folklore edited by Margaret Mills, Peter Claus and Sarah Diamond gives a sense of its range across the region (Mills et al. 2003).

docs.title: 10.2 Cultivators
docs.text:
Peasant farming is the largest body of folk knowledge in India, and its history is told in Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna. Its main features can be summarised here. Farmers classify soils by colour, texture, depth and water-holding capacity, and match crops and varieties to each; they sow mixtures of cereals, pulses and oilseeds that spread risk and maintain fertility; they select and store their own seed; and they time their work by the rains, the stars and the flowering of trees. When the agricultural chemist J. A. Voelcker toured India for the government in 1889–91, he concluded that Indian cultivators were in many respects as skilled as British farmers, and that their main difficulties were shortages of water, manure, fuel and credit rather than ignorance (Voelcker 1893).

Farmers’ knowledge has its own theory as well as its own practice. In a village of western Uttar Pradesh in the 1980s, the anthropologist Akhil Gupta found that farmers described soils, crops, fertilisers and weather in the language of “hot” and “cold” qualities and of balance, a language shared with ideas about food and the body. Chemical fertilisers, for example, were judged “hot” and thought to need balancing. Gupta argued that this was not a survival of ignorance but a coherent way of understanding the new technology of the Green Revolution, which farmers adopted and judged on their own terms (Gupta 1998).

Much of this knowledge is stored in sayings. In the Hindi-speaking north they are attributed to Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī (Section 6.2); in Bengal to Khanā, a legendary woman astrologer; and in every region there are rhymes about which crop to sow after which rain, how to judge a bullock and what a red sky at evening means. Their reliability varies. Many encode real experience of local soils and seasons; others are matters of luck or belief. They should be read as records of what farmers observed and valued, not as forecasts.

The Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s replaced many local varieties with high-yielding ones that needed irrigation, fertiliser and pesticide. It raised yields of wheat and rice greatly and ended the threat of famine in much of India; it also made farmers dependent on purchased inputs and made much local seed knowledge redundant. Movements for the revival of local seed and of millets, such as the Deccan Development Society’s work with Dalit women farmers in Telangana (Section 5.11), are attempts to recover what was lost without giving up what was gained.

docs.title: 10.3 Herders
docs.text:
Pastoralists of many castes, the Raika (Rebari) and Gujar of Rajasthan and Gujarat, the Dhangar of the Deccan, the Gaddi of Himachal Pradesh and the Kuruba of Karnataka among them, hold a knowledge of animals, grass and routes that settled farmers lack. Some are Scheduled Tribes; most are not. Their breeding of animals suited to heat, drought or mountain pasture, and their care of sick animals, are described in Sections 2.15 and 7.10.

Arun Agrawal’s study of Raika shepherds who migrate each year with their flocks from western Rajasthan shows that their knowledge is as much social as ecological. Households travel together in camps that decide jointly on routes, on where to halt and on the division of work, and that negotiate with farmers for the right to graze harvested fields in exchange for manure. Agrawal argues that these decisions are made through a skilled combination of leadership and consultation, and that the herders’ success depends on reading markets and politics as closely as pasture (Agrawal 1999). As fields have been irrigated and commons enclosed, the routes have become harder to use, and many herding families have settled or sent their young people to other work.

docs.title: 10.4 Fishers
docs.text:
India’s coastal fishing communities, the Mukkuvar and Paravar of the far south, the Koli of the western coast, the Pattanavar of the Coromandel coast and many others, hold a knowledge of the sea that is among the most exact in rural India. It includes the location of fishing grounds and reefs, found far from land by lining up landmarks on the shore; the habits and seasons of fish; the currents, winds and swells of the monsoon seas; and the building and handling of boats suited to surf beaches without harbours. The kaṭṭumaram of the Coromandel coast, a raft of logs lashed together, gave English the word “catamaran”.

Kalpana Ram’s study of Mukkuvar women on the coast of Kanyakumari shows the social side of this knowledge. Men go to sea; women trade fish, manage household money and credit, and hold the networks on which the family depends ashore, and a Catholic parish organisation shapes much of village life (Ram 1991). Ajantha Subramanian’s history of the same coast traces how the Mukkuvar have claimed rights over their stretch of sea, against mechanised trawlers from outside, against the state and sometimes against the church, and how they have used both custom and the language of citizenship to do so (Subramanian 2009). The conflict between small-scale fishers and trawlers, which began with the mechanisation of fishing from the 1950s and 1960s, led to strikes and to a fishworkers’ movement in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and seasonal bans on trawling during the monsoon breeding season were introduced in Kerala from the late 1980s. Fishers’ knowledge of fish seasons was one of the arguments for those bans.

Fishers also live with the most dangerous weather on the coast. Their own reading of wind and swell, and the local knowledge of safe places described in Section 6.6, are now combined with forecasts broadcast by radio and mobile phone, which have made going to sea less dangerous than it was a generation ago.

docs.title: 10.5 Artisans and the Village Economy
docs.text:
In the classic picture of the north Indian village drawn by the missionary William Wiser in the 1930s, potters, carpenters, blacksmiths, barbers, washermen, leatherworkers and others served the landowning families under hereditary arrangements, receiving fixed shares of grain at harvest and gifts at festivals in return for their work. Wiser called this the jajmānī system (Wiser 1936). Later scholars have questioned how far it was ever a single system, and how far it described an ideal more than a practice; Susan Wadley’s restudy of Wiser’s village over sixty years shows how money wages, migration and politics have dissolved most of these ties (Wadley 1994). But the picture captures something real: in a caste village, craft knowledge was hereditary, learned within the family from childhood, and tied to a place in a system of obligation.

The crafts themselves, pottery, metalwork, carpentry, weaving, dyeing, leather and the rest, are described in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru. What matters for this chapter is the form of the knowledge. Much of it is tacit: the potter’s judgement of clay and fire, the smith’s reading of the colour of hot iron, the weaver’s sense of tension in the warp. It was learned by watching and doing, not from instruction, and it was protected by the fact that outsiders could not easily acquire it. When factory goods undercut village crafts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, this knowledge did not simply disappear; much of it moved into small workshops in towns, into repair trades and into the craft revival, but the hereditary link between knowledge and caste was loosened.

docs.title: 10.6 Dalit Knowledge
docs.text:
Some of the most important folk knowledge in India has been held by Dalit communities, and it has been doubly devalued: as unlettered knowledge, and as the knowledge of castes regarded as polluting. Leatherworkers knew how to flay, tan and work hides, and supplied the village with water bags, harness, sandals and the heads of drums (Volume 17). Dalit drummers played at weddings, funerals and festivals, and in Tamil Nadu the frame drum (paṟai), long a mark of the low status of those who played it, has become in recent decades a symbol of Dalit pride; Zoe Sherinian has studied how Dalit Christian musicians made it part of a theology of liberation (Sherinian 2014). In much of north India the midwives who attended births were women of low or Dalit castes, valued for their skill but regarded as polluted by the work, as Patricia Jeffery and her colleagues showed for western Uttar Pradesh (Jeffery et al. 1989). In Maharashtra the Mahars, as village servants, were watchmen, messengers and keepers of the village’s knowledge of its boundaries, called as witnesses when boundaries were disputed (Zelliot 1992).

Dalit thinkers have argued that this knowledge deserves recognition as knowledge. Kancha Ilaiah’s Why I Am Not a Hindu (1996) contrasted the productive skills of the labouring castes, in farming, herding, leatherwork, pottery and washing, with a Brahmanical tradition that, in his account, despised labour and claimed knowledge for itself (Ilaiah 1996). His argument has been criticised for idealising the labouring castes and for its sweeping picture of Brahmanical thought, but it put a real question on the agenda. Gopal Guru and Sundar Sarukkai have pursued that question in philosophical terms, asking why Dalits have so often been treated as sources of experience to be studied rather than as theorists in their own right (Guru and Sarukkai 2012). Their question applies to this whole volume, which describes the knowledge of others largely from published scholarship.

B. R. Ambedkar’s campaigns, among them the Mahad satyāgraha of 1927 for the right of Dalits to draw water from a public tank (Section 4.11), and the anti-caste movements that followed, also changed the relation between Dalits and inherited occupations. Many Dalits have deliberately abandoned hereditary work, such as the removal of dead animals, as a step towards dignity, even where it meant giving up a skill. That choice is part of the history of folk knowledge too: not every knowledge that disappears is a loss to those who once carried it.

docs.title: 10.7 The Village Goddess and Her Specialists
docs.text:
The religion of the village is a body of knowledge in its own right. In much of south India, as the missionary bishop Henry Whitehead described early in the twentieth century, each village had its own goddesses (grāmadevatā), worshipped not by Brahmin priests but by priests from other castes, with animal sacrifice at the great festivals and with a part for Dalit drummers and servants in the rites (Whitehead 1916). The goddess protects the village from epidemic and misfortune; her festival marks its boundaries and renews its unity, while also displaying its hierarchy. The goddesses of smallpox and fever, Śītalā in the north and Māriyammaṉ in the south, are discussed in Section 7.11.

Village religion also has its specialists of possession and healing. In Tamil Nadu the cult of Draupadī as a village goddess, studied by Alf Hiltebeitel, combines a local retelling of the Mahābhārata, performed over many nights in street theatre, with a firewalk in which devotees cross a bed of embers; its main patrons are the Vanniyar, a large cultivating caste (Hiltebeitel 1988). Shrines of hero-gods such as Tejājī in Rajasthan (Section 8.6) and of the snake goddess Manasā in Bengal are places where snakebite victims are taken and where possessed mediums speak for the deity. Possession, as Chapter 7 explains, can offer a language for distress, and it can also delay treatment; both are part of the picture.

docs.title: 10.8 Bards, Genealogists and Epics
docs.text:
Caste society had its own keepers of memory. In Gujarat and Rajasthan, hereditary genealogists, the Bāroṭs, Bhāṭs and Cāraṇs, kept written registers of the births, marriages and deaths of their patron families and visited them periodically to bring the record up to date and to recite the family’s origin and history. A. M. Shah and R. G. Shroff showed in the 1950s that these genealogists were also mythographers, who supplied their patrons with legends of descent that supported claims to status (Shah and Shroff 1958). Their records were used to settle disputes over marriage and inheritance, and they show how oral and written memory worked together in village India.

The community epics introduced in Chapter 8 belong mostly to this caste world. In Andhra Pradesh the epic of the heroes of Palnāḍu, about a war between related ruling houses, is sung by bards for the castes that claim descent from its heroes; Gene Roghair published a study and translation, and Velcheru Narayana Rao showed that each Telugu folk epic belongs to particular castes, whose values and place in the social order it expresses (Roghair 1982; Blackburn and Ramanujan 1986). In the Kongu region of Tamil Nadu, Brenda Beck recorded the story of the twin brothers and their sister known as the Annanmār Katai, the epic of a cultivating caste (Beck 1982). In western Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, Susan Wadley studied Dhola, the epic of Raja Nal, sung mostly by singers of low caste for mixed village audiences (Wadley 2004). These epics carry knowledge of local history, of land and of kinship, and they are often the form in which a caste remembers who it is.

docs.title: 10.9 Women’s Songs, Proverbs and Riddles
docs.text:
Women’s song is the largest and least recorded part of village oral literature. Women sing while grinding grain at the hand mill, while transplanting rice, at weddings, at births and at deaths. In Maharashtra the grinding songs (ovī) sung at the hand mill form an enormous body of short verses on work, family, devotion and the hardships of married life, and collectors have recorded them in very large numbers. Gloria Goodwin Raheja and Ann Grodzins Gold showed for north India that such songs do not simply repeat the ideals of kinship that men and texts describe; they comment on them, complain of them and sometimes mock them (Raheja and Gold 1994). The songs are discussed further in Section 8.9.

Proverbs and riddles, whose working is described in Section 8.2, are as abundant in caste villages as among Adivasis. Many concern farming and weather; many others concern caste and kinship, and some of these carry the prejudices of the village, about women, about lower castes and about outsiders. Collections that print them without comment preserve the prejudice along with the wit, and a careful reader needs to notice both.

docs.title: 10.10 Change and Survival
docs.text:
Village folk knowledge has been changing for as long as it has been recorded. The forces at work are the same as for Adivasi knowledge: migration to towns, schooling in standard languages, the market in seeds, fertilisers and factory goods, the decline of hereditary occupations and new media. But the loss is not uniform. Some knowledge has moved into new settings, as when village songs are sold on cassettes and online, or a potter’s family makes goods for urban markets. Some has been abandoned by choice, as when Dalit families leave degrading work. And some has been revived and reinterpreted, as in the movements for local seed and millets or the Dalit use of the paṟai.

What village and Adivasi knowledge have in common is that both were long treated as raw material for others, whether for the state, the scholar or the market, and both are now being claimed by their holders. What separates them is that the first grew up inside the caste order and the second, for the most part, outside it or against it. Holding both in one volume makes it easier to see that “folk” is not a single thing, and that the question of who holds a knowledge, and on what terms, matters as much as what the knowledge is.

Key Points

  • Most rural knowledge in India is held by cultivators, herders, fishers and artisans of caste villages; caste distributes that knowledge by birth and fences it in.

  • Farmers’ knowledge has its own theory as well as practice, as Gupta’s account of “hot” and “cold” agronomy shows; herders’ and fishers’ knowledge is social and political as well as ecological.

  • Dalit communities have held important skills, from leatherwork and drumming to midwifery, that were devalued with the castes that held them; Dalit thinkers have argued for their recognition as knowledge.

  • Village goddesses, bards, genealogists and community epics keep the memory and the religious knowledge of caste communities.

  • Not every disappearing knowledge is a loss to its holders: some has been abandoned deliberately as a step towards dignity.

docs.text:

  • Gupta (1998): farmers’ knowledge and the Green Revolution in a north Indian village.

  • Agrawal (1999): the migrating camps of Raika shepherds.

  • Subramanian (2009): fishers, rights and the sea in south India.

  • Whitehead (1916): the village goddesses of south India.

  • Raheja and Gold (1994): women’s songs and stories in north India.

  • Ilaiah (1996) and Guru and Sarukkai (2012): Dalit arguments about knowledge and theory.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Tribal Governance: Councils, Customary Law and Self-Rule
11.1 Introduction: Governance as Knowledge
docs.text:
Adivasi communities have their own institutions for settling disputes, allocating land and forest, organising festivals and rituals, and dealing with outsiders. These institutions embody accumulated experience about how to live together in particular places. They are also political institutions, with their own hierarchies and exclusions, and they have been reshaped by colonial rule, by the Indian state and by the communities themselves.

Jaipal Singh’s claim in the Constituent Assembly that Adivasis had democracy to teach the rest of India (Chapter 1) rested on the village assembly, in which all adult men, and in some communities women too, could speak. This chapter describes such institutions, the constitutional and legal framework within which they now operate, and the debates about their strengths and limits.

The rules these institutions apply are usually called customary law: the norms and procedures by which a community regulates land and inheritance, marriage and divorce, disputes, offences and ritual duties. Customary law is usually unwritten, differs from community to community, and changes through practice and deliberation. Its sanctions include compensation, fines (often paid as a feast for the village), ritual purification and, in serious cases, boycott or expulsion. It is often called “restorative” rather than “punitive”; that is partly true, but boycott and expulsion can be severe, and customary law can also enforce inequalities, especially of gender.

docs.title: 11.2 Village and Regional Councils
docs.text: Adivasi governance typically has two levels: a village headman and council, and a federation of villages for matters that concern several villages or relations with outside powers.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Santal
docs.text: A Santal village is headed by the mãjhi (headman), assisted by the paranik (deputy), the jog mãjhi (who supervises the conduct of young people and ceremonies), the goḍet (messenger) and the nāeke (village priest). Villages are grouped under a parganā. Disputes are settled first in the village assembly in front of the headman’s house; serious matters go to the parganā. Historically the annual great hunt also served as the occasion for a council of the whole region (lo bīr), which dealt with the gravest offences (Archer 1974).

docs.title: 11.2.2 Munda, Ho and Oraon
docs.text: Among the Munda, each village has a secular headman (the muṇḍā) and a priest (the pāhan). Groups of villages form a paṛhā under a mānkī. Among the Ho of Kolhan (Singhbhum), the British formalised this muṇḍā–mānkī system as the basis of local administration under Wilkinson’s Rules in the 1830s, a rare case of a colonial government governing through an Adivasi institution. Among the Oraon the village has a pāhan and a mahto, and villages form paṛhā federations with their own flags and emblems (Roy 1912).

docs.title: 11.2.3 Gond
docs.text: Gond villages in central India usually have a headman and a priest, and in many areas they were integrated into the revenue systems of Gond and later Maratha and British rulers through offices such as the paṭel and the village watchman (koṭvār). In Bastar, villages were grouped into parganās under mājhīs, and important matters were discussed at regional gatherings and at the annual Dasara festival in Jagdalpur. Nandini Sundar’s history of Bastar shows how these institutions were reshaped by the princely state, colonial administration and independent India (Sundar 1997).

docs.title: 11.2.4 North-East India
docs.text: The communities of North-East India have a great variety of institutions. Among the Khasi, the village council (dorbar shnong) under a headman (rangbah shnong) manages village affairs, and groups of villages form himas (chiefdoms) under a syiem. Ao Naga villages were traditionally governed by the putu menden, a council of elders drawn from the clans, and Angami and other Naga villages had their own councils; the Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act of 1978 gave village councils statutory form. Among the Mizo, hereditary chiefs ruled villages until their rights were abolished in the 1950s.

docs.title: 11.2.5 Naga Village Government in the Ethnographic Record
docs.text:
The early ethnographies of the Naga hills, written by colonial administrators who were also careful observers, describe village governments of great variety. J. H. Hutton described Angami villages as largely self-governing communities divided into clan wards (khel), with little hereditary authority and decisions reached by discussion among the elders (Hutton 1921). J. P. Mills described the Ao village council, in which representatives of the clans served for a fixed period and then handed over to the next age group (Mills 1926). Among the Konyak, by contrast, powerful hereditary chiefs (aṅgh) ruled over groups of villages. These differences show that there is no single “tribal” form of government: Adivasi communities include both strongly egalitarian and strongly hierarchical polities. The colonial ethnographies remain valuable, and are read today by Nagas themselves, though they were written from the standpoint of the ruling power. They also describe the villages as they were in the 1910s and 1920s. Since then Naga village government has changed a great deal: the Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act of 1978 turned customary councils into statutory bodies with defined powers over village administration, land and the settlement of disputes; most Nagas became Christians, and village churches and church associations now share moral authority with the councils; and state programmes have been channelled through village councils and development boards. The descriptions above are therefore historical, and present practice varies from village to village. The institutions described in this section are summarised in Table 11.1.

Table 11.1. Some customary governance institutions Community Institution Structure Santal Mãjhi, parganā Village headman and officials; regional head Munda Muṇḍā, pāhan, paṛhā, mānkī Headman and priest; federation of villages Ho Muṇḍā–mānkī Formalised under Wilkinson’s Rules (1830s) Oraon Pāhan, mahto, paṛhā Priest and secular headman; federation Gond (Bastar) Headman, priest, mājhī Village and parganā (Sundar 1997) Khasi Dorbar shnong, hima Village council; chiefdom under a syiem Ao Naga Putu menden Council of clan elders

docs.title: 11.3 How Assemblies Work
docs.text:
Village assemblies typically meet in an open space, often under a tree or near the shrine of the village deity. Disputes are heard in public, witnesses speak, elders deliberate, and decisions are sought by consensus: discussion continues until no one is willing to hold out further. Decisions may be sealed by an oath, an offering or a shared meal. Public hearing makes the process transparent and allows the whole village to enforce the outcome.

The limits are equally important. In most communities, women do not sit in the assembly or speak there except as parties or witnesses; younger men defer to elders; and the families of the headman and of the founding lineages often have more say than later settlers. Consensus can mean that the powerful prevail and the weak are silenced. Many Adivasi women’s organisations have argued for women’s full participation in customary councils, and the reservation of seats for women in statutory panchayats (from 1993) has brought many Adivasi women into public office for the first time.

docs.title: 11.4 The Legal Framework of Self-Government
docs.text:
The Constitution and a series of later laws give Adivasi communities a framework of protection and self-government in several layers. Because these instruments recur throughout the volume, they are explained here once, together; other chapters refer back to this section. Figure 11.1 shows how they fit together, and Table 11.2 lists the main laws in order of date.

Figure 11.1. The main legal instruments for Adivasi land, forests and self-government and how they relate, as explained in Section 11.4. The list of Fifth Schedule states is as of 2026; the diagram is a schematic of legal relationships, not a map, and omits many other laws (Table 11.2).

docs.title: 11.4.1 The Fifth Schedule
docs.text:
The Fifth Schedule applies to Scheduled Areas in ten states: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan and Telangana. Its protective provisions were prepared in the Constituent Assembly by a sub-committee on the excluded and partially excluded areas outside Assam, chaired by A. V. Thakkar. Each such state has a Tribes Advisory Council, three-quarters of whose members are to be Scheduled Tribe members of the state legislature. The Governor may direct that an Act of Parliament or of the state legislature shall not apply, or shall apply with modifications, in a Scheduled Area, and may make regulations to prohibit or restrict the transfer of land by or among Scheduled Tribe members and to regulate money-lending. Governors have very rarely used these powers independently of state governments, and many Tribes Advisory Councils meet seldom. B. D. Sharma (1931–2015), who served as Commissioner for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the late 1980s, campaigned for decades for the Schedule to be used as intended (Section 12.4).

In Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997), the Supreme Court held that the lease of land in a Scheduled Area to private, non-tribal companies for mining violated the protective intent of the Fifth Schedule and the state’s land transfer regulation. The judgment was widely welcomed by Adivasi organisations, though its scope was later narrowed in practice.

docs.title: 11.4.2 The Sixth Schedule and the North-East
docs.text: The Sixth Schedule, which grew out of the recommendations of the Constituent Assembly sub-committee chaired by Gopinath Bordoloi (Section 1.8), applies to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. It provides for Autonomous District Councils, elected bodies with powers to make laws on land, forests, inheritance, marriage, village administration and social customs, and to run village courts under customary law. There are ten such councils: three in Assam (the Bodoland Territorial Council, created in 2003, and the councils of Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao), three in Meghalaya (the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills councils), one in Tripura, covering the tribal areas of the state, and three in Mizoram (the Chakma, Lai and Mara councils). Their record is mixed. They have protected land and customary institutions, but they have often been short of funds and capacity, and dominated by the largest community in their area, to the disadvantage of smaller groups. In addition, Articles 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram) provide that no Act of Parliament on Naga or Mizo religious or social practices, customary law and procedure, or the ownership and transfer of land shall apply unless the state legislature so decides. These provisions give customary institutions in the North-East far stronger protection than in central India.

docs.title: 11.4.3 PESA, 1996
docs.text:
The 73rd Amendment to the Constitution (1992) created a uniform three-tier system of elected panchayats, but excluded Scheduled Areas until Parliament extended it with suitable modifications. Following the report of a committee chaired by Dileep Singh Bhuria (1995), Parliament passed the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA). The Act requires state laws on panchayats in Scheduled Areas to be consistent with customary law, social and religious practices and the traditional management of community resources. Every gram sabha (village assembly) is declared competent to safeguard the traditions and customs of the people, their cultural identity, their community resources and their customary mode of dispute resolution. The gram sabha approves plans and programmes and identifies the beneficiaries of government schemes. It, or the panchayat at the appropriate level, must be consulted before land is acquired for development projects, and its recommendation is required for mining leases for minor minerals. Panchayats and gram sabhas are given ownership of minor forest produce and powers to prevent the alienation of land and restore land unlawfully alienated, to manage village markets, to control money-lending and to regulate the sale of intoxicants.

PESA has been called the most radical decentralising law in India, and one of the least implemented. Many states took years, some more than two decades, to frame rules; state laws often diluted the powers of the gram sabha; consultation before land acquisition was frequently a formality; and many gram sabhas did not know their powers. Where communities and supporting organisations have used PESA together with the Forest Rights Act, as in parts of Maharashtra and Odisha, the results have been significant (Section 14.5).

docs.title: 11.4.4 The Forest Rights Act, 2006
docs.text:
The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) is the most important recognition of Adivasi rights since independence. Its preamble acknowledges that the forest rights of these communities were not recognised when state forests were consolidated in the colonial period and after independence, resulting in “historical injustice”.

The immediate background was an eviction drive. In 2002, following a Supreme Court case on forest encroachments, the Ministry of Environment and Forests directed states to remove encroachers from forest land, and large numbers of Adivasi and other families who had cultivated forest land for generations, but held no title, were evicted. Adivasi and forest-dweller organisations came together in a national Campaign for Survival and Dignity and, with allies in Parliament and among scholars, pressed for a law that would recognise their rights. The bill was strongly opposed by parts of the forest service and by some wildlife conservationists, and its final form reflected compromises between these positions.

The Act recognises, among other rights, the right to hold and live on forest land under cultivation before 13 December 2005 (up to four hectares); ownership of minor forest produce and the right to collect, use and sell it; community rights such as grazing, fishing and the use of water bodies; rights to the habitat of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups; and rights to intellectual property and traditional knowledge related to forest biodiversity. Most important for self-government are the rights over community forest resources: the right to protect, regenerate, conserve and manage forests that the community has traditionally used. Scheduled Tribes qualify if they are resident in the forest area where they claim rights; “other traditional forest dwellers” must show residence over three generations (75 years). The process begins in the gram sabha, which receives and verifies claims; committees at the sub-division and district level then decide. Titles to land are to be issued jointly in the names of both spouses where the claimant is married. Relocation from areas declared critical wildlife habitat is allowed only with the free and informed consent of the gram sabha and with resettlement.

Implementation has been slow and uneven. Large numbers of individual claims have been rejected, often for lack of documents, without proper reasons or without a hearing; forest departments have sometimes obstructed claims; and community forest resource rights have been recognised far less often than they could have been. Where they have been recognised, as at Mendha-Lekha in Maharashtra and in parts of Odisha, gram sabhas have begun to manage and sell forest produce themselves (Section 14.5). The fragility of these rights was shown in 2019. In Wildlife First v. Ministry of Environment and Forests, a case brought by conservation groups challenging the constitutionality of the Act, the Supreme Court in February 2019 ordered state governments to evict forest dwellers whose claims had been rejected, an order that could have affected well over a million households. After protests and an application by the central government, the Court stayed its order later the same month and asked the states to review the rejections.

docs.title: 11.4.5 Rights and Conservation
docs.text:
The dispute between forest-rights campaigners and conservationists deserves a fair statement, since both sides argue from real concerns. Conservationists who opposed the bill, and those who later challenged the Act in court, made three main arguments. Titles to individual plots inside national parks and tiger reserves could fragment the remaining habitat of wide-ranging animals. The promise of title could encourage fresh clearing by people hoping to have it recognised, especially where the cut-off date was hard to verify. And weak verification could give land to claimants who were not eligible. They pointed out that the forests at issue are often the last refuges of species found nowhere else. Supporters of the Act replied that most claims concerned land long under cultivation; that many claims were rejected for want of papers rather than of eligibility; that the Act already provides a procedure for voluntary relocation from critical wildlife habitat; and that community forest rights give villagers a stake in protecting the forest against outside timber, mining and plantation interests.

The evidence does not yet settle the argument. Studies of the ecological effects of the Act are few, recent and mostly local. Cases such as Mendha-Lekha and the Soliga of the BRT hills (Section 2.4) show communities managing forests with care once rights were recognised, while the petitioners in the 2019 case argued that the claims process had led to fresh encroachment in many districts. Neither kind of example shows what happens on average, and the answer probably differs between individual titles, which can turn forest into farmland, and community forest rights, which are rights to manage and use rather than to clear. What can be said is that the conflict is not simply one of people against wildlife. Many forest dwellers have long lived alongside wild animals (Section 2.12), and many conservationists now accept that protected areas are hard to defend without the cooperation of those who live in and around them.

docs.title: 11.4.6 The Biological Diversity Act, 2002
docs.text: The Biological Diversity Act, India’s law under the Convention on Biological Diversity, applies throughout the country.
