docs.title: 13.1 Introduction: The Ethics of Recording
docs.text:
To record knowledge that might be lost seems an obvious good. But the history of documenting Adivasi knowledge is ambiguous. Records have preserved songs, stories, plant names and languages that would otherwise have disappeared; they have also been made without consent, kept far from the communities concerned, used to classify and control them, and used commercially without benefit to them. This chapter looks at that history, at participatory and community-controlled alternatives, and at the documentation of languages.

Principles of Ethical Documentation

  • Free, prior and informed consent of the community and of individual knowledge holders.

  • Community ownership and control of records, including decisions about access.

  • Respect for restricted knowledge: some knowledge is meant only for initiates, for one gender, or for particular occasions.

  • Benefit-sharing from any use of the records.

  • Do no harm: records should not expose communities to appropriation, ridicule or danger.

  • Support for living practice: documentation should complement, not replace, the continued practice of knowledge.

docs.title: 13.2 Colonial and Early Ethnography
docs.text:
The first large records of Adivasi life were made by colonial officials, missionaries and scholars: census reports and district gazetteers; compendia such as H. H. Risley’s The Tribes and Castes of Bengal (1891) and Edgar Thurston’s Castes and Tribes of Southern India (1909) (Risley 1891; Thurston and Rangachari 1909); and monographs by missionaries such as Stephen Hislop and P. O. Bodding and by scholars such as Sarat Chandra Roy (Hislop 1866; Bodding 1925; Roy 1912, 1915). These works preserve much that would otherwise be lost, and they are still used, including by Adivasi scholars and activists.

They were also shaped by colonial purposes and assumptions. Risley used anthropometry to rank castes and tribes by race; the census assigned communities to fixed categories that hardened identities; ethnographers collected data and departed, without obligation to the people they studied. The categories of “tribe”, “animist” and “criminal tribe” were partly products of this knowledge-making.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Old Ethnographies, New Uses
docs.text: Colonial ethnographies have had unexpected afterlives. Naga, Khasi and Ao readers consult Hutton, Mills and Gurdon for information about their own clans, customs and history (Hutton 1921; Mills 1926; Gurdon 1907); Munda and Oraon litigants have cited Roy’s descriptions of customary tenure in land disputes (Roy 1912); and revival movements draw on recorded myths and songs to recover forgotten rituals. Such uses show that the records belong, in a sense, to the communities they describe. They also show the danger of treating an outsider’s snapshot of one moment as the definitive statement of a community’s “true” custom.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Verrier Elwin
docs.text: Verrier Elwin (Chapter 1) produced the largest body of writing on the Adivasis of central and north-eastern India: monographs on the Baiga, Muria and Saora, collections of myths, songs and folktales, and studies of tribal art (Elwin 1939, 1947, 1949, 1951, 1955). He worked closely with Indian collaborators, above all Shamrao Hivale, and with Adivasi informants and assistants whose role was not always acknowledged. His work is sympathetic and vivid, but also reflects his own preoccupations; Ramachandra Guha’s biography assesses it critically (Guha 1999). Elwin’s autobiography, The Tribal World of Verrier Elwin (1964), gives his own account (Elwin 1964).

docs.title: 13.2.3 Photographs
docs.text: Photography was part of documentation from the start. Colonial photographers produced “type” portraits of tribal people for ethnological albums, often posed and sometimes partly undressed, which reinforced the image of Adivasis as exotic and primitive. Later photographers such as Sunil Janah, who travelled with Elwin in the 1940s, made more sympathetic portraits, but the images still circulated far from the people photographed. Such photographs are now valuable historical records, and some communities have used them to recover knowledge of past dress, ornament and architecture; but their use raises questions of consent and dignity that apply equally to photography today.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Anthropology after Independence
docs.text: The Anthropological Survey of India (founded 1945) and university departments of anthropology produced many studies after independence. The Survey’s People of India project, directed by K. S. Singh between 1985 and 1992, compiled brief profiles of several thousand communities, including all the Scheduled Tribes (Singh 1994). The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya (National Museum of Mankind) in Bhopal has built large collections of Adivasi art and architecture and invited Adivasi artists and builders to create works on its grounds. Increasingly, Adivasi scholars such as Virginius Xaxa and Ram Dayal Munda have written about their own communities and challenged the assumptions of earlier ethnography (Xaxa 1999).

docs.title: 13.3 Participatory Documentation
docs.text: Participatory approaches treat communities as partners rather than sources of data. Community members are trained as researchers and work in their own language; records are made in that language first, with translations clearly marked, and audio and video capture performance and practice as well as words. The community reviews the records before they are finished and decides what is too sensitive to record at all. The most successful projects tie documentation to support for living practice, such as apprenticeships, seed exchanges and performances, so that the record does not become a substitute for the thing recorded.

docs.title: 13.4 People’s Biodiversity Registers
docs.text:
People’s Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) record the biological resources of a village or local body, their uses, and the knowledge associated with them. The methodology was developed in the 1990s by Madhav Gadgil and colleagues, who saw the registers both as a record of knowledge and as a tool for local communities to manage their resources and claim a share in benefits from their use (Gadgil et al. 2000). The Biological Diversity Act, 2002, and its rules require every local body to constitute a Biodiversity Management Committee and prepare a PBR.

In practice many registers were prepared hastily, often by consultants or officials rather than by communities, especially after the National Green Tribunal set deadlines for their completion. Their quality varies greatly. They also raise questions of ownership and access: a register that lists a community’s knowledge of medicinal plants may, if publicly accessible, make that knowledge easier to appropriate.

docs.title: 13.5 The Honey Bee Network
docs.text: The Honey Bee Network, started around 1988–89 by Anil K. Gupta at the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad, set out to find, document and support grassroots innovations and traditional knowledge held by farmers, artisans and other people with little formal education. Its name reflects its principle: like a honey bee, it should take from the flowers without harming them and help them to pollinate. The network publishes newsletters in several Indian languages so that knowledge circulates among practitioners, insists that every entry be credited to the person who provided it, and supports innovators in seeking protection and investment. It led to the creation of the Society for Research and Initiatives for Sustainable Technologies and Institutions (SRISTI) and, in 2000, of the government-supported National Innovation Foundation. The network has compiled a very large database of innovations and practices.

docs.title: 13.6 Archives and Digital Records
docs.text:
Digital media make it possible to record performance, speech and practice in sound and image, to store large collections, and to return copies to communities. Important collections relating to Adivasi and folk traditions are held by the Archives and Research Centre for Ethnomusicology (ARCE) of the American Institute of Indian Studies in Gurugram, the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the Central Institute of Indian Languages, and international language archives. Online platforms such as Sahapedia publish essays and recordings on folk traditions.

Digital archives also raise problems. Many Adivasi villages lack reliable internet access, so communities may be the last to see their own records, while records held on distant servers can be used by anyone, including for commercial purposes. A recording of a song without its setting, meaning and rules of performance keeps only part of the knowledge. And the principle of open access can conflict with a community’s rules about who may hear or see certain things.

Community archives, in which a community or its organisation holds and manages its own records, are one response. Another is to attach community-defined access conditions to records held in institutional archives. Adivasi communities have also used new media to speak for themselves: community radio stations in Adivasi languages; CGNet Swara, a mobile-phone service started in 2010 in central India on which people can record and listen to news reports in Gondi and Hindi; and video and social media made by young Adivasi journalists, film-makers and musicians. These are not archives in the usual sense, but they are part of how knowledge is now shared.

At Tejgadh in eastern Gujarat, the Bhasha Research and Publication Centre founded by G. N. Devy established in 1999 an Adivasi Academy, which runs courses, a museum and a library, and publishes literature in Adivasi languages. State Tribal Research Institutes, set up in most states with large Adivasi populations, hold reports, photographs and recordings, though their records are often difficult to access.

docs.title: 13.7 Museums and Return
docs.text:
Museums in India and abroad hold large collections of Adivasi objects (weapons, ornaments, textiles, ritual objects, musical instruments) and, in some cases, human remains, collected by colonial officers, missionaries and anthropologists, often without the consent of the communities. Communities and scholars increasingly ask for these collections to be shared, interpreted with the communities, and in some cases returned. In Nagaland, a collaborative initiative begun in 2020 has worked with Naga communities on the return of Naga ancestral remains held in a British university museum, with attention to how communities wish such remains to be received.

In India, museums such as the Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya in Bhopal, the state tribal museums and community museums run by Adivasi organisations have experimented with exhibitions designed and built by members of the communities represented. Such approaches change the museum from a place where communities are displayed into a place where they represent themselves.

docs.title: 13.8 Contact, Protection and the Gaze
docs.text:
The ethics of documentation are sharpest for the small communities of the Andaman Islands. The Jarawa had little peaceful contact with outsiders until the late 1990s. The Andaman Trunk Road, built through their reserve from the 1970s, brought settlers, poachers and tourists, some of whom treated the journey as a “human safari”. After a video of Jarawa women being made to dance for tourists was published in 2012, there was national outrage, and the authorities restricted tourist traffic and photography along the road. Disease, alcohol and exploitation brought by contact pose grave risks to such communities.

The Sentinelese of North Sentinel Island have consistently rejected contact. Indian policy since the 1990s has been to protect them by leaving them alone, enforcing an exclusion zone around the island. In 2018 an American missionary who landed on the island illegally was killed by the islanders, an event that drew renewed attention to the policy of non-contact. For such communities, the most ethical form of “documentation” may be none at all: respect for their choice to remain apart.

docs.title: 13.9 Genetic and Biomedical Research
docs.text: Adivasi communities have been studied not only by ethnographers but also by geneticists and medical researchers, for whom small, relatively isolated populations are of particular interest. Blood and DNA samples from Andaman Islanders, Munda-speaking peoples and others have contributed to major studies of human population history (Narasimhan et al. 2019). Such research can benefit communities, for example by identifying inherited conditions such as sickle cell disease and guiding health services. But it also raises questions of consent (were participants told what their samples would be used for?), of the storage and reuse of samples, of how findings about a community’s “origins” are reported and used in politics, and of benefit. Elsewhere in the world, indigenous communities have objected strongly to the use of their samples for purposes they had not agreed to. Ethical guidelines for research in India, issued by the Indian Council of Medical Research, treat tribal communities as needing special protection and call for community as well as individual consent.

docs.title: 13.10 Languages
docs.text:
Adivasi knowledge is held in Adivasi languages; their linguistic history and scripts are also discussed in Volume 10, Śabda Vidyā. The 2011 Census recorded 121 languages with ten thousand or more speakers (22 scheduled and 99 non-scheduled), grouping thousands of reported mother tongues under them (Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India 2013). Many Adivasi languages are counted as “mother tongues” under larger languages, which conceals their distinctness. The People’s Linguistic Survey of India, a volunteer project led by G. N. Devy from 2010, recorded some 780 languages and warned that many were in danger.

The first systematic survey of the languages of India, the Linguistic Survey of India directed by George Abraham Grierson and published between 1903 and 1928, recorded specimens, grammatical sketches and vocabularies of hundreds of languages and dialects, including many Adivasi languages for which it remains an important early record. Its classifications, made largely through correspondence with officials and missionaries, were sometimes wrong, and many smaller languages were missed or merged with their neighbours. The People’s Linguistic Survey was conceived partly as a response, in which speakers themselves described their languages.

UNESCO’s atlas of endangered languages (2009) listed nearly two hundred languages of India as vulnerable or endangered, more than for any other country, most of them Adivasi languages; its assessments, based on limited data, have been debated, but the trend they describe is not in doubt.

Only a few Adivasi languages have official recognition: Santali and Bodo were added to the Eighth Schedule in 2003, and several states recognise tribal languages for education and administration (Sikkim, for example, recognises Lepcha and Limbu among its official languages, and Jharkhand recognises Santali, Mundari, Ho, Kharia, Kurukh and other languages as second official languages). Most Adivasi children are still taught in a language that is not their mother tongue, which contributes to high drop-out rates and to the loss of the language within a few generations.

docs.title: 13.10.1 Speakers and Status
docs.text:
Census figures show both the size of the largest Adivasi languages and the extent of language shift (Table 13.1). Bhili/Bhilodi, with about ten million speakers in 2011, was the largest language of India outside the Eighth Schedule, larger than several scheduled languages; Santali had more than seven million. Yet the number of Gondi speakers, about three million, is far smaller than the number of people who identify as Gond, many of whom now speak Hindi, Marathi or Telugu as their first language. The figures also conceal internal variety: “Bhili/Bhilodi” and “Gondi” are each umbrella labels under which the census groups many mother tongues that their speakers name separately.

Demands for inclusion in the Eighth Schedule have been made for many of these languages, among them Bhili, Gondi, Ho, Mundari, Kurukh, Khasi, Garo and Kokborok. Inclusion brings recognition by the Sahitya Akademi, use in national examinations and a stronger claim on state support; it also, as the Santali case shows, raises the question of which script and which variety will be standard (Chapter 8, Section 8.14).

docs.title: 13.10.2 Standardisation
docs.text: Writing a language down raises the question of which dialect becomes the standard. Gondi, for example, is spoken in many varieties across several states, some of them barely mutually intelligible, and speakers have been schooled in Hindi, Marathi, Telugu or Odia. Efforts by Gond organisations and linguists to compile a common Gondi vocabulary and standard have had to balance unity with respect for local speech. In the most sustained of these, a series of meetings held over about four years and organised by the citizen-journalism network CGNet Swara, with the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, brought together Gondi speakers from six states to agree on common words: for each word the variants of the different regions were compared and one was chosen by vote. The resulting standard vocabulary of some three thousand words, printed in Devanagari, was released in 2018; its compilers regarded it as a first step towards a full dictionary. Whether such a standard will be taken up in schools depends on state governments, since Gondi has little official status in any state. Similar debates surround the choice of script (Chapter 8). Standardisation can strengthen a language by giving it a written norm for schools and media; it can also marginalise the speech of smaller groups within the community.

docs.title: 13.10.3 Documentation and Revival
docs.text: Language documentation projects record grammar, vocabulary and texts, often with community members as researchers. The Central Institute of Indian Languages in Mysuru (founded 1969) has worked on tribal languages and on mother-tongue-based education. Adivasi communities themselves have developed scripts (Ol Chiki for Santali, Warang Citi for Ho, Tolong Siki for Kurukh), published textbooks and literature, and set up schools teaching in their languages. Language revival is most successful when the language is used in schools, media and public life, not only recorded.

docs.title: 13.10.4 Radio, Telephone and the Internet
docs.text:
Since the 1990s the means of recording and circulating Adivasi speech have passed increasingly into Adivasi hands. Regional stations of All India Radio have long broadcast programmes and news in some Adivasi languages, but the decisions about content were made elsewhere. Community radio, licensed in India from the mid-2000s, has allowed some stations in Adivasi regions to broadcast in local languages under local management. In central India CGNet Swara, begun in 2010 by the journalist Shubhranshu Choudhary, adapted the idea of citizen journalism to places with mobile phones but little internet: callers record reports and songs by telephone in Gondi, Hindi and other languages, which are checked by moderators and made available to other callers and online. Its reports have drawn attention to unpaid wages, failures of the ration system and police abuses, and it has also served as an archive of songs and stories in Gondi.

The encoding of Adivasi scripts in Unicode (Table 8.1) has made it possible to type them on phones and computers, and Santali has had its own edition of Wikipedia, in the Ol Chiki script, since 2018. Video-sharing platforms carry a large and largely unstudied production of songs, dance and short films in Santali, Kurukh, Mundari, Ho, Gondi and the languages of the North-East, made by Adivasi musicians and studios for Adivasi audiences in India and among migrants. Documentary film-makers such as the Oraon director Biju Toppo, working with the Ranchi collective Akhra, have recorded movements against displacement from within. These media do not by themselves protect a language or a body of knowledge; but they reverse, at least in part, the history described at the beginning of this chapter, in which recording was something done to Adivasi communities by others.

Key Points

  • Documentation has preserved knowledge but has also been extractive; consent, community control and benefit are essential.

  • People’s Biodiversity Registers, the Honey Bee Network and digital archives are important but imperfect tools.

  • For communities such as the Sentinelese, respect for their choice of isolation outweighs any wish to document.

  • Language is the foundation of knowledge; mother-tongue education and community scripts are key to its survival.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Indigenous Knowledge in Policy and Education
14.1 Introduction: Beyond the Dichotomy
docs.text:
This volume has described the ecological, medical, literary, artistic, political, hydrological, culinary and calendrical knowledge of Adivasi and folk communities. This final chapter asks how such knowledge can be given its due place in the policies and institutions of a modern state, in ways that serve the communities who hold it.

Integration carries risks. It can become appropriation: the selective use of indigenous knowledge without recognition or benefit to its holders. It can become distortion: the extraction of “useful” elements from living systems while ignoring their context. And it can become patronage: the display of indigenous knowledge as heritage while its holders remain poor and powerless. The approach favoured here is sometimes called epistemic pluralism.

Epistemic Pluralism

Epistemic pluralism holds that different knowledge systems can each be valid in their own domains, and that the most productive relation between them is dialogue rather than hierarchy. It rejects both the view that one system (usually modern science) is the only legitimate source of knowledge on every question, and the view that all claims are equally valid and cannot be compared. Where claims overlap, for example on whether a remedy works or a water structure recharges groundwater, they can and should be tested; where they concern meaning, value or identity, communities speak for themselves (Agrawal 1995; Sillitoe 1998).

docs.title: 14.2 Adivasi Knowledge and “Indian Knowledge Systems”
docs.text:
This volume belongs to a series on Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā, the knowledge traditions of India, a subject that has received new official attention since the National Education Policy of 2020. That framework raises a question that Adivasi scholars have put sharply: is Adivasi knowledge to be treated as part of a single Indian tradition whose centre is Sanskrit learning, or as a set of traditions in their own right?

The evidence of this volume points to the second answer. Adivasi knowledge has interacted with Sanskritic, Islamic, Christian and modern scientific knowledge for centuries, but it was developed by peoples with their own languages, religions, histories and institutions, and it should not be described as a folk or “lost” form of the Vedic or classical traditions. Presenting it in Sanskrit categories, however respectfully, risks repeating the absorptive framing that Adivasi movements have rejected. A plural understanding of Indian knowledge, in which Adivasi, Dalit, Islamic, Christian, regional and classical traditions each have their own place, is both more accurate and more just.

docs.title: 14.3.1 Mother Tongue and Curriculum
docs.text:
For most Adivasi children, school begins in a language they do not speak at home. Educationists have long argued that early schooling in the mother tongue, with a gradual transition to the regional language and English, improves learning and helps languages survive. Odisha has run a multilingual education programme in several tribal languages since the mid-2000s, and other states have produced primers in Santali, Gondi, Kurukh, Mundari, Ho and other languages.

The National Education Policy 2020 recommends that, wherever possible, the medium of instruction until at least Grade 5 should be the home language or mother tongue, and it calls for the inclusion of Indian knowledge systems, including tribal knowledge and indigenous and traditional ways of learning, in the curriculum. These are welcome commitments. Their realisation depends on teachers who speak the children’s languages, materials written with communities, and a curriculum that treats Adivasi knowledge as knowledge rather than as folklore.

docs.title: 14.3.2 Residential Schooling
docs.text: Much Adivasi education takes place in residential schools and hostels: government āśram schools, Ekalavya Model Residential Schools (from the late 1990s), mission schools and large private institutions. They have brought education to remote areas, but they also separate children from their families, languages and the practical learning of village life. The experience of residential schooling in other countries, where it contributed to the loss of indigenous languages and to serious abuse, is a warning. Many Adivasi educators argue for schools rooted in the community, with local teachers and calendars that fit the agricultural year.

docs.title: 14.3.3 Universities
docs.text: The Indira Gandhi National Tribal University at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh was established by Act of Parliament in 2007, with a mandate to promote higher education and research on tribal art, culture, traditions, languages and knowledge. Central tribal universities have since been established in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, and universities such as North-Eastern Hill University in Shillong and Rajiv Gandhi University in Arunachal Pradesh have long had programmes on the cultures of the North-East. Ranchi University’s department of tribal and regional languages, built up by Ram Dayal Munda and others from the 1980s, was a pioneer in teaching Adivasi languages at university level.

docs.title: 14.4 Biodiversity Law and Traditional Knowledge
docs.text: International and Indian law on biodiversity and traditional knowledge, the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Nagoya Protocol and the Biological Diversity Act, is explained in Sections 11.4 and 12.10. For the purposes of this chapter the main point is that benefit-sharing payments under these laws have so far been small and have rarely reached the communities whose knowledge was used.

docs.title: 14.5 Forest Self-Government: Mendha-Lekha
docs.text:
The village of Mendha-Lekha in Gadchiroli district of Maharashtra, a Gond village, has become a symbol of Adivasi forest self-government. From the 1980s, under the slogan māvā nāṭe māvā rāj (“our village, our rule”), its gram sabha took decisions by consensus, refused permission for outsiders to cut its forest, protected the forest itself, and set up study circles to discuss issues ranging from forest management to the rights of women. Its leaders, among them Devaji Tofa, worked with supporters from outside the village, while insisting that decisions be made by the village.

In 2009 Mendha-Lekha was among the first villages in India to have its community forest rights recognised under the Forest Rights Act. In 2011 it became the first gram sabha to obtain a transit pass to harvest and sell bamboo from its own forest, a right long monopolised by the forest department and paper mills, and it used the income for village development and forest protection. The village later placed its land under collective ownership. Following its example, many other gram sabhas in Gadchiroli and elsewhere in Maharashtra and Odisha have claimed community forest rights and begun to manage and market forest produce, with varying success.

The experience of Mendha-Lekha shows what PESA and the FRA can mean in practice when a community is organised and has time and support. It also shows that self-government is hard work, depends on leadership and unity, and can be undermined by conflicts within and outside the village.

docs.title: 14.6 Forest Produce and Livelihoods
docs.text: For many Adivasi households, forest produce is the main source of cash, and the terms on which it is sold determine whether forest knowledge brings any benefit. Historically, collectors sold to traders and state agencies at low prices and were often paid in kind or in advance against debt. Several policies have tried to change this. In 2013 the central government introduced minimum support prices for a list of minor forest produce, under which state agencies are to buy produce if market prices fall below the support price; and from 2018 the Van Dhan programme has supported groups of forest-produce gatherers, many of them women, to process and market produce. Where gram sabhas hold community forest rights, as at Mendha-Lekha, they can sell produce such as bamboo and tendu leaves directly. The Forest Rights Act also requires that titles to land be issued jointly in the names of both spouses where the claimant is married, a provision that, where implemented, gives Adivasi women a recorded right in land for the first time. These measures have been unevenly implemented, but they point to the principle that the people who hold forest knowledge should share in its value.

docs.title: 14.7 Tourism
docs.text: Tourism is increasingly promoted in Adivasi regions as a source of income: homestays in Nagaland, Meghalaya and Arunachal Pradesh, festivals such as the Hornbill Festival, visits to living root bridges and sacred forests, and craft villages. Community-run tourism, in which villages decide how many visitors to receive, set the rules and keep the income, can bring benefits and pride in local knowledge. Tourism controlled by outside operators has often done the opposite, treating communities as spectacles, as in the “human safaris” to the Jarawa reserve (Chapter 13), damaging sacred sites, and taking most of the profit. The difference lies, again, in who controls the decisions.

docs.title: 14.8 Recognition of Knowledge Holders
docs.text: Recognition matters. In recent years national honours have been given to several holders of community knowledge: the Kani healer Lakshmikutty (Padma Shri, 2018) and Tulsi Gowda of the Halakki Vokkaliga community of Karnataka, known as an “encyclopedia of the forest” for her knowledge of tree species and her work in raising seedlings over decades (Padma Shri, 2020), among others. Artists such as Jivya Soma Mashe, Bhuri Bai and Mithila painters have received the same honours (Chapter 9). Such recognition raises the status of knowledge that was once dismissed. It is most meaningful when accompanied by support for the communities and practices from which the knowledge comes.

docs.title: 14.9 Health Care
docs.text:
India’s Ministry of AYUSH (Āyurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Homoeopathy) supports the classical systems of traditional medicine. Folk and tribal healers have little place in this framework. Several states and non-governmental organisations have documented local health traditions, promoted the cultivation of medicinal plants by communities, and trained village healers to recognise conditions that need referral. Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), village women appointed under the National Rural Health Mission from 2005, have become a bridge between communities and health facilities in many Adivasi areas.

The aim, from the point of view of public health, is not to make folk healers into substitutes for doctors, but to make good health care available to Adivasi communities, to respect patients’ own understanding of illness, and to evaluate traditional remedies honestly (Chapter 7). Adivasi communities have some of the worst health indicators in India, including high rates of malaria, tuberculosis, malnutrition and maternal and child mortality, and sickle cell disease is common in many central Indian communities (Government of India 2014). Respect for traditional knowledge is no substitute for the public health services to which they are entitled.

docs.title: 14.10 Lessons from Elsewhere
docs.text:
Other countries offer both warnings and examples.

  • Canada: from the late nineteenth century until the 1990s, indigenous children were sent to residential schools designed to remove them from their languages and cultures. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which reported in 2015, documented the abuse and loss that resulted, and called for the restoration of indigenous languages and knowledge in education.

  • New Zealand: from 1982 Māori communities established kōhanga reo (“language nests”), pre-schools in which young children are immersed in the Māori language by elders. The movement, followed by Māori-medium schools, helped to reverse the decline of the language and has been imitated around the world.

  • Norway, Sweden and Finland: the Sámi have elected parliaments with advisory and some administrative powers over language, culture and reindeer herding.

  • Latin America: the constitutions of Bolivia and Ecuador recognise indigenous peoples’ self-government and, in Ecuador’s constitution of 2008, rights of nature itself, partly inspired by indigenous ideas of the earth.

These examples differ greatly from Indian conditions, and none is without problems. But they show that indigenous languages can be revived, that self-government can be given institutional form, and that the damage done by assimilationist schooling can be long-lasting.

docs.title: 14.11 Research Partnerships
docs.text: Much of the knowledge in this volume reached print through research by outsiders. The principles that ought to govern future research with Adivasi communities are now widely agreed, even if often ignored. Research should begin only with the free, prior and informed consent of the community, given through its own institutions, as well as of the individuals concerned. Communities should help decide what is studied, so that research answers their questions as well as the researcher’s. Those who contribute knowledge or labour should be credited by name, as authors where appropriate, rather than reduced to anonymous “informants”. Findings should go back to the community in its own language and in a usable form; any commercial use should be governed by agreements that benefit the community, as the Biological Diversity Act requires; and a community may decline to take part or restrict what is published (Section 13.1). Adivasi universities, research institutes and organisations, and Adivasi scholars in mainstream institutions, are increasingly setting these terms themselves.

docs.title: 14.12 A Dialogue of Knowledges
docs.text:
The aim of the approaches discussed here is not to preserve Adivasi knowledge in museums, databases or policy documents, but to make it possible for communities to continue, develop and apply their knowledge, on their own land and in their own languages, in dialogue with other knowledge systems. Such a dialogue treats indigenous knowledge as knowledge, not as raw material to be validated and appropriated by others. It tests claims where they can be tested, and it expects scientists and officials to learn from communities as well as to teach them. Above all it depends on material conditions, secure rights to land and forest, self-government, livelihoods, health and education, without which knowledge cannot be practised.

Modern Relevance: Indigenous Knowledge and Sustainability

International bodies such as the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change now recognise the knowledge of indigenous peoples and local communities as relevant to biodiversity conservation and climate adaptation (Nakashima et al. 2012). Much of the world’s remaining biodiversity lies in lands managed by indigenous peoples. In India, as elsewhere, conservation that excludes or displaces forest communities has often been both unjust and ineffective.

docs.title: 14.12.1 The Long View
docs.text: The knowledge described in this volume was built up by many generations of observation, experiment, argument and teaching, and it continues to change. What it calls for is respect, rather than nostalgia or the absorption of Adivasi traditions into someone else’s story: expressed in political action that secures the rights of the communities who hold this knowledge, in education that takes it seriously, and in scholarship that listens to what Adivasi people say about themselves.

docs.title: 14.13 Proposals and Their Difficulties
docs.text:
Earlier chapters have described many proposals made by Adivasi organisations, scholars and official bodies such as the High Level Committee of 2014 (Government of India 2014). They are gathered here, with the objections they meet, so that the reader can weigh them rather than take them as settled.

On land and self-government, the proposals are to implement PESA in every Fifth Schedule state without diluting the powers of the gram sabha; to use the Governor’s powers under the Fifth Schedule to protect land; to implement the Forest Rights Act fully, above all its community forest rights; to require the free, prior and informed consent of the gram sabha for projects on Adivasi land, as in the Niyamgiri decision; and to resettle fairly those already displaced. The objections are of two kinds. State governments and industry argue that a village veto over mines, dams and roads would let a few hundred people block projects that serve millions. Some conservationists argue that individual forest titles can fragment wildlife habitat (Section 11.4.4). The second objection is partly empirical and can be tested; the first is a question of how the costs of development are to be shared, which law alone cannot settle.

On customary institutions, the proposal is to recognise village councils and customary law while guaranteeing the rights of women and dissenters within them, and to enforce the laws against witch-hunting. The difficulty is that the two halves pull against each other: strengthening customary authority can strengthen the exclusion of women from land and councils (Section 11.7), and Adivasi women’s organisations have been among the sharpest critics of uncritical praise of custom.

On knowledge and its use, the proposals are to protect oral traditional knowledge in law, with community control and benefit-sharing; to support documentation and archives controlled by communities, and to return copies of old records to them; to record sacred groves and community lands correctly in land records; and to test widely used remedies and weather signs with their holders as partners. Here the difficulty is practical. Knowledge that is shared across many villages, or across the line between tribe and caste, has no single owner with whom benefits can be shared, and the registers meant to protect knowledge can make it easier to copy (Section 13.4).

On education, health and food, the proposals are mother-tongue education in the early years with curricula prepared with communities; health, nutrition and education services of the quality other citizens receive; the inclusion of millets and gathered foods in public nutrition programmes; and a census code for Sarna and other indigenous religions for those who wish to use it. These meet fewer principled objections, but they cost money and require teachers, health workers and officials who speak Adivasi languages, which most states have been slow to provide.

None of these proposals is new, and most have been made by Adivasi organisations themselves for decades. Whether they are adopted is a political question. What this volume can contribute is an account of the knowledge at stake, and of the evidence for and against the claims made on its behalf.

Key Points

  • Integration of indigenous knowledge risks appropriation, distortion and patronage; dialogue among knowledge systems is the goal.

  • Mother-tongue education and curricula prepared with communities can give Adivasi knowledge its place in schools.

  • Mendha-Lekha shows what PESA and the FRA can achieve when a community is organised.

  • Secure rights, fair markets and good public services are the material conditions for the survival of Adivasi knowledge.
